draw from the same 72 mnemonics.** The other 77 were covered only statically -- assembled, and
checked that no VEX prefix survives, which says nothing about what the result computes.

**The gap was structural.** `build()` writes every case as `%xmmA,%xmmB,%xmm0`, and
`vmovaps %xmm1,%xmm0` has no middle operand, so the largest mnemonics in the binary could not
be expressed. Nothing pointed at it because the figure everyone quotes -- "233 cases from 49
mnemonics" -- counts `len(CASES)`, the case SPECS, and calls them mnemonics. The real count
was 72.

Five two-operand moves in three shapes each closes **185,000 patches, a third of the total**,
from fifteen cases, and both oracles pick them up automatically.

**`vcomiss` and its family are deliberately absent.** 30,760 patches that write FLAGS, and this
harness observes sixteen xmm registers -- a case for one would compare the wrong thing and
pass. That is the vacuous pass this file is full of, and writing it knowingly would be worse
than the gap. It wants a different observation and is recorded rather than bodged.

#### The first version of the cases could not fail, and only the sabotage said so

The reference for a whole-register move is `return b`. Sabotaged to `return a`, the suite
passed 1,984 lowerings.

The cases passed `source` as BOTH `src1` and `src2`, so the harness loaded one register twice:
`a` and `b` held the same bytes, `return a` and `return b` were the same answer, and the
reference could not be wrong. **A case whose operands cannot disagree cannot test which one the
lowering keeps.** With `src1` set to the destination's prior contents the sabotage fails on
every pattern.

That is the third control this session that could not fail, after two sabotages that never
applied. **The discipline is not that the mistake gets avoided -- it is that sabotaging every
new check catches it before it ships**, and all three were caught inside the hour they were
written.


### Finding 210 -- the flags, which 31,479 patches write and nothing observed

Classifying the still-uncovered mnemonics by WHAT THEY WRITE, because that decides whether the
harness can reach them at all:

```
71,074 patches in 81 uncovered mnemonic(s)
  31,479  writes FLAGS only         5 mnemonics   vcomiss 23,168, vucomiss 6,450
  19,253  writes nothing            1             vzeroupper
  12,794  writes an xmm register   54
   5,937  writes a general register 10
   1,611  writes memory            11
```

**A case for a flag mnemonic in `lowering_test` would have passed while comparing bytes neither
side touched.** That harness loads sixteen xmm registers and compares sixteen xmm registers
against a reference returning `__m128i`; `vcomiss` writes none of them. The gap was not a
missing case but a missing OBSERVATION, and adding the case without the observation would have
turned a known gap into a green tick.

`vex_oracle` captures the flags now -- masked to the six arithmetic bits, since the ambient
ones differ between qemu and silicon and are nobody's result, and preceded by a deterministic
`xor` so an instruction that writes no flags leaves the same value on both sides. The five
mnemonics live in `build_flags()`, which `lowering_test` does not consume and which shares
`finish()` with `build()` so both go through one assembling path rather than two.

**Sabotaged, every flag lowering comparing the wrong register: 58 unexplained differences, all
in those mnemonics.** The channel is live.

#### Building it in three steps is what found the defect

The observation went in ALONE first, and the existing 248 cases failed. One `span` was serving
as the output size, the printed length AND the input stride, so growing it for the flags slot
moved the input pointer 272 bytes per pattern instead of 256 and every case after the first
read misaligned bytes. **Isolated, that is one variable.** Added together with new cases it
would have been new and old failures at once, with nothing to say which was which.

`span` was not a bug while input and output were the same size. It became one when they
diverged, and nothing in the code said the two were equal by definition rather than by
coincidence.

#### And the hazard named in the design was one this instrument cannot see

The justification written for this work said a prefix strip landing on `ucomiss` instead of
`comiss` would be caught here. **It would not.** That pair differs only in whether a QNaN
raises the invalid-operation flag in MXCSR; their EFLAGS results are identical, and this
harness compares EFLAGS.

What it catches is any lowering whose FLAGS differ -- a wrong register, a wrong operand order,
a wrong instruction -- which is real and covers 31,479 patches. It is not the NaN-signalling
case. **A probe checked against the mechanism its author had in mind rather than against the
failure it must catch** is this file's own recurring finding, and it was written here into the
justification rather than the code. MXCSR is a different slot and a separate piece of work.


### Finding 211 -- MXCSR, and the five sabotages it took to prove one channel works

Finding 210 closed the flag mnemonics against EFLAGS and recorded that the `comiss`/`ucomiss`
distinction was still invisible: that pair sets identical EFLAGS and differs only in whether a
QNaN raises the invalid-operation flag in MXCSR. This adds that observation.

The exception flags are STICKY, so each case resets MXCSR to `0x1f80` first; without it a case
would inherit whatever the previous one raised and the verdict would depend on case ordering --
reproducible, wrong, and stable enough to look deliberate.

#### The comparison had to be split, and the measurement forced it

With MXCSR observed, 22 existing cases differed -- all on the `edges` pattern, all in
`dst_is_src1` and `dst_is_src2`, never `distinct`. The bytes said why:

```
vex (under qemu)   0x20   = PE
low (native)       0x22   = PE | DE
```

**qemu does not model the denormal flag.** The `edges` pattern puts a denormal in `%xmm0`, and
only the aliased shapes read `%xmm0` -- `distinct` reads `%xmm1` and `%xmm2`, whose values are
XOR-shifted and not denormal. So the aliasing was a coincidence of which registers each shape
happens to read, not a property of aliased lowerings.

Masking DE out would have been an exemption wider than its reason, excusing the class the
channel exists to catch. Instead the lowered side is run under qemu as well, and the STATUS
slot is compared against that while the REGISTERS are still compared against the native run:

```
registers   qemu-VEX  vs  native-SSE    the lowering must be right on real silicon
status      qemu-VEX  vs  qemu-SSE      one translator on both sides, so a difference is ours
```

**The claim is narrower and the narrowing is the point.** The status comparison no longer says
"raises what the original raises on this hardware"; it says "raises what the original raises
with the translator held constant". A qemu error affecting both forms equally is invisible to
it. The register comparison does not share that limit, and saying so is cheaper than
discovering it later.

#### Five sabotages, and only the fifth was a control

```
1  string anchor matched two lines           assertion caught it
2  shell escaping mangled the pattern         assertion caught it
3  replace() silently did not match           assertion PASSED, edit did not apply
4  capture removed from BOTH sides            applied, symmetric, 0 differences
5  lowered side reports a masked-off MXCSR    312 differences
```

**Number 3 is the one to remember: the assertion checked that the line CONTAINED the anchor,
not that the replacement happened.** Verifying the anchor is not verifying the edit. The fix
was to replace the line by index and then grep the modified file -- check the artifact, not the
operation.

**Number 4 applied perfectly and still proved nothing.** Removing the capture from both
programs made them agree on its absence. **A sabotage has to break the two sides
DIFFERENTLY**, or it tests only that the harness is self-consistent, which it always is. That
is Finding 209's undiscriminating operands in another costume, and the second time in two hours.

#### And a no-op edit that read as a result

The first attempt at the split spliced at `(REGISTERS - 1) * 32`. `run()` returns BYTES at
`SLOT` each; the printer works on `.hex()` at 32 each. Two units in one function, no name
distinguishing them, and the wrong constant silently in range: `b[:480]` was the whole buffer,
`emulated[480:]` was empty, and the comparison never changed.

The run then produced the same 22 differences with the same `0x20` against `0x22` -- and the
obvious reading was available and wrong: *holding the translator constant did not help, so the
lowering really does raise a different flag.* What refused it was that the output was
byte-for-byte identical to the previous run. **A changed comparison that produces an unchanged
result has not been changed.**


### Finding 212 -- the item I priced last was nearly free, and four instruments failed proving it

Finding 209 ranked the 54 xmm-writing mnemonics below the flags group: "the largest amount of
work for the smallest gain", because each needed a hand-written GCC reference. **That was
wrong.** The reference burden belongs to `lowering_test` alone; `vex_oracle` compares against
the ORIGINAL INSTRUCTION and needs none. Building `build_flags` for Finding 210 is what showed
the route, and re-measuring turned 54 references into 58 mnemonics with zero.

```
xmm-writing mnemonics with no case   53      14,098 patches
can be lowered                       53      no refusals
usable as cases in the harness's convention  58 entries, 1 excluded
oracle cases                        248  ->  316
```

**Written in the harness's convention, not the binary's.** The shipped operands name `%rax`,
`0xb0(%rbx)`, `0x8(%r8)` -- registers this harness does not control, so a case copied verbatim
would read uninitialised state and could agree OR differ for reasons unrelated to the lowering.
Only mnemonics whose every source is an xmm or an immediate are here. The GPR- and
memory-sourced ones need a deterministic input first and remain open.

#### Four instruments failed, and none of them was the rewriter

**A rip-relative lowering with no pool.** `vpermilps` lowers to `pand -13(%rip),%xmm15`, and
the harness emits no constant pool, so the displacement pointed at whatever followed and the
oracle died of SIGSEGV. It is excluded by a BEHAVIOURAL detector -- lower twice at different
pool addresses and see whether the bytes move -- rather than by name, because a name list would
be correct today and silently wrong the moment another lowering learns to use the pool.

**A misleading crash index.** The last case PRINTED was `vpcmpgtq`, which disassembles to
`movaps` plus `pcmpgtq` and cannot fault. stdout is block-buffered into a file, so the buffered
tail was lost when the process died: the last printed index is a lower bound on progress, not
the crash site. The bytes were right and the index was an artefact of how the output was
captured.

**A probe polluting the harness's bookkeeping.** `vex_oracle` wraps `lower_vex` to record one
original per case and asserts the counts match. The pool detector's two extra calls per case
made it 434 for 316, and the gate refused. Without that assertion the probe's calls would have
been interleaved into the recorded originals and every case compared against the WRONG one --
differences that look like lowering defects and are nothing of the kind. `LOWER_VEX` is bound
at import now: **the probe is not a case and must not be counted as one.**

**And twelve real differences that were not defects.** `vrcpps` and `vrsqrtps` are specified
only to a relative error of about 1.5 * 2^-12 with the low mantissa implementation-defined:
`vex 0000803f` against `low 00f07f3f` is 1.0 against 0.99976 and neither is wrong. The lowering
is a prefix strip, so both sides run the same instruction and the difference is hardware
against emulator. They are compared against the EMULATED lowering now, which asks the
answerable question -- is the strip faithful -- rather than one the ISA declines to answer.

#### Three comparison modes, each with its reason written down

```
registers, normally        qemu-VEX  vs  native-SSE   must be right on real silicon
status slot                qemu-VEX  vs  qemu-SSE     qemu does not model DE
approximate instructions   qemu-VEX  vs  qemu-SSE     the ISA pins no exact result
```

**An exemption whose justification is recorded can be re-examined when the reason changes; one
added to make a run go green cannot, because nobody knows what it was for.** That is the
difference between these three and an ignore list.

**And the first sabotage was invalid.** Flipping a bit in the opcode produced SIGILL rather
than a wrong answer -- a crash is not a comparison. Flipping the modrm's low bit, so the
lowering reads the wrong register, gives 312 differences.


### Finding 213 -- deterministic general registers, and a filter that misread three of nine

A mnemonic whose source is a general register could not be a case: the harness controls `%rdi`
and `%rsi` and nothing else, so `vcvtsi2ss %rax,...` would read whatever the C driver left.
That is not a missing case but a case that could agree OR differ for reasons unrelated to the
lowering -- the failure this file records more than any other, arriving as an input rather than
as an observation.

`vex_oracle` loads `%rax`, `%rcx` and `%rdx` from the input buffer now, so their values vary
across all seven patterns rather than being one constant. Three constraints, and each would
produce a harness that LIES rather than one that fails:

  * **caller-saved only.** `%rbx` and `%r12`-`%r15` belong to the caller, and these are
    functions the harness calls in a loop -- clobbering one corrupts the driver, and the
    corruption appears as comparison differences that diverge as the loop proceeds.
  * **never `%rdi` or `%rsi`**, which carry the pointers.
  * **after the `xor`**, because `mov` writes no flags and the deterministic flag state of
    Finding 210 has to survive to the instruction.

The control ran first: 316 existing cases, GPR setup in place, 0 unexplained. Then the six new
mnemonics, and 322 cases still agree.

#### The filter misread three of nine, and adding them would have been the bug it fixes

Selecting GPR-source mnemonics by "starts with `%` and not `%xmm`" also matches `%ymm`. So
`vcvtps2ph`, `vextractf128` and `vextracti128` came back labelled GPR-source when their source
is a 256-bit register.

**Adding them would have been worse than leaving them out.** The harness loads only the low 128
bits, so a `%ymm` source reads an upper half NOTHING DEFINED -- the same uninitialised-input
defect this item exists to remove, reintroduced by the fix for it. They are recorded as
deliberately absent, needing a 256-bit input, rather than silently dropped.

#### The sabotage tests the machinery, not the cases

Corrupting the lowered bytes would show the cases can fail and say nothing about whether the
GPR setup is load-bearing. Feeding the two sides DIFFERENT values from the input buffer tests
exactly that: 29 differences of a possible 42, the rest coinciding because some patterns give
the same answer either way.

#### Where the oracle now stands

```
233  this morning
248  + two-operand moves       185,000 patches   a shape the expansion could not express
258  + flag-only mnemonics      31,479           a new observation
316  + xmm-source mnemonics     14,098           no reference was ever needed
322  + GPR-source mnemonics      ~9,000          deterministic register inputs
```

Each step needed a different thing, and none of them was "write more cases of the kind already
there". **What remains uncovered is recorded with its prerequisite** -- memory-sourced
mnemonics, and the `%ymm`-source ones -- which is the difference between a gap somebody can
pick up and a gap nobody knows about.


### Finding 214 -- an item created by misreading three characters, closed at 0

Finding 213 recorded `vcvtps2ph`, `vextractf128` and `vextracti128` as needing a 256-bit input
before they could be oracle cases, and put that on the list. It is worth nothing, and the row
existed because of a misclassification followed by a misreading.

**The misclassification:** selecting GPR-source mnemonics by "starts with `%` and not `%xmm`"
also matches `%ymm`, so three lane instructions were labelled GPR-source. Excluding them was
right; recording them as a future item assumed they were patched at all.

**The misreading:** the destination table showed `vextractps` with 1,221 memory and 403
general-register patches, and it was read as `vextractf128`. Three characters apart, and
completely different instructions -- `vextractps` extracts a float element and has a legacy
form; `vextractf128` moves a 128-bit lane and does not.

That misreading raised a real alarm, and it was worth checking rather than dismissing.
`lower.py` says a lane-1 extract needs "the Y2 shadow slot for this register", which only a
region provides -- so an IN-PLACE patch of one would read a half that does not exist on an
SSE-only CPU, and nothing in the tree would catch it: the bytes decode, no VEX survives, the
boundaries reconcile.

```
in-place patches of vextractf128, vextracti128, vinsertf128,
vinserti128 and vcvtps2ph:                                       0
```

**None, and by construction rather than by luck.** 256-bit sites are never patched in place --
the rule `stale_upper_reads` relies on to decide which readers survive. So `vex_oracle`, which
tests the in-place path, can never need a 256-bit input.

**The coverage question for 256-bit work belongs to `span_oracle`**, which executes spans and
regions and gained its missing passenger case in Finding 208. That is where a lane extract's
correctness is tested when a region carries one -- and where Finding 205's `NO_LEGACY_FORM`
defect was found.

**The cost of checking was one pass; the cost of building would have been a 256-bit input
channel for zero patches.** A row on the list is a claim like any other, and this one had never
been priced -- it was carried straight from the sentence that excluded the mnemonics, which is
exactly the shape of the four stale scope numbers already recorded today.


### Finding 215 -- the general register as a RESULT, and 95.2% re-derived rather than added up

Re-measured from the patch list rather than summed from the day's commits, which is the check
the four stale scope numbers here all failed:

```
in-place patches   547,716 across 126 mnemonic(s)
executed coverage  521,643  (95.2%)  in 106 mnemonic(s)
remaining           26,073  in 20 mnemonic(s)
  19,253  vzeroupper -- writes nothing, correctly excluded
   6,244  13 mnemonics whose DESTINATION is a general register
     576   6 mnemonics with a memory source
```

`vcvttss2si %xmm1,%eax`, `vmovmskps`, `vextractps`, the `vpextr*` family: their whole result
lands in a GPR, and the harness compares sixteen xmm registers. A case for one would have
compared bytes neither side touched and passed -- the same shape as the flags before Finding
210, and the mirror of Finding 213, which needed the register as an INPUT.

`vex_oracle` dumps `%rax` now. **The order is the correctness argument**: it goes before the
flags capture, because `pushfq`/`popq %rax` destroys it, and it can go there only because
`movq` writes no flags so the deterministic flag state still reaches the `pushfq`. Reversed,
the GPR result would become the low bits of EFLAGS on both sides equally -- a self-consistent
harness measuring nothing.

Control first: 322 existing cases with the slot in place, 0 unexplained. Then nine mnemonics,
and 331 cases still agree.

#### Two sabotages, and the pair is what says anything

```
blank the slot on the lowered side       2,236 differences -- nearly every comparison
flip the modrm of the gpr_dest cases        41 differences -- exactly the nine mnemonics
```

The first proves the slot is compared and cannot distinguish that from the cases working: every
case loads `%rax` since Finding 213, so blanking it moves everything. The second proves each of
the nine depends on its own lowering, and all nine appear. **A control that fails everywhere
shows the channel exists; one that fails precisely where it should shows the cases use it.**

#### A generator error no test would have caught

It emitted `vpextrq $0x1,%xmm1,%eax`, taking the destination width from the template rather
than from the mnemonic. `vpextrq` moves 64 bits: written with `%eax` it assembles to a
DIFFERENT INSTRUCTION, and the case would have tested that one -- passing, because both sides
run the same wrong thing. Operand width is a property of the mnemonic and the pattern could not
know it.

#### What moved the coverage was observations, not cases

```
xmm registers   the original          53% of patches
EFLAGS          Finding 210           +31,479
MXCSR           Finding 211           the comiss/ucomiss distinction
%rax as input   Finding 213            +9,000
%rax as result  Finding 215            +6,244        95.2%
```

Every one unlocked a CLASS. The cases were never the scarce thing.


### Finding 216 -- the memory-sourced forms, and 96.5% of the in-place path executed

The last uncovered class with a source the harness could reach: 576 patches in six mnemonics.

**They are not new instructions.** `vcvtsi2ssl`, `vcvtpd2psx` and the rest are the same opcodes
already covered in register form -- `objdump` prints the size suffix precisely because a memory
operand leaves the width ambiguous, so they arrive at the case list as distinct mnemonic
strings. The gap was therefore not in the lowering's coverage of an instruction but in the
case list's NAMING: the register form was tested, and the memory form goes through a different
path in `lower_vex`, the one that adjusts a displacement rather than rewriting a modrm, which
nothing had executed.

Written against `%rdi`, the input buffer, because the shipped operands read `0x8(%r8)`,
`(%rbx)`, `0x48(%rsp)` and a rip-relative displacement -- none of which the harness controls.
`%rsp` would be the worst of them: reading it is harmless, and a lowering that adjusted the
displacement would address into the harness's own frame.

**The sabotage was chosen for what these cases test.** Flipping the last byte's low bit -- the
trick used for the register cases -- changes a register field in some encodings and a
displacement in others, so a pass would be ambiguous. Flipping bit 4 moves the DISPLACEMENT,
which is the code path these exist for: 39 differences, in all six mnemonics.

```
in-place patches   547,716 across 126 mnemonic(s)
executed coverage  528,374  (96.5%)  in 120 mnemonic(s)
remaining           19,342  in 6 mnemonic(s)
  19,253  vzeroupper
      89  vmovlps, vmovhpd, vmovntps, vstmxcsr, vldmxcsr
```

**`vzeroupper` is not an item and should not become one.** It is patched to NOPs, and the
argument is that an SSE-only CPU has no upper half to zero. A case would compare xmm registers
neither side touches -- the low 128 bits are unchanged by `vzeroupper` and by `nop` alike -- so
it would pass while the entire semantic difference lives in bits the test machine does not
have. That is a question this harness cannot ask, and saying so is worth more than a green
tick.

**The 89 that remain are stores**, and the bucket label misfired again for the same reason as
Finding 215: the classifier reads sources, and these have a memory DESTINATION. They want an
observation of written memory, which is the sixth such addition and the last one the in-place
path has left.


### Finding 217 -- the stores, and the end of the in-place path at 124 of 126 mnemonics

The last class whose effect the harness could not see: 89 patches whose whole result is the
memory they write. `vex_oracle` gained a sixteen-byte scratch region INSIDE its compared
buffer, so the two sides differ exactly when the stored bytes differ and a case that writes
nothing there costs nothing -- the driver memsets the whole buffer before each call.

```
in-place patches   547,716 across 126 mnemonic(s)
executed coverage  528,459  (96.5%)  in 124 mnemonic(s)
remaining           19,257  in 2 mnemonic(s)
```

**Both survivors are recorded exclusions, not gaps.**

`vzeroupper` is 19,253 of them, patched to NOPs. A case would compare xmm registers neither
side touches -- the low 128 bits are unchanged by `vzeroupper` and by `nop` alike -- while the
entire semantic difference lives in upper halves this machine does not have. **The harness
cannot ask the question**, and a case would be a green tick for nothing.

`vldmxcsr` is 4, and it crashed the run before it was excluded. `LDMXCSR` raises #GP if any
reserved bit of its operand is set, and every buffer here holds arbitrary bytes: the input is
pattern data and the scratch is `0x5a5a5a5a`. Both are invalid MXCSR values. A valid operand
means a buffer existing for one instruction with four patches, which is more machinery than the
coverage buys. The diagnosis was confirmed by removing it and watching 341 cases pass, not
inferred from the fault.

#### Three invalid sabotages in one day, each of which produced output

```
the anchor matched but the edit never applied     assertion checked containment, not replacement
the capture was removed from BOTH sides           applied, symmetric, agreed on the absence
the displacement was flipped out of bounds        crashed instead of differing
```

**Each ran to completion and printed something that looked like a verdict.** The third is the
sharpest: a blanket modrm flip would have been worse still, since `stmxcsr` is `/3` and
`ldmxcsr` is `/2` -- one bit apart -- so the sabotage would have silently turned the store into
the load that had just crashed the run, and the crash would have been read as the sabotage
working.

Replacing the lowered store with NOPs is asymmetric, in bounds, and cannot fault: 28
differences across all four stores.

#### What the day did to this harness

```
233 cases  ->  341        53% of in-place patches  ->  96.5%
observations added: EFLAGS, MXCSR, %rax in, %rax out, a store region
```

Five observations and six case lists, and **not one of the five was "more cases of the kind
already there"**. Every class that opened needed the harness to be able to SEE something new;
the cases were never the scarce thing. The two that stay shut are shut because the machine
cannot hold the state, which is a different sentence from "nobody has written it yet".


### Finding 218 -- 440 swallowed calls, and nothing had ever executed one

The detour path measured the way the in-place path was:

```
detour candidates   242,927 across 129 site mnemonic(s)
site coverage       242,790  (99.9%)   137 sites in 7 mnemonics uncovered
swallowed           92,683 across 183 mnemonic(s)
  executed by an oracle case            83,601
  covered by a fixture rather than one    6,052   mov, jmp, lea, je, nop
  executed by NOTHING                     3,030   in 62 mnemonics
```

The sites were nearly all covered already, because the in-place case list names the same
mnemonics. The passengers were not, and the largest of them is `call` at 440 -- with `verify`
reporting 384 in the shipped stub section, "every one an instruction a window covered and
re-emitted". **The path has run in production since Finding 86 built it and nothing had
executed one.**

Structural checking cannot close it. `verify` proves a re-emitted call's target still begins an
instruction; it cannot prove the DISPLACEMENT was recomputed for the stub's address, nor that
the RETURN ADDRESS -- which now points into the stub -- leads somewhere execution continues.

`swallowcall` does: a four-byte site that cannot hold a jump, a `jne` blocking backward
widening, and a five-byte `call` the window must therefore swallow.

#### The first version failed on a mechanism it was not testing

It returned 5. The helper sat inside `func_end`, so both halves were ONE `.pdata` function, and
the rewriter believed `rsp` stayed at `_start`'s frame throughout -- so the helper's stub
borrowed the callee home space at `(%rsp)`, which inside a function entered by `call` is the
RETURN ADDRESS. It saved `%xmm1` over it and restored `%xmm1` from it.

**The rewriter reasoned correctly from what the binary told it.** Real binaries do not put a
call target inside its caller's `.pdata` range: a called helper is its own function, a leaf,
and a leaf lends nothing -- which is exactly what `no home space to borrow` refuses. The
fixture had arranged for that refusal never to be asked.

The helper is after `func_end` and in pure SSE now. Both halves matter: outside the range it is
not rewritten, which isolates the test to the call's re-emission; pure SSE means an AVX-less
CPU runs it unmodified.

#### Three sabotages, and the first two edited code the path never reaches

```
close_stub's displaced loop, twice     stub bytes IDENTICAL -- the pass meant nothing
build_stub's displaced loop            call 0x14000103d -> 0x140001041, answer 30 -> 3
```

There are three `emit_swallowed` call sites and the plain path uses the third. Both failed
attempts asserted that the anchor LINE matched -- it did -- and neither checked that the output
changed. What settled it was diffing the sabotaged stub against the real one and finding them
byte-identical.

**Asserting on the source proves you edited something; only the artifact proves you edited the
thing that runs.** That is the fourth time today the two were confused, and the corrupted call
is worth seeing: it still returns, and answers 3 instead of 30. Silent, not a crash.

#### And two measurements of the passengers were wrong before this one

`entry[2]` gave addresses rather than mnemonics -- caught because a column of instruction names
held `5446595600`. Then counting only `preceding` and not `displaced` gave 2,251 passengers of
the real 92,683: **2.4% of the population**, with a coverage percentage computed over it. The
number that exposed that was not a check but a fixture suite containing `swallowjmp` and
`crossblock` appearing to swallow two instructions in total.


### Finding 219 -- the swallowed conditional branches, and two fixtures that proved nothing

The suite swallowed `jmp` and `je`. Starfield swallows `jbe` 182 times, `ja` 132, `jb` 126 and
`jae` 66, and a re-emitted branch whose displacement was not recomputed transfers control
somewhere else. **`verify` cannot catch that**: it proves every target still BEGINS an
instruction, which a wrong displacement satisfies by landing on a different valid one.

`condswallow` swallows all four, and took three versions to be worth anything.

```
v1  a `cmp` after each site      windows widened FORWARD; four cmps swallowed, no branch
v2  branches not taken           all four swallowed, green, and passed the sabotage
v3  branches taken               clean 3, sabotaged 5
```

**v1 would have passed `check-pe`.** The arithmetic was right and the rewrite was right; the
fixture simply tested nothing it was written for. A window takes the cheapest widening
available and only a branch target blocks the forward one -- which is why `condbefore` gets its
`je` swallowed, a fixture I had read and modelled on without seeing the part that made it work.
Running `collect` before wine caught it in seconds.

**v2 is the one worth keeping.** It swallowed exactly the four branches it named, ran green,
and was provably useless: with every branch arranged to fall through, moving each re-emitted
target by two bytes changed nothing, because **a branch nobody takes does not care where it
points.** Every structural property of that fixture was correct. Only the sabotage could show
it. It is *a test can name the hazard exactly and cover only the safe path*, written after
reading that entry.

v3 makes each branch taken and skipping a poison: taken correctly, `%xmm5` keeps its 3; a
branch re-emitted two bytes out lands mid-instruction and the answer becomes 5.

#### And aiming the sabotage took four attempts

```
close_stub's displaced loop        stub bytes identical
build_stub's displaced loop        stub bytes identical
short-branch opcodes 0x77 etc.     stub bytes identical
build_stub's PRECEDING loop, 0f 8x  bytes differ, answer 3 -> 5
```

The branches here PRECEDE their sites and are in `preceding`; the swallowed `call` of Finding
218 FOLLOWED its site and was in `displaced`. Same mechanism, opposite list. And a branch
re-emitted into a stub is far from its target, so the two-byte form is widened to `0f 8x
rel32` -- a sabotage keyed on `0x77` matches nothing.

**Every wrong attempt returned a plausible number.** What separated them was diffing the
sabotaged stub against the real one: three said IDENTICAL, and identical bytes cannot be a
result.


### Finding 238 -- the switch floor gets a control, and an indirect jump poisons the walk

The last coverable check. `verify` fails when dispatches are recognised and no table
resolves, because that is what a broken resolver looks like -- Finding 196 built the floor
after an image base added twice returned zero tables for a whole build and the totals read
as neutral. It needed BOTH halves built: no fixture contained a dispatch, and no corrupted
image can express "the resolver read nothing".

The sabotage is not an invented breakage. It adds the base a second time, which is the
defect the floor exists for: every span lands 0x140000000 too high, `at` resolves nothing,
and every dispatch is still recognised.

```
switchtable, normal      rc=0   dispatches=1 tables=1 targets=2
switchtable, sabotaged   rc=1   1 switch dispatch(es) recognised and no table resolved
wine                     rewritten 77, want 77
```

**An indirect jump poisons `upper_half_read_later` for everything BEFORE it.** The first
layout put the dispatch on a dead path inside the function and the fixture returned 29:
the forward walk cannot resolve where `jmp *%rcx` goes, so it answers "read", which
declined the live-path pair and left surviving VEX where the program runs. Moving the
dispatch past the `ret` fixes it -- the walk stops at the return, and the dispatch is still
in the listing for a static resolver. **A conservative answer at one site is a refusal at
every site before it**, which is not obvious from reading either piece of code.

**And the table entries must be literal RVAs.** The assembler cannot fold
`symbol - 0x140000000` without a relocation, so the first version assembled the
displacement and both entries as `0` -- which made the fixture trip the check with no
sabotage at all. Hardcoding them makes the fixture brittle to layout changes, and loudly
so: if the RVAs go stale the table stops resolving and `check-verify` goes red.

**Twenty minutes went to a stale artifact.** `switch_dispatch` returned `0x0` while objdump
showed `0x1060`, because `make build/pe-switchtable.exe` rebuilds the binary and the `.asm`
listing is a separate target. Reading a listing generated before the fix is this file's own
artifact-not-plan rule, met from a direction nobody had listed.

### Finding 252 -- a run borrowed a register its own passengers use

**138 windows in the shipped image carried wrong bytes**, and had done since runs learned to
borrow. It was found by a fixture built to test something else entirely.

#### What it does

A run carries an upper half across a span in a reserved xmm. Where nothing is dead it borrows
a live one, saves it, and restores it -- `assign_helpers`, the `lendable` branch. That branch
chose from

    free = set(VOLATILE_XMM) - taken - set(own)
    for position in list(stores) + [load_at]:
            free -= xmm_numbers(plain[position][3])

which excludes the registers the lifetime's own load and stores name, and **nothing between
them**. A run swallows what lies between into the same stub, and those passengers are
re-emitted BETWEEN the carry-load and the carry-store. The comment said it picked "a register
the run does not itself name"; the passengers are the run.

The save and restore protect the CALLER's register across the stub and say nothing about the
middle of it. From the shipped image, site `0x1404dab63`, stub `0x1489b27e1`:

    movups %xmm0,(%rsp)          save the borrowed xmm0
    movups 0x20(%r10),%xmm0      the carried upper half
    ...
    movups 0x10(%r11),%xmm0      a PASSENGER overwrites it
    movups 0x30(%r11),%xmm0      and again
    ...
    movups %xmm0,0x20(%r11)      stores the PASSENGER's value as the upper half
    movups (%rsp),%xmm0          restore

Both directions are wrong: the passenger destroys the half in flight, and a passenger that
merely READS the register reads the half instead of its own value.

#### The scale, and the cost of fixing it

    runs that borrow a helper                      347
      a PLAIN passenger names the borrowed one     171
        and the window is PLACED in the image      138

    after the fix          before
    run  2,045 / 6,717     2,053 / 6,797      -8 windows, -80 sites
    plain 179,097/241,291  179,093/241,285    +4 / +6, picked up
    detours    202,836        202,838         -2
    stub refusals   37             46         -9

**Only 8 of the 138 lost the run**; the rest simply get a different, non-clashing register. So
the correction cost eight windows, not a hundred and thirty-eight.

**And the failure mode changed direction.** `noxmm` computed **10** where the same arithmetic in
legacy SSE gives 77; with the fix the run declines, the VEX survives and the program dies at 29.
A silently wrong answer became an honest refusal, which is the trade this project makes
everywhere else.

**The frontier pays 18 sites for it**, and `make detour-verify` holds on the result:

    VEX in .text  805,131 -> 5,691   was 5,673
    removed             799,440      was 799,458, still 99.3%

That is the whole price of the correction, and the status lines in `project.md` and `README.md`
move with it -- caught by `make status`, which failed on all three claims before they were
updated. A number that justifies the work is a number that has to be re-taken when the work
changes, and the gate is what makes that automatic rather than remembered.

#### `check-run-borrow`, and why its pass is 29

The gate asserts 29 and names 10 as the defect. That is worth stating because **29 is not a
lowering** -- it is an illegal instruction. A gate that could only tell "worked" from "crashed"
would have called the broken build the healthier one, and this is the case where the crash is
the correct outcome. Proved by reverting the one line in a scratch copy: the fixture returns 10
and the gate rejects it.

#### Three things about the finding, which are the reusable part

**It came from a fixture built for something else.** `noxmm` exists to hold every volatile xmm
live so the GPR mover of Finding 251 can be tested. The defect fell out of it. That is now the
third time this session a measurement aimed at one question has answered a different and more
important one.

**The first probe measured nothing and looked clean.** Its print sat in `report_units`, which
returns early without `--shadow-regs=all`, and the run was made without the flag. An empty
result from a probe that cannot print is indistinguishable from a genuine absence -- and it
would have read as "no clashes found".

**The second probe over-counted, at 236.** It asked whether ANY member names the borrowed
register, and `assign_helpers` does exclude the lifetime's own load and stores. The question
that matters is narrower -- a PLAIN passenger -- and it gives 171 built and 138 placed. A
number that is easy to compute is not thereby the number the claim needs.

**`make check` was green throughout.** Nothing in the suite exercises a borrowing run with a
clashing passenger, which is why the fixture had to come from outside it.

### Finding 354 -- a forward hammock takes a site that borrows

**The build of Finding 353 stopped at `0x140bbc1db`**, after first faulting at
`0x142a481c6`. Both are the same shape: the second arm of a ternary, or the last
arm before a join.

    140bbc1d3  jbe    0x140bbc1db
    140bbc1d5  vsubss %xmm6,%xmm0,%xmm0
    140bbc1d9  jmp    0x140bbc1df          rel8, the join
    140bbc1db  vsubss %xmm0,%xmm6,%xmm0    four bytes, dst == src2
    140bbc1df  vcomiss 0x4347c59(%rip),%xmm0

Finding 353's census had already called `0x140bbc1db` "ok": one rel8 way in, and
room for its slot. **The forward hammock was never asked.** `dst == src2` with
no dead xmm makes the lowering a `("spill", n)` strategy, and `collect` offered
hammocks only to sites with no strategy at all. A probe that ran `collect` alone
and logged both hammock walks found neither one called for either site.

**The exclusion was right for the backward hammock and only inherited by the
forward one.** A backward hammock's labels point at instructions BEFORE the site,
which the plain path lays out and the spill path does not. A forward hammock's
labels come after the site, and the spill path closes before they do: the save,
the lowering, the restore and any `STACK_CLOSE` all come before the first
passenger. So a branch to a held label skips a bracket that is already shut. The
two things that could open after it are refused already:
  * a block pointer planted for a borrowing passenger is refused in
    `build_stub`;
  * a borrowing passenger is refused in `forward_hammock`.

So `collect` offers the forward walk to a spill site too, and `build_stub` lets
the pair through. Every other strategy is still refused.

**Measured on the full image, against Finding 353's build:**

| | Finding 353 | Finding 354 |
|---|---:|---:|
| short sites holding their own targets | 143 | 186 |
| declined: next instruction is a branch target | 49 | 7 |
| frontier rows (5 of them switch-table bytes) | 254 | 214 |
| detours | 203,328 | 203,368 |

That is 40 sites, both of the faulting ones among them. The 7 that remain are
refused for "a passenger transfers control".

**`fwdspill` is the fixture.** It is `fwdhammock` with three changes:
  * the site is `vsubss %xmm0,%xmm1,%xmm0`;
  * an indirect `jmp` leaves no xmm provably dead, so the site borrows `%xmm2`;
  * `%xmm2` is read at the end.

It answers 107. Measured three ways:
  * HEAD declines the site, which faults (29);
  * this change answers 107;
  * with the held label aimed at the stub's first byte, the loop re-runs the
    save and the subtraction and answers 103.

### Finding 353 -- a hammock holds what follows the site, and a rel8 jumps through a slot

**The other survivor Finding 351's build stopped on, `0x142a61561`**, is one case
of a rotation switch:

    142a61560  ret
    142a61561  vaddss %xmm4,%xmm3,%xmm0      a switch target, four bytes
    142a61565  vxorps 0x24a5103(%rip),%xmm4,%xmm1   <- jmp rel8 at 0x142a615c9

It cannot widen back over the `ret`. Its next instruction is reached by a
`jmp rel8` from below, which cannot reach a stub, so Finding 351's re-aim does not
apply. No `int3` padding lies within reach of either jump.

**The window's own padding is within reach.** Taking the next instruction as a
passenger makes the window 12 bytes, and only five are its jump. So
`forward_hammock` walks forward from a short site whose next instruction is a
target, holds every target among the passengers, and accepts each way in from
outside that can be re-aimed:

  * a rel32 is rewritten as in Finding 351;
  * a rel8 (`jmp` or `jcc`) is rewritten to a five-byte slot in the window's
    padding, `start + 5` for the first such target. `apply` writes a
    `jmp rel32` there to the stub's copy.

The window grows until it holds the jump and every slot. A passenger must not
transfer control, and must not borrow. A branch into the middle of the stub skips
whatever the stub set up before it, and a block pointer planted for a borrowing
passenger is that, so `build_stub` refuses such a window. The labels need no
second pass: the site's lowering is already in the body when the passengers go
down, so each held one's offset is the body's length at that point.
`HAMMOCK_FORWARD` names the slots, and `place_stubs` refuses conflicts as in
Finding 351.

**`verify` follows a rel8 through its slot.** The rewritten byte must land on a
slot inside the same window, and the slot's `jmp rel32` must land in that
window's stub.

**The first build failed `verify` on 18 lost boundaries and a branch target**,
and the cause was the padding. `apply` filled the window with jump and nops,
then wrote each slot over the start of a multi-byte `nop`. Where the window ran
one byte past its last slot, the `nop`'s trailing `00` was left behind, and the
sweep read it as the start of an instruction that ran into the code after the
window. `apply` now pads again from the last slot to the window's end.

**`fwdhammock` is the fixture**, built to reach exactly this:
  * the site is named by a rel8 from below, so neither widening back nor the
    backward hammock can take it (the first version named it from above, and
    the backward hammock took it);
  * a loop's `jmp rel8` returns to the held `addl`;
  * a one-byte `cltd` leaves the window one byte past its slot.

It returns 77 and the original 29. With the short jump put back, `verify` fails
three checks and the copy crashes. With the re-pad turned off, `verify` fails on
a lost boundary.

Measured 2026-10-19:

    verify, VEX in .text      804,953 -> 278   before (Finding 352)
                              804,953 -> 254   forward hammocks

24 sites, `0x142a61561` among them, and none newly surviving. 42 jumps re-aimed in
all. Ten fewer in-place patches, because a forward window takes a VEX passenger
that was patched in place before. `verify` passes, with the same OPEN line.

### Finding 352 -- a lone 256-bit site jumps short too

**Finding 351's build ran 104 seconds and stopped on two survivors.**
`0x142a61561` (a `vaddss`, Finding 353) faulted first, and three seconds later
`0x142a059a7`:

    142a059a1  je     0x142a05a60
    142a059a7  vmovups (%rcx),%ymm0        four bytes, the survivor
    142a059ab  mov    %rbx,0x8(%rax)       a chained .pdata fragment starts here

The load's next instruction begins a chained unwind fragment
(`UNW_FLAG_CHAININFO`), which the target set counts as a function start, so
`ymm_run` stops there before reaching a store. The unit window, Finding 246's
lowering that keeps the upper half in the permanent slot, cannot widen forward
over the fragment start or backward over the `je`. Eight bytes of `int3` padding
sit just above the function, within a `jmp rel8`'s reach. But Finding 331's
trampoline was offered only on the plain path, which a 256-bit site never
reaches.

**The unit window takes the trampoline now.** `unit_candidate` accepts a window of
the site alone when a slot is within reach (`unit_trampoline`, asked without
claiming because the ladder walks rungs it never takes), and `seat_unit` claims
the slot for the one candidate kept. The rest is Finding 331's machinery
unchanged: `apply` writes the short jump and the slot's `jmp rel32`, and `verify`
excuses the padding. The dropped-window alternatives skip a short window, since
only `seat_unit` claims a slot.

**`tramp256`** in `check-shadow-pe` is the shape: a four-byte `vmovups` load
between a never-taken `jne` naming it and a never-taken `jne` naming its
successor, with padding after `func_end`, and a later store of the register. The
upper lane of the copy is 77. Without slots the load stays VEX and the program
dies (29). With `TRAMPOLINE_RULE` off it dies too.

**Crossing a chained fragment boundary was measured and not taken.** Only 14
survivors have a chained fragment start from 16 bytes before them to 32 after, and a window that moved
a fragment's prologue saves into a stub would unwind with the wrong fragment's
codes.

Measured 2026-10-19:

    verify, VEX in .text      804,953 -> 283   before (Finding 351)
                              804,953 -> 278   lone 256-bit sites jump short

Five sites, `0x142a059a7` among them. `verify` passes, with 200 lost boundaries
all inside trampoline padding, and the same OPEN line.

### Finding 351 -- a jump from outside a hammock is re-aimed rather than refused

**The survivor at `0x140d80afd` that stopped Finding 350's run is a short site
where every instruction is a branch target**, each reached by rel32 jumps from
elsewhere in the function:

    140d80af9  vxorps %xmm1,%xmm1,%xmm1   <- je   at 0x140d80b81
    140d80afd  vaddss %xmm1,%xmm2,%xmm1   <- jmp  at 0x140d80bad, 0x140d80bc7
    140d80b01  vcomiss %xmm7,%xmm1        <- jmp  at 0x140d809bc, 0x140d809d1

Forward widening swallows `0x140d80b01` and backward widening swallows the site,
and both are targets. The site's own `vaddss` cannot be patched in place: written
as `addss %xmm2,%xmm1` it would keep xmm1's upper lanes where VEX takes xmm2's. No
`int3` padding lies within reach of a `jmp rel8`. Finding 336's hammock was refused
too, because it holds a target only when every branch to it is inside the window,
and these come from after it.

**A rel32 jump is a pointer that can be rewritten.** The hammock now accepts a
target reached from outside the window when every outside way in is a direct jump
whose last four bytes are its displacement (`reaimable`). The jump stays where it
is, and `apply` rewrites its displacement to the stub's copy of the target.
`build_stub` already lays out a label for every preceding instruction and for the
site; it now also records each held target's offset in `HAMMOCK_LABELS`, which is
correct at any stub address because every piece's length is position-independent.

A rel8 cannot reach a stub, and a table, a relocation or a `lea` cannot be
rewritten, so those still refuse. The jump must also lie inside a function range
and outside every data island, so that a run of data that happens to decode as
`e9 xx xx xx xx` is never edited.

**Two windows may not share a re-aimed jump.** A window that moved the jump would
carry it into a stub still aimed at the held target, which is padding now.
`place_stubs` places windows in address order and refuses whichever comes second:
a hammock whose jump lies in a placed window, or a window covering a jump a placed
hammock re-aims. It refused nothing in Starfield.

**`verify` asks the image, not the plan.** For each jump a placed hammock re-aims,
the rewritten bytes must match the original except for the displacement, and the
new target must lie inside that window's own stub. Only then does a held target
reached from outside count as held. Restoring the original jump in a copy of the
rewritten `reaim` fixture failed three checks: this one, "direct branch targets
no longer begin an instruction" and "land inside a placed window". The copy
faulted under wine.

**`reaim` is the fixture** for 0x140d80afd's shape. A `jbe` that is always taken
reaches the site only through a `jmp.d32` from below the window, and the
instruction after the site is a branch target, so the site can only be held. It
returns 77, the original dies of an illegal instruction (29), and a jump left
aimed at the window crashes.

Measured 2026-10-19:

    verify, VEX in .text      804,953 -> 290   before (Finding 350)
                              804,953 -> 283   re-aimed jumps

Seven sites, `0x140d80afd` among them, with 10 jumps re-aimed. "Reached from after
it" no longer refuses anything. Of the 99 hammocks still refused, 84 are "an
instruction it would swallow will not move", which is the next lever in this
group. `verify` passes with the same OPEN line (510 register-addressed operands,
Finding 341).

**What this does not cover.** A forward window -- the site and the target after it
-- would hold the target among the instructions after the site, and `build_stub`
lays out labels only for those before it. Of the eight sites listed beforehand as
forward candidates, four converted through the backward window instead
(`0x140d80afd`, `0x1419c76fb`, `0x14211253b`, `0x1422964af`). Four still survive:
`0x141a32dbc`, `0x141a544fa`, `0x14169b320` and `0x141746614`. Of the five listed
as backward candidates, `0x140301787` and `0x1421d4746` still survive.

### Finding 350 -- a caller holds what its callee leaves alone, so `ret` frees nothing by itself

**Starfield got past Finding 349's crash and faulted inside a stub**: an access
violation at `0x148ded821`, `movups %xmm1,0x20(%r9,%r14,1)`, with `r9` holding
`0x3f9d9be33f800000` -- two floats, 1.0 and 1.23, used as a pointer. Half a second
later another thread stopped on the survivor at `0x140d80afd`.

**The original code keeps `r9` live across a call.** `0x142920cac` loads `r9`, calls
`0x142ccb870`, and stores through `r9` after it returns. The ABI makes `r9` volatile,
but the compiler allocated registers across the whole program: it knew `0x142ccb870`
never writes `r9`, and relied on it. The stub for `vmovups (%rdx),%ymm0` at
`0x142ccb8af` moved the upper half through `r9` without saving it, because
`gpr_live_out` modelled a `ret` as reading `rax` and `rdx` and nothing else. The same
error appeared in five places, all trusting what the ABI permits a callee to do rather
than what this program relies on. `gpr_effect` had already refused that trust for a
call, on `__chkstk`'s evidence:

  * a `ret`, in `gpr_live_out` and `xmm_live_out`;
  * a `ret` and a call in `scratch.dead_from`, `dies_here` and the checker `walk`,
    which killed xmm1-5 and xmm4-5;
  * the region helper's closing call, seeded with nothing live after it;
  * `scratch.function_scope` and `gpr_function_scope`: a register a function never
    names was taken as free everywhere in it, though a caller may hold it across the
    whole function.

**Now the answer is the clobber set the compiler would have computed.**
`scratch.clobbers` runs over the same ranges as `function_scope`. For each function it
counts the registers its reachable instructions certainly write, adds the sets of the
functions it calls directly (to a fixed point), and counts everything for an indirect
call, whose target follows the standard convention.

  * At a `ret`, a volatile register is live unless the function clobbers it.
  * At a call, xmm4/5 die only where the callee clobbers them and does not read them,
    because `__vectorcall` passes arguments there.
  * xmm0-3 are always live at a `ret`, since `__vectorcall` returns a homogeneous
    aggregate in them. This is not hypothetical. `0x1403a30fe` calls `0x140368fc0`
    and then takes xmm0, xmm1, xmm2 and xmm3 as four results -- an `XMMATRIX`. The
    old rule killed xmm1-3 at every `ret`, so a stub at the end of such a function
    could have destroyed three rows of a matrix.

Two choices keep the clobber set from being too large, which is the unsafe direction.
Writes are recognised from a census of every last operand in the listing: a positive
list for GPRs, and for vector registers everything but the compares to flags. Only
code reachable from the entry counts, so jump-table bytes decoded as instructions add
nothing.

**The entry point and the exports clobber everything** (`patch.standard_entries`,
279 functions in Starfield). The loader and other modules call them knowing nothing of
them. Without this, `make check` failed on the `spanblock` fixture. Its only function
is the entry point and writes only `eax`, so no GPR was left without TEB scratch,
which a fixture image cannot import.

Being called from outside says what a function clobbers, not what it reads. The first
version marked those functions as reading every xmm register too, as it rightly does
for an indirect call, whose callee may take `__vectorcall` arguments in xmm4 and
xmm5. That emptied `span_helper`'s whole-function answer. With `--shadow-regs=all`,
the `unaligned256` fixture then lowered the high half of its `vmulps` without a
helper, as `mulps 0x10(%rax),%xmm0` on an operand 8 bytes off alignment. The fixture
returned 5 for 77. That is Finding 341's open class, reached by losing a helper
register.

`longpair` parks an upper half in a register its function never names, xmm1 or
xmm2. Both were free only by the old `ret` rule, so the fixture now zeroes them just
before its `ret`.

Where no clobber set is registered, a `ret` keeps every register live and a call kills
nothing. That costs a scratch and never a value. The selftests build their fixtures'
clobber sets the same way. The two cases that asserted the ABI rule are now pairs:
"a ret reads a register the function never writes" and "... does not read one it
clobbers".

Measured 2026-10-19:

    verify, VEX in .text      804,953 -> 264   before (Finding 349)
                              804,953 -> 290   clobber sets

All 26 newly surviving sites were converting before and relied on the ABI rule. 23
are now "next instruction is a branch target": hammocks whose passengers no longer
find a scratch. 3 are lost to an overlap. In the rebuilt image the stub at
`0x142ccb8af` saves `rcx` and uses `r11`, which `0x142ccb870` writes in its epilogue;
`r9` is untouched. `verify` passes with the same OPEN line (510 register-addressed
operands, Finding 341).

**What this does not cover.** Upper ymm halves are still dead at every call. MSVC
emits `vzeroupper` before calls -- `0x142920d14` is one -- so its own code treats them
that way. Direct calls to an address with no range contribute no clobbers, which is
sound and costs sites.

### Finding 349 -- a passenger may borrow through TLS, and a VEX form kills its destination

**Starfield got past Finding 348's crash and stopped 52 seconds after load on an
illegal instruction at `0x142437e05`**: `vmulps (%rax),%xmm1,%xmm6`, a survivor, and
one of the 34 sites Finding 348 cost. It is four bytes between two five-byte `vmulps`
in a chained fragment, and its forward neighbour would not ride along. Two causes,
both fixed.

**A passenger was offered a borrow only where the frame lends one.** Its memory
operand may be unaligned, so the neighbour needs a register to `movups` into, and with
none dead it borrows one. `swallowed_borrow` asked `borrow_offset` alone. `build_stub`
has planted a TLS block for a borrowing forward passenger since Finding 182, but only
when the window lends no frame slot, and nothing at collection offered one there.
After Finding 348 a split function lends nothing, so the path mattered. Now, under
`--spill=tls`, a forward passenger is offered a borrow where neither it nor the
window's start lends a frame slot and two GPRs are dead across the window. The start
has to lend nothing as well: `build_stub` takes `base` from the start, and a start that
lends would save the passenger into the frame at an address `borrow_offset` refused.
A preceding or hammock passenger gets no block from `build_stub`, so it is not
offered one. Worth 19 sites, 326 -> 307, and not this one: only `rcx` is provably
dead there.

**The liveness scan counted every VEX non-destructive form as reading its
destination.** `scratch.kills_of` knew the plain moves and the zeroing idioms. So
`vshufps $0x88,%xmm0,%xmm1,%xmm5`, which writes `xmm5` whole from `xmm0` and `xmm1`,
left `xmm5` live, and the same went for `xmm2` -- both dead from `0x142437e05` to
their writes. A three-operand instruction in `lower.NDS_MNEMONICS` or a compare form now
kills its register destination when that register is not also a source. That is the
ISA's rule for VEX.128 and VEX.256 (`dst = op(src1, src2)`, upper bits zeroed). It is
also the shape `lower_vex` already emits as `movaps src1,dst; op src2,dst`. A
merge-masked EVEX operand (`{%k}`) does read the destination and is excluded.

**`scratch.walk` cannot vouch for this**, because it calls the same `kills_of`. The
rule rests on the ISA definition, not on a second implementation. The rebuilt image's
`verify` is the check on the result.

Measured 2026-10-19, both in one build:

    verify, VEX in .text      804,953 -> 326   before (Finding 348)
                              804,953 -> 307   TLS passenger borrow only
                              804,953 -> 264   with the liveness rule

`0x142437e05` converts. Of the 35 addresses that survive in Finding 348's build and
not in Finding 347's, 24 convert now and 11 still survive -- among them `0x1406d6933`,
the passenger after a closed stack allocation. The rest of the gain is sites that
survived both before and after Finding 348: 264 is 28 below Finding 347's 292. No site
that converted in Finding 348's build survives in this one. `verify` passes, with the same OPEN line
(505 register-addressed operands, Finding 341).

### Finding 348 -- the zeroed frame pointer was a borrow into a split function's shadow

**The crash every Steam run since Finding 342 has stopped on is a rewrite bug, and
this is it.** `0x141e92950` saves its caller's `rbx` and `rbp` into its own shadow --
entry `0x8(%rsp)` and `0x10(%rsp)` -- then zeroes `rbp` for its own use and reloads both
at exit. The stub for the `vandps`/`vcomiss` window at `0x141e92a90` borrowed `xmm1`
with `movups %xmm1,0x70(%rsp)`: at that depth, 16 bytes over exactly those two slots.
The restore gave back `xmm1` and nothing else, so the function returned a float's
halves as `rbx` and `rbp`. A scalar's upper half is usually zero, the caller's
`lea 0x88(%rbp),%rcx` became `0x88`, and the game wrote through it at `0x1422CC4BE` --
with `rbx` zero too, as every crash dump showed.

**Why the borrow analysis said the shadow was free:** MSVC split the function across
five `.pdata` entries, four of them chained (`UNW_FLAG_CHAININFO`). The prologue that
writes the shadow is in the first, the site in the fourth, the epilogue that reads it
in the fifth. `shadow_depths` follows the chain for the frame size, so the
displacement was right, but asks "is the region still read from here" over the one
entry's instructions, and the fourth fragment never mentions it. Of 236,427 entries,
56,269 are chained fragments of 25,581 functions.

**The fix:** a chained fragment, or a function that has them, lends neither its shadow
nor its callee home space. Its sites take the TLS spill instead. The parent is read
from the `RUNTIME_FUNCTION` after the fragment's unwind codes, and every one of the
56,269 names a real `.pdata` start.

**A second bug, found by the audit that measured the first.** When a site takes the
stack fallback (Finding 204), `build_stub` sets `base = 0` to address its own 16 bytes,
and nothing reset it after `STACK_CLOSE`. A passenger after it then saved its borrow
at `(%rsp)`, inside the function's frame again (`0x1406d6927`). `base` is `None` after
the close now, so such a passenger refuses.

Measured with a scratch audit of every stub store to the stack, by window, against
the stores the window's own instructions make:

    stores in split functions that are no original store    15,410 -> 10
    stores after a closed stack allocation                      28 -> 0

The 10 left are original stores the audit cannot match: a `vextractf128` to the
stack, and the members of one long copy run beyond its lookahead. **The cost is 34
sites**, 292 -> 326 by `verify`'s count: 27 from the chained rule and 7 from the
reset. `verify` passes on the result.

**This rested on a gap no gate covers.** `verify`'s store check (Finding 342) looks at
stores to fixed addresses. A borrow save is matched by its own restore, so the store
audit filed it as "saved and restored" and never asked whose slot it was. Nothing
in `check-pe` builds a function with chained unwind info. A fixture that does is the
open half of this finding.

### Finding 347 -- the listing ran out of step into 165 function starts

`build/text.asm` was one linear `objdump` sweep. Data embedded in `.text` -- a switch
table, mostly -- decodes as instructions, and the last of them can run past the data
into the function after it. The sweep is then out of step until the encodings line up
again, and the listing shows phantom instructions where the real ones are.

Measured 2026-10-17 against `.pdata`: **165 of 236,427 function starts were not
instruction boundaries**, and two of them only looked like one, because they sat
on a continuation line of a 9-byte `movabs`. An address-keyed read of the listing (the
first count, 163) takes such a line for a boundary. Decoding from each start until it
meets the sweep, and diffing the VEX sets:

- **Two real VEX instructions were missing**, `vmovss 0x4(%rcx),%xmm0` and
  `vmovss (%rcx),%xmm4` at `0x1424bfb74`/`0x1424bfb79`. They open the function at
  `0x1424bfb70`, which follows a switch table. Nothing counted them, nothing converted
  them, and `7bdaf976` shipped them as VEX.
- **No phantom VEX**: no instruction the rewriter converted was a misreading, so the
  out-of-step stretches corrupted nothing.
- The other 1,483 direct-branch and call targets off a boundary hold no real VEX
  either. The 31 that start with a VEX byte decode as `(bad)`, which is data.

`tool/resync.py` now sits after `objdump` in the listing rule. Where a row straddles a
`.pdata` start, the bytes before the start become one `(bad)` row and the code is
decoded afresh from the start until a boundary agrees with the sweep. It fails rather
than guesses when the two do not agree within 256 bytes. It also fails when a second
start falls inside the fresh decode, and when any start in range is still off a
boundary at the end. On Starfield: 165 spliced, none left, and exactly the two
`vmovss` gained against the old listing's VEX set.

**`patch.disassemble` reads through the same filter**, for the original image and the
patched one. Both `verify` and `frontier` read their counts from it. Without the
filter, the first `verify` of the new build refused one lost boundary at
`0x1424bfb7b`: that address is a boundary only in the old out-of-step reading of the
original, and the patched bytes no longer decode to it. Through the filter, the
original reads **804,953 VEX** (two more, exactly the pair) and 164 undecodable
VEX-prefixed rows, 16 fewer, because those were artifacts of the same misreading. The
rebuilt image passes `verify`: `804,953 -> 292`, 804,661 removed. Its survivor roll
is the old one line for line, since the pair converts in place.

Only `.pdata` starts are trusted for this. A branch target can sit inside data that
merely decodes, and restarting there would manufacture the phantom instructions this
removes.

### Finding 346 -- what the 36 overlap survivors are, measured 2026-10-16

Measured by replaying `place_stubs` on the candidate list `frontier` hands it (the
`7bdaf976` build), logging `rescue_seat` and the chained `build_stub` at every placed
window that ends exactly on one of the 36. Every one of them is stranded the same way:
a neighbour's window ends on the site and the next window starts after it, so only
the rescue could take it, and the rescue does not.

- **29, all 256-bit: the passenger has a `unit` strategy.** `rescue_seat` takes a
  passenger with no strategy or a `spill` one, because `moved_instruction` lowers
  only the plain rules. These are the `vdivps`/`vmulps`/`vsubps` blocks around
  `0x142db9f76` and `0x142dcc161`, plus `0x14374e704` under a 93-byte run. Taking them
  means chaining unit lowerings into one window.
- **5, scalar: the seat is found and the extended stub refuses.** The reasons are
  `the window will not hold one borrow displacement` and `a displaced instruction
  will not move`: the passenger needs a borrow the extended window cannot give it.
  The five are `0x1406d6923`, `0x140d72ab6`, `0x1422d6ab0`, `0x142489c0f` and `0x1426cfe8b`.
- **2: the rescue is never asked.** `0x1426aeac1` and `0x1426aeb09` are both branch
  targets, sitting after a `jne`/`vmovaps`/`jmp` diamond whose join is also a branch
  target. Their only candidate widens backwards over the whole diamond, and the
  window before it took the `jne`.

So the 29 and the 5 are the unit-lowering and passenger-borrow work this tree has
stopped on, and the bucket holds no placement-order gain like Finding 345's.

**The 13 `lost to a refused stub` are the same two classes.** `build/stub-refused.txt`
lists 15 refused windows. 14 are `unit`, and their refusals name the span emission,
`no direct SSE form` or `the FMA would not lower`. The one plain window is the 51-byte
hammock at `0x142295d4f` that carries `0x142295d7e`. Each of its 13 instructions lowers
on its own under any internal-target map. Rebuilt with `emit_swallowed`'s reasons
exposed, it refuses at its `vmovss (%rax),%xmm0` passenger, which borrows xmm1: `the
window will not hold one borrow displacement`.

**And the 70 `next instruction is a branch target`.** These counts are from the
`7bdaf976` apply log, by the backward fallback's reason: 50 sites are themselves branch
targets, 11 follow an instruction that does not fall through (a `jmp`, or a `call`
whose return would land mid-window), and 13 have a predecessor that will not move. A
neighbour tally over the 102 `will not move` and these 70 together names what refuses:
- `vextractf128 $1,%ymm,%xmm`: 41 forward and 46 backward. Only span code lowers it.
- 256-bit `vmovups`: about 40 forward.
- Aliased scalars such as `vaddss %xmm4,%xmm9,%xmm4`, which need a scratch the passenger
  does not have. 9 forward, 20 backward.

`0x1411bf3d5`/`0x1411bf3d9` is the scalar shape: two aliased `vaddss` stranded between
a placed window and a branch target, each the other's only neighbour. None of this is
reachable without span lowering, passenger borrows or re-aimed outside branches.

`place_stubs` takes candidates in address order, and two can share an address: a
neighbour alone, and a short site widened backwards over that neighbour. Collection
order put the narrow one first, so the wide one -- which removes both -- was lost to
an overlap wherever the rescue could not seat the site. `0x1406f62fc` is the shape: a
`vmulps` between a `vbroadcastss` and an unaligned `vdpps (%rdx)`, the forward
neighbour refused by Finding 341's guard.

Sorting by address and then by window, widest first, measured on Starfield 2026-10-16:
294 -> 292 survivors, `lost to an overlap` 44 -> 36. The two gained are `0x1406f62fc`
and `0x142d8d67b`; the other six rows that moved are the same sites now tried and
refused rather than overlapped, which is why `refused` reads 15 against 11. No site
was lost: a wide window that will not build commits nothing, so the narrow one still
places. `verify` passes (1,425 stub RIP stores inside, 505 `OPEN` as before), and so do
`check`, `check-pe`, `check-shadow-pe` and `check-spill`. Nothing in the 36 that remain
was examined.

Run in the game 2026-10-16 (`7bdaf976`): the sixth reproduction of Finding 342's
stop, unchanged -- the null write at `0x1422CC4BE` with `rbp` zero, 156 s after the
image loaded, then the illegal instruction at `0x140D80AFD`. Neither gained site is
on that path, so the two are neither a fix nor a regression there.

### Finding 344 -- an A/B against the stack borrows, inconclusive so far

The zeroed `rbp` of Finding 342 is suspected of coming from a stub's stack save, and
the project already keeps the switches that compare binaries for exactly that:
`--shadow=off` takes the caller's 32-byte shadow away, `--fallback=off` the per-site
stack borrow. Built with both (`e7a6d007`, 2026-10-15), `verify` passes and 2,031 sites
survive against 294 -- 1,750 of them `no home space to borrow`. A null write at
`0x1422CC4BE` again would clear the borrows; getting past it would implicate them.

**The run, 2026-10-15, answered neither**: 47 seconds in it stopped on
`vsubss %xmm0,%xmm7,%xmm0` at `0x142BE520D`, a site this build left in place and the
default build lowers.

**Each switch alone, 2026-10-16:** `--fallback=off` leaves 1,535 and keeps
`0x142BE520D` as a survivor, so it cannot get further. `--shadow=off` leaves 327 --
33 more than the default, none of them that site -- and `verify` passes. It removes
the borrow the suspicion is about, a save placed in the caller's shadow space by
`rsp_depths`. **Its run, 2026-10-16, stopped 44 seconds in** on
`vmulps (%rax),%xmm1,%xmm6` at `0x142437E05`, one of its 33 extra survivors -- inconclusive
again, and the default build (`fcca7c16`) is back in the game directory.

**Whole-switch A/B has reached its limit here.** Every switch that removes a borrow also
leaves sites the default lowers, and the game reaches some of them on the way to 147
seconds. A conclusive comparison needs the borrow withheld only where it can be withheld
without a survivor -- a per-site control in the borrow code, which does not exist.

### Finding 343 -- what two survivor classes are made of, measured 2026-10-14

Read from the Finding 342 build's frontier (294 survivors), to choose the next lever.
Nothing in the code changed.

**`next instruction will not move`, 102 -- the largest class -- is a span problem, not
a placement one.** Of the 202 neighbours either side of these sites, 85 are
`vextractf128` and 73 a 256-bit `vmovups`, and the apply log's refusal reasons agree:
"no direct SSE form and not a sequence" 88 and "the swallowed neighbour is 256-bit, and
only the span emission lowers one" 77. Typically the site sits between two neighbours
that each got a one-instruction window of their own (`0x1404a572a`), so neither
widening has anywhere to go. Lowering a 256-bit neighbour as a passenger needs the slot
machinery, so this class belongs to the shadow-register work.

**`outside .pdata`, 30, is mostly code nothing is known to enter.** A read-only scratch
audit (outside.py's own `chunks`, `split_refused` and `classify`, against the report
mode's `known` set) puts the sites in eleven chunks:

    uncalled, ends in ret       0x1407c7570, 0x1407c7590 (12 sites) -- no call, jump,
                                lea or relocation names them; packed after a ret
    called, runs off the end    0x140732160, 0x140e43c7e/c94/c99, 0x1413fcbf0,
                                0x14234c563 -- the piece ends at a cut, not a transfer
    accepted by the report      0x1414c3ce0, 0x1422cf7a0 -- refused in `collect`, whose
                                recut uses entries and outside jumps (Finding 338)
    contains (bad)              0x1422cf7ed

The twelve uncalled sites can execute only if something reaches them by an address no
table records. Treating them as code would widen the oracle on no positive evidence,
which is the trade `leaf_ranges` refuses. At 30 sites the class does not justify that.

### Finding 342 -- a GPR mover's RIP store landed one slot load past its target

**Found by the store audit of Finding 341** (every stub store against the stores of the
instructions its window replaced): after setting aside 57,162 stack stores that the same
stub reloads -- borrowed-register saves -- 179 stores
were left, all `mov %rax,disp(%rip)` writing the upper half of a 32-byte store to a
global, each 7 bytes past its target:

    original  vmovups %ymm0,0x145fafde8         upper half at ...df8 and ...e00
    stub      mov %rax,...  # 0x145fafdff        and ...e07

`gpr_move_half` emits a store as the slot load and then the memory store, and handed
`encode_mem64` the pair's start as the store's position; a RIP displacement is
measured from the end of its own instruction, so every such store landed one slot load
(7 bytes) high, over the next variable. The memory side is placed where it is emitted
now. It is silent corruption of program data and a candidate cause of the zeroed frame
pointer above -- **not established**; the next Steam run of this build says.

Gates, `check-vex` and `verify` pass on the build, and the store audit of it finds no
unexplained store: the 179 moved into "inside an original store", 70,293 -> 70,472.
It is the build in the game directory, and **its Steam run, 2026-10-14, ended exactly as
before** -- the null write at `0x1422CC4BE` 147 seconds in, then the survivor at
`0x140D80AFD` -- so this was not what zeroed the frame pointer. That stays open.

**~~The stack stores are ruled out~~ -- they are not.** A borrowed-register save
reloads the REGISTER afterwards and leaves the stack slot holding the register's value,
so each of those 57,162 stores changes memory permanently and is safe only where the
slot is dead. Classified by the function's own unwind data (scratch script, not in the
tree): 35,797 land in the outgoing home area of a function that makes calls, past its
prologue -- dead between calls; **571 are in a window inside the prologue and 3,493 in
a function that makes no call**, where the slot may be a pushed register or a live
local; 17,295 are in chained entries and 6 outside `.pdata`, unclassified. A save at
the top of the stack after `push %rbp` and before the frame is allocated would put an
xmm register's low bytes where `pop %rbp` reads them -- the zeroed-`rbp` shape. The
twelve direct callees of the crashing caller were checked and none has such a store;
deeper callees were not. Separately, no stub writes `rbp` more often than its window's
originals (49 windows checked). **The 571 and 3,493 are the next thing to check**, and probably
weaker than they look: `window_borrow` places a save in the caller's 32-byte shadow
space by the `rsp` depth `rsp_depths` models at every instruction, prologue included,
and refuses a function that references that region itself or copies `rsp` toward it.
The audit compared offsets against the frame after the prologue only, so it cannot
see what the depth model already accounts for. Check a sample of the 571 against
`rsp_depths` before treating them as a cause.

**`ripstore`, in `check-pe`, is the fixture**: `noxmm` with both memory sides
RIP-relative, every volatile xmm live across a load and a store kept apart by integer
filler, and a `guard` after `sink` that the misplaced half would overwrite. It returns
77; built by a copy of `detour.py` with the fix reverted it returns 12, and `verify`
fails it with one stray RIP store, where the fixed build passes with 3. It is not in
`check-shadow-pe`, because `--shadow-regs=off` carries it correctly by the `run`
lowering and that gate requires `off` to fail.

**`verify` now checks the class**: every RIP-relative store in a stub (`rip_store`
reads target and width from objdump's text) must lie inside a RIP store among the
instructions its window replaced, mapped through `placed`'s stub ranges. Against the
pre-fix image it fails naming exactly the 179; against the committed build it passes,
1,425 stub RIP stores all inside; `check-verify` passes on all 49 fixtures.

### Finding 341 -- legacy SSE needs a 16-byte operand aligned, and VEX did not (step 1 of 2)

**Step 1 is committed and is the build in the game directory.** Selftest, the three
gates and `check-vex` pass; on Starfield `verify` passes with 6,262 RIP operands that
need alignment all aligned, no hazard at any in-place site, and **678 stub instructions
`OPEN`** -- the 256-bit emitters, first `0x1489b9b8d mulps 0xf0(%rbp),%xmm0`. Survivors
286 -> 294 (289 real). Step 2 below is what the next session picks up.

**The control for step 1 is the fixture, not `verify`.** `verify` cannot tell from an
image's bytes which emitter wrote a stub instruction, so a hazard in a `lower_vex` stub
is counted `OPEN` like a 256-bit half, and `verify` passes the `--align-guard=off`
`unaligned` image. Running it is what discriminates: 77 against 5. `verify`
discriminates again once step 2 makes `OPEN` a failure. Its in-place half skips sites
inside a placed window: a window's jump at `0x141d5c2b6` put `0f ef 06` at the next
site, read as `pxor (%rsi)`, a false hazard.

The 286 build (Finding 340) ran 158 seconds, the longest yet, and died in a stub at
`0x148BC1982` on `EXCEPTION_ACCESS_VIOLATION` reading `0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF` -- a #GP:

    original  1418ed680  vmulps -0x8(%rax),%xmm2,%xmm1     any address
    stub      148bc1982  mulps  -0x8(%rax),%xmm1           16-byte aligned only
              rax = 0xa09ef3a0, so the operand is at ...398
