**Nothing in the rewriter asked whether the program's own memory operands are aligned**
-- only its slots (Finding 152). A census of the shipped image, alignment-requiring
legacy forms whose original was VEX, excluding `movaps`/`movdqa` and the non-temporals
whose VEX forms required alignment already:

    in place  pointer        663     stub  pointer        3,300
    in place  rsp, %16==0      7     stub  rsp, %16==0      593
    in place  rip, aligned    87     stub  rip, aligned   6,175
    rip, unaligned: none

**Step 1, in the working tree.** `patch.ALIGNMENT_FREE` lists, by (map, pp, opcode), the
legacy forms whose memory operand needs no alignment; `needs_alignment` is the rest.
`sse_encoding(..., guarded=True)` refuses such a form with a non-RIP operand, and only
the two callers with a fallback ask: the in-place pass, whose site becomes a detour,
and `lower_vex`, which loads with `movups` into the scratch -- or into the destination
for an exactly commutative op, `EXACTLY_COMMUTATIVE` -- and runs the op register to
register (`unaligned_split`). `collect` asks the liveness scan for a scratch for such a
site. `verify` reads the image's bytes (`alignment_hazard`, objdump `-w`): an in-place
hazard or an unaligned RIP target fails; stub hazards print as `OPEN`, counted.
`--align-guard=off` restores the old encoder. Fixture `unaligned` in `check-pe`: 77
rewritten, 5 (the #GP) with `--align-guard=off`, 29 original; `verify` fails the `off`
image naming both `mulps`.

**Guarding every caller was tried first and is the wrong order**: the 256-bit emitters
write `op mem,xmm` halves through `narrow_piece` (about twenty callers) with no scratch,
so they refused, 207 sites came back as survivors -- 256-bit arithmetic, `vmulps`,
`vaddps`, `vandps`, `vsubps`, `vpaddq` -- and `splatop`, `permilps` and `pshufb1`
failed. The vzeroupper's `nopl (%rax)` was a false positive in the first check; `0F
18`-`0F 1F` are excluded.

**The step-1 build ran through Steam on 2026-10-14 for about 470 seconds**, three times
the longest before, and no alignment fault recurred. It ended on a survivor at
`0x140D80AFD`, a 4-byte `vmulss` filed `next instruction is a branch target`: it and the
instruction after it are both entered by jumps from elsewhere in the function
(`0x140d80bad`, `0x140d80bc7` and `0x140d809bc`, `0x140d809d1`), so neither a widened
window nor Finding 336's hammock can take it. One second earlier the main thread took
a first-chance access violation in unmodified code, `mov %rdx,(%rcx)` at
`0x1422CC4BE` with `rcx = 0x88` -- a member of a null object -- which the game
survived; whether it is the game's own or a wrong value from the rewrite upstream is
not established.

**The null write is not the game's own: a frame pointer came back zero.** Measured on a
second run, 2026-10-14, the same pair 162 seconds in. The caller at `0x141e8c098`
passes `lea 0x88(%rbp),%rcx`, and `rbp` is its frame pointer, set once at
`0x141e8bd4f` from `rax - 0x78` and never written again in the function -- so a
callee returned with `rbp` zero. None of the sixteen backtrace frames is in the stub
section, and the one stub the function itself enters (`0x148c7c17a`) does not touch
`rbp`. The stub section holds about forty instructions that write `rbp`; they look like
moved originals (`pextrq $1,%xmm0,%rbp`), and checking each against its site is the
next step. **This was the corruption lead, and Finding 348 explains it:** a borrow wrote into a
split function's shadow over its saved `rbp`. Whether the game gets past it is for
the next run to say. What follows is the search as it went. First place
to look: `0x140f14380`, the last call before the bad one, whose stubs store to
`(%rsp)` -- compare each against its original instruction. Reproduced on a third run
2026-10-14, 96 seconds in, a fourth at 142, and a fifth 2026-10-15 at 147 on the same `fcca7c16` build -- the
null write with `rbp` zero, then `0x140D80AFD` on another thread half a second later.

**That callee looks innocent, by an audit of every stub's stores** (a scratch script,
not in the tree): each store a stub makes to program memory, against the stores of the
instructions its window replaced, resolving RIP targets and setting aside slot storage.
On the committed build: 70,292 inside an original store, 42,696 own storage, 57,328
not -- of which 46,502 are `(%rsp)` and 10,647 `disp(%rsp)`, the borrowed-register save
area, and 179 RIP. The four in `0x140f14380` are `movups %xmmN,(%rsp)` after its
`push %rdi; sub $0x20,%rsp`, inside its own outgoing home space and clear of the `rbx`
it saved at `0x10(%rsp)` on entry. So the zeroed `rbp` comes from deeper, and the
question to ask of those 57,000 is which ones fall outside the frame their function
has allocated at that point -- a frameless leaf, or a window before the prologue ends.

**What the 678 are, measured on the committed build 2026-10-13** (`alignment_hazard`
over `objdump -w` of `.avxsse`): `mulps` 218, `addps` 201, `subps` 72, `andps` 52,
`paddq` 32, `mulpd` 25, `addpd` 21, `addsubps` 14, `blendvps` 12, `pcmpeqb` 12. By
base: `r11` 272, `rcx` 184, `rax` 65, `r8` 36, `rbp`/`rsp`/`rbx` 18 each, `rdi` 16.
**Most of the `r11` ones are the stubs' own slots**, `0x32a0(%r11)` onwards at
offsets that are multiples of 16: the TLS template declares 16-byte alignment and the
slot sits at a 16-byte offset, so they are aligned wherever the loader honours that --
a heap allocation on x64 does. `verify` cannot see that from one instruction; the
emitter knows it is addressing a slot and should say so, or move it with `movups`
as Finding 152 did for the stack. The other ~400 are the program's data through
`rcx`, `rax` and the rest, and are the real exposure.

**Half of the ~400 program-data hazards are one shape, measured 2026-10-14**: the unit
lowering's memory form, 205 of 398 with a slot move beside them --

    movaps %xmm4,%xmm0;  mulps 0xf0(%rbp),%xmm0       low:  dst = src1 op mem
    movups 0x32e0(%r11),%xmm6;  mulps 0x100(%rbp),%xmm6   high: helper = slot op mem+16

The low half can load `mem` into the helper, which is free until the high half. The
high half needs a second register: either do it FIRST, borrowing the low destination
to hold `mem+16` (sound only where that destination is not also src1, whose low half
must survive), or have the unit strategy find a second dead xmm and refuse without
one. That is the design to build; it was not started.

**Step 2's first part landed 2026-10-14: the unit lowering's `lane` and `lanemem`.**
`narrow_piece` takes a `scratch`; given one, a half legacy SSE needs aligned goes
through `unaligned_split`. The low half passes the helper, free until the upper half;
the upper half passes `second_helper`, which the unit already takes when two xmm are
dead, and without one emits as before. `OPEN` fell 678 -> 505 with no survivor added
(294). Fixture `unaligned256` in `check-shadow-pe`: 77, 5 with `--align-guard=off`,
29 with `--shadow-regs=off`. The first remaining hazard is an upper half with no
second helper, `mulps 0x100(%rbp),%xmm6` at `0x1489b9b9f`.

**The 505 that remain** include the ~270 slot operands through `r11` above, which a TLS
block the loader aligns makes safe; the rest are upper halves with one helper and the
other 256-bit emitters.

**Step 2, rest open: the other 256-bit emitters.** Give `narrow_piece`'s callers the same
`movups` fallback -- they have helper registers (span/unit pools) but `narrow_piece`
is not told one -- then make `verify`'s `OPEN` line a failure. The census says up to
3,300 pointer and 593 stack operands in stubs; how many come from the 256-bit paths
is unmeasured. Until then those faults stay possible wherever the game's data is
not aligned.

### Finding 340 -- the stale-read repair is off by default, on the holder's decision

The 636 build ran through Steam on 2026-10-12 for 123 seconds, the longest run yet, and
every illegal instruction in it was the one site, `0x14374DCDC`, on nine threads.
Finding 339 had measured what withholding writers for a surviving reader costs. **The
holder decided on 2026-10-13 that `--stale-repair=off` is the default**: the image is
for machines without AVX, where such a reader faults before it reads. The image stops
being right on an AVX machine wherever a reader survives, and `--stale-repair=on`
restores that.

The default image is Finding 339's `off` measurement: **281 real instructions left of
804,946**, 286 by `verify`'s count with the five table rows.

Two controls test the repair itself and now ask for it: `staleupper`, which breaks the
image, and `conservative`, which breaks the code. Under the new default the second
passed `verify`, correctly, because there was no longer anything to catch.

**And a Makefile hazard surfaced on the way.** `check-pe` built `sse-regioncarry.exe`
under `--shadow-regs=off` to prove the region strategy places, overwriting the fixture
`check-verify` reads under the default. Any edit to `tool/detour.py` rebuilt it before
the next `check`, so it never showed; a Makefile-only edit did not, and `check-verify`
failed on six boundaries and a clobbered register in an image built under other flags.
The region check writes `sse-regioncarry-off.exe` now, and a second `make check` after
`check-pe` passes.

### Finding 339 -- the stale-read repair costs 350 sites on the machines this is for

The 636 build's last run died at `0x14374DCDC`, `kept: its window was withheld`, whose
blame chain ends at a `vcmpgt_oqpd` with no SSE form (Finding 338). Every reader
`stale_upper_reads` reports is a surviving 256-bit VEX instruction -- 256-bit sites are
never patched in place, so a reader outside every placed window is VEX by construction.
On a machine without AVX such a reader faults before it reads anything, so the stale
value it would have read is never observed there. The repair keeps the image right on
an AVX machine, and on the machines this project is for each withheld writer is only one
more site that faults, earlier.

`--stale-repair=off` measures it. `stale_upper_reads` reports nothing, so the repair
loop withholds nothing, `apply` reverts no in-place patch for it, and `verify` says that
it did not check rather than passing quietly. Measured on 2026-10-12 over the same
listing:

                                         on      off
    VEX in .text                        636      286
      kept: its window was withheld     358        0
      kept: a repair left it in VEX       8        0
    detours                         202,365  202,382

Both include Finding 337's five table rows, so `off` leaves 281 real instructions of
804,946 -- 99.97%. Every other `verify` check passes on the `off` image, and the
game's fatal site is rewritten in it.

**The default stayed `on`, and changing it was the holder's decision** -- taken in
Finding 340: it gives up
correctness on an AVX machine, which Finding 333 called "the price of not writing wrong
bytes". `off` is the better image for a CPU without AVX and the worse one anywhere
else.

### Finding 338 -- a leaf function is cut only at an entry, and ends at its switch table

The 685 build of Finding 337 ran through Steam on 2026-10-12 and stopped 79 seconds in
on `EXCEPTION_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION` at `0x14087DA4D`, a `vmovss` filed `declined: outside
.pdata`. Its function is a setter with no unwind data, reached through a vtable at file
offset `0x4b50c68`:

    14087da40  mov    0x8(%rcx),%rdx
    14087da47  cmpb   $0x0,0x44(%rdx)
    14087da4b  jne    14087da5e               over its own store
    14087da4d  vmovss 0x56150bb(%rip),%xmm0   the fault
    14087da55  vmovss %xmm0,0x40(%rdx)
    14087da5e  ...

**`split_refused` cut it at its own `jne`'s target.** A refused chunk is recut at every
known address (Finding 313), so the piece from `0x14087da40` ended at the conditional
jump and was refused; the docstring called that the right direction to be wrong in, and
the game reached it. `split_refused` now takes `entries` -- `INDIRECT_TARGETS` plus every
direct call's destination -- and cuts at a known address only when it is one of those or
a jump from outside the chunk reaches it. That cuts less and never more, so every piece
still starts at an entry and is held to the same strict conditions.

That build ran 73 seconds and met two more setters of the same family, at `0x14087DB47`
and `0x14087D7AE`, each dispatching through a switch whose table follows it. Since
Finding 337 the table's rows are `(bad)`, so the last piece ran into them and was
refused for holding data. `chunks` now takes the resolved table rows as `data` and ends
a chunk at them as at `int3`; and a trailing `nop` -- the table's alignment -- is no
longer what "ends in a transfer" reads, since padding is not where a function ends.
`outside.control` checks each rule on the game's shapes and fails with any of them
removed. `--leaf-entries=off` restores the old oracle.

    VEX in .text                       685 ->  636
      outside .pdata                    74 ->   30

636 includes Finding 337's five table rows: 631 real instructions left of 804,946.
Fourteen sites the first cut rule refused, among them `0x1402b2c42`, came back with the
table rule; why cutting less had refused them was not established.

The same run's fatal fault was elsewhere: seven threads at `0x14374DCDC`, a 256-bit
`vperm2f128` at the entry of a packed-double math routine, `kept: its window was
withheld`. Its blame chain ends at the `vcmpgt_oqpd` at `0x14374eb63`, which has no SSE
form. **Whether to keep withholding writers for a reader that faults anyway is the
holder's question**: the repair exists so the image stays right on an AVX machine
(Finding 333's "the price of not writing wrong bytes"), and on a machine without AVX a
withheld writer is only one more site that faults. The withheld class is 358.

### Finding 337 -- a switch table that decodes as VEX is data, and was being rewritten

The 677 build of Finding 336 ran through Steam on 2026-10-11 and stopped about 95 seconds
in, twice, identically: two and then three worker threads took
`EXCEPTION_ACCESS_VIOLATION` on executing `0x2137919E9`, an address outside the image,
with `rdx` holding the same value. The 805 and 880 builds had stopped on survivors before
reaching this point, so it is older than Finding 336 rather than caused by it -- a build
with `--hammock=off` stopped 54 seconds in on the survivor at `0x140D3672E` that 336
removes, which is why that build could not answer the question.

The second run's backtrace named the dispatch:

    140d355af  movzbl 0xd35718(%rax,%r13,1),%eax     r13 = __ImageBase
    140d355b8  mov    0xd35710(%r13,%rax,4),%edx
    140d355c0  add    %r13,%rdx
    140d355c3  jmp    *%rdx

and the table it reads had been rewritten:

    original   140d35710  c5 55 d3 00  fc 55 d3 00     RVAs 0xd355c5, 0xd355fc
    rewritten  140d35710  e9 19 79 d3  07 55 d3 00     a detour's jmp rel32

`c5 55 d3 00` is a valid VEX.256 `vpsrlq (%rax),%ymm5,%ymm8`, and a window was placed
over it with the `cld` after it as a passenger. `0x140000000 + 0xd37919e9` is the fault.

**Every data guard was keyed on `(bad)`.** Finding 225's islands cluster what objdump
refused, so a table that decodes end to end is in no population -- which `verify`'s own
comment on the island check said. `switch_targets` had read this exact table since
Finding 174 to block its targets, and never kept its bytes. It now records every table it
reads in `SWITCH_DATA`: the dword table over its entries, and the byte table a two-level
dispatch reads first (`switch_index`), bounded by the dispatch's `cmp` and cut at the
first byte that is not a valid slot. `switch_data_rows` turns the rows overlapping them
into `(bad)`, so the candidate loop, passengers and `verify` refuse them as they refuse
any island; the in-place patches, which `build_patches` reads from the listing directly,
are filtered by span. `data_islands` adds the tables as exact spans rather than
clustering their rows: the first build clustered them with the 256-byte gap and swept in
real code between neighbouring tables, and `verify` failed on four islands holding
correct in-place patches. The slot cut exists because the first version's 256-byte
fallback, taken where no `cmp` is found, ran the table at `0x141823748` into the next
function's prologue and kept three real VEX instructions as data.

`verify` checks that no byte of any table changed. **Against the 677 build it fails**,
naming 4 tables, first `0x140c55714`; against this one it passes, 2,383 spans. Five rows
the listing counted as VEX instructions are table bytes -- `0x140c55716`, `0x140d35710`
and Finding 225's `vphsubd` pool at `0x142c4079a` -- so the denominator is 804,946, not
804,951. `--switch-guard=off` restores the old behaviour. There is no PE fixture: a
table entry that decodes as a lowerable VEX instruction needs an RVA whose third byte is
a VEX opcode, which puts the target past 1 MB; the control is the game build above.

**677 -> 685 survivors** by `verify`'s count over the same listing, five of which are the
table bytes above: 680 real instructions left of 804,946. The 202,359 detours and
520,334 in-place patches are against 202,363 and 520,338.

### Finding 336 -- a window may hold branch targets that only its own branches reach

The 805 build of Finding 335 ran through Steam on 2026-10-10 and stopped 61 seconds in,
on a worker thread, on `EXCEPTION_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION` at `0x140D3672E` -- a survivor
filed `declined: next instruction is a branch target`:

    140d36726  jbe    72e
    140d36728  vsubss %xmm4,%xmm7,%xmm0       one arm, then jmp 732
    140d3672c  jmp    732
    140d3672e  vsubss %xmm7,%xmm4,%xmm0       the other arm -- the fault
    140d36732  vcomiss %xmm3,%xmm0            the join

An absolute difference. The site is four bytes and a Class C lowering wants seven, so it
needs a detour; it is the `jbe`'s target so it cannot be swallowed backward, and the
join after it is the `jmp`'s target so it cannot widen forward. **200 of the 805
survivors were this class**, the largest left, and Finding 331's `jmp rel8` reaches only
where `int3` padding is within 127 bytes -- here it is 286 away.

**The branch into the site comes from six bytes above it.** A window may hold a target
when every way into it is a direct branch from inside the same window: the stub
re-emits those branches aimed at its own copy of the target, and the original bytes,
padding now, are reached by nothing. Measured before building: of the 200, 159 have
every branch into the site within 64 bytes and none of them a call.

`hammock_window` walks back from the site until every branch target strictly inside the
window, the site included, is reached only from inside it and the window holds five
bytes. It ends at the site, so the join stays outside. A target that is also reached
INDIRECTLY -- a relocation, `.pdata`, exception data, a switch table, an address taken
by `lea` -- is refused, since a table cannot be re-aimed; `analysis_context` now keeps
those apart as `INDIRECT_TARGETS`, where `blocked` had merged them with the direct ones.
`build_stub` emits the swallowed instructions twice: once to learn where each lands,
then with every branch to a held target aimed at that label. Lengths are
position-independent -- a re-aimed branch is always rel32 -- and the second pass is held
to the first's rather than trusted to it. Earliest-start placement lets the hammock win
over the other arm's own window, which it contains; that arm is lowered inside it.

The game's site becomes one window from `726` to `732`:

    jbe    <stub copy of 72e>
    movaps %xmm7,%xmm0; subss %xmm4,%xmm0; jmp 732
    movaps %xmm4,%xmm0; subss %xmm7,%xmm0; jmp 732

**`verify` asks both halves of the claim of the output.** A held target is excused from
"still begins an instruction" and from "lands inside a placed window" only where the
listing, read again in `verify`, shows every branch naming it inside that window and it
is not indirect. And a new check reads the stub section: no branch there may land
inside a placed window past its jump -- which is what a branch moved and not re-aimed
does. With the re-aim removed the `hammock` fixture returns 5 rather than 77, silently,
and that check fails naming `140004030 -> 0x140001022`; nothing else in `verify` did.

**`hammock`**, in `check-pe`, is the absolute difference with the sandwiched arm taken:
29 original, 77 rewritten, 29 with `--hammock=off`.

**805 -> 677.** 128 short sites took a hammock and 137 could not:

      an instruction it would swallow will not move      110
      a target it would hold is reached indirectly        12
      the branches in are out of reach                    11
      a target it would hold is reached from after it      4

`declined: next instruction is a branch target` falls 200 -> 71. The 110 are the next
lever and the same walls as everywhere else -- a swallowed 256-bit neighbour, which only
the span emission lowers, and aliased forms with no scratch. `make detour-verify` passes
on the 677 build with 154 targets held, and the compare audit of Finding 334 is clean.

### Finding 335 -- where only some paths zero an upper half, the writer clears the slot

The 880 build of Finding 334 ran through Steam on 2026-10-10 and stopped 45 seconds in
on `EXCEPTION_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION` at `0x1424E3B5B` -- not a wrong byte this time but a
survivor, `kept: a repair left it in VEX form`:

    1424e3b35  vmovups 0x20(%rax,%rcx),%ymm0     one path loads all 256 bits
    1424e3b55  jmp 1424e3b5f                     and skips the zeroing
    1424e3b57  mov 0x70(%rsp),%edx               a branch target
    1424e3b5b  vxorps %xmm0,%xmm0,%xmm0          the other zeroes them -- the fault
    1424e3b5f  vmovups %ymm0,0x0(%rbp)           a branch target, reading both

**Finding 333 refused the store and the repair did the rest.** The store reads ymm0's
slot, and no constant written at the store is right when one path brings a loaded value
and the other a zero, so 333 refused it as `an upper half zeroed on some paths only`.
The store then survived as VEX, a surviving 256-bit reader needs the machine upper half
really zeroed, and the repair kept the `vxorps` as VEX for its sake. That pairing is
what 333's 78 sites were, and the game reached one of them.

**So the clear moves to the writer, which is the only place that knows which path ran.**
`zeroed_uppers` now returns the VEX.128 writers behind each partial field --
`CLEARING_WRITERS`, 24 writers behind 25 readers here: 7 zeroing idioms, 13 register
copies like `vmovdqu %xmm0,%xmm2`, and scalars. Such a writer is not patched in place,
since four bytes have no room for a clear; it is offered only as a `narrow` member of a
unit window, which stands the block up exactly as for a 256-bit site and emits the
lowered write followed by `span_slot_zero`. Taken as a plain passenger anywhere else it
is refused in `moved_instruction`, because a passenger is emitted without the clear. A
writer that places nowhere stays VEX and faults where it stands -- it never leaves a slot
wrong. The reader's refusal goes, since every path now leaves the slot right.
`--writer-clears=off` restores Finding 333's behaviour.

The game's site is `[b57, b5f)` widened back over the `mov`, which starting on a branch
target is allowed because the target becomes the jump:

    148d05965  mov    0x70(%rsp),%edx
    148d05969  mov    %gs:0x58,%r11
    148d05972  mov    0x5a5a5a5a(%r11),%r11      the index, filled by the callback
    148d05979  xorps  %xmm0,%xmm0
    148d0597c  movq   $0x0,0x32a0(%r11)          ymm0's slot
    148d05987  movq   $0x0,0x32a8(%r11)
    148d05992  jmp    0x1424e3b5f

**`partslot`**, in `check-shadow-pe`, is the shape with the zeroing on the path taken:
77 with the writer clearing, 29 with `--writer-clears=off` (the store left as VEX and
faulting), 29 with `--shadow-regs=off`.

**880 -> 805**, of the 78 Finding 333 cost:

      kept: a repair left it in VEX form              24 ->   8
      declined: ymm value has no known upper half     15 ->   2
      kept: its window was withheld                  397 -> 358
      declined: 256-bit: arithmetic rather than a copy  34 -> 25
      declined: a slot-clearing writer would not place   0 ->   1

Five writers stay VEX: the `vminss` above, and four `vmovdqu` register copies at
`0x1434d8...` whose windows were withheld. Each was patched in place before and is a
survivor now, where its reader was the survivor before -- a writer runs on one path and
its reader on all of them, so the exposure shrank rather than moved. The 8 left as
`a repair left it in VEX form` are the same mechanism for a different reason and are
the next sites a run would meet.

`make detour-verify` passes on the 805 build, and the compare audit of Finding 334 is
clean on it: 0 of 25,929 RIP operands outside the image, every `cmp` one of the eight
named predicates.

### Finding 334 -- a compare's predicate is in the mnemonic, and three emitters lost it

The 830 build of Finding 333 ran through Steam on 2026-10-09, past the allocator hang,
and faulted 46 seconds in: `Unhandled page fault on read access to 0000000104895590 at
address 0000000148D92303`, on the main thread, in `.avxsse`. The stub there held

    original  c5 f8 c2 1d 85 b2 11 02 04   vcmpneqps 0x211b285(%rip),%xmm0,%xmm3
    stub      0f c2 1d 85 32 b0 bb fd      cmpps $0xfd,-0x444fcd7b(%rip),%xmm3

-- the old displacement's first byte, then the new displacement written one byte late,
over the predicate. **objdump folds a compare's predicate into the mnemonic**, so
`vcmpneqps` has no `$` in its operands, and `lower_vex` decided whether an immediate
followed the RIP field by looking for one in the text. It wrote the displacement over
the last four bytes. **507 stubs** in that binary pointed outside the image this way:
366 `cmpps`, 140 `cmpss`, 1 `cmpsd` -- every RIP-relative compare `lower_vex` moved.

Checking the rebuilt stubs for predicates above seven found the second: `cmpps $0x41`
and `$0x44`, which are no predicate at all. `lanereg3`, `lanereg`, `lanealias` and
`lanemove` rebuilt their tails as opcode and modrm, dropping the imm8 after it, so the
CPU took the next instruction's REX as the predicate and that instruction lost it --
`movups 0x32d0(%r11)` ran as `0x32d0(%rbx)`. **49 stubs.** `vcmpltps %ymm2,%ymm0,%ymm1`
reaches `lanereg3` rather than `immreg3` for the same reason: no `$`.

With the predicate kept, the third: 8 stubs carried `$0x1e`, GT_OQ. SSE `0F C2` reads
imm8[2:0] and calls the rest reserved, so it ran as NLE -- **true on a NaN where GT is
false**, a wrong mask rather than a fault. `has_direct_sse_form` refuses VEX-only
predicates by mnemonic, but only `lower_vex` asks it; the span paths narrow each half
and call `sse_encoding` directly. The guard is there now: 16-23 are 0-7 with the QNaN
signalling flipped and the same mask, so they become imm8 & 7 (16 stubs, `$0x12` and
`$0x16`); 8-15 and 24-31 are refused.

**Each one was invisible to every check in the tree** for the reason Finding 303 met
from the other side: the fixtures that carried a compare predicate (`cmpconst`) took it
through `narrow_piece`, which Finding 303 had fixed, and no fixture put one through the
other three routes. Three now do -- `cmpimm` in `check-pe` (a 128-bit RIP compare into
a stub: 29 original, 77 rewritten, and the old rewriter emits `cmpunordps` against
`0x13fd01d63`), `cmpreg` in `check-shadow-pe` (the register form: 29 off, 77 with
slots, and the old one emits `$0x41`), and `REFUSED_PREDICATES` in `lowering_cases.py`,
asked of `sse_encoding` because the first version asked `lower_vex`, which refused them
by name, and passed with the guard removed.

**The price is 50 sites, 830 -> 880**, and it is the third guard only: the first two
fix bytes and refuse nothing. Frontier against Finding 333's build:

      kept: its window was withheld                 356 -> 397
      declined: 256-bit: arithmetic rather than a copy  26 -> 34
      lost to a refused stub                         16 -> 17

The four GT_OQ sites are refused and the rest is the sign rule cascading from them
through the repair. A compare SSE cannot express is the operand-exchanged form in
`lower.py`; carrying that into the span paths would win them back, and is not built.

**Measured on the rebuild, every `cmp` in `.avxsse` now decodes as one of the eight
named predicates** -- 4,023, none with an explicit `$`, none of 25,926 RIP operands
outside the image -- and `make detour-verify` passes. `check-vex`, run because
`lower_vex` changed: 2,387 comparisons, 0 unexplained.

### Finding 333 -- a VEX.128 zeroing patched in place left the slot stale, and the game hung on it

Run through Steam on 2026-10-09, at the copyright holder's request, the 752-site build
passed the presence check that held Finding 323's run, loaded 50 DLLs and raised no
exception -- then stopped: one thread, 0.56 s of CPU, asleep in a futex for thirteen
minutes. Its Windows stack, read out of `/proc/<pid>/mem`, waits in `WaitOnAddress`
under `0x140323460`, a spin lock the allocator takes at `0x1422d161a`. **A wait with no
other thread in the process is a lock nobody will ever release**, so the question was
what had written the lock word, not who held it.

The allocator is the function the original dies in, and the first thing past the
original's fault is this:

    1422d2bf4  vpxor   %xmm0,%xmm0,%xmm0      all 256 bits of ymm0
    1422d2bf8  vmovdqu %ymm0,-0x51(%rbp)       32 zero bytes over a local

Rewritten, the `vpxor` is `pxor` in place and the store is a `unit` stub that takes its
upper sixteen bytes from ymm0's permanent slot. **The slot held `0x149518590` and
`0x209370000`** -- read from the frozen process, the last 256-bit value anything wrote
to ymm0 -- so the store put two pointers where the original put zeros.

`unit_candidate`'s own docstring names the hole: "one VEX.128 write left in place
zeroes a machine upper half while the slot keeps the old value". `stale_upper_reads`
never sees it, because it asks only about readers that SURVIVE; a reader inside a
window takes its upper half from the slot, and no in-place patch writes a slot.

    lowered 256-bit upper-half reads                       25,124
      every path in through a VEX.128 write                11,088
      some paths only                                          20
      producers that are the xor zeroing idiom             11,076

**The fix is at the reader, where the zero is known.** `zeroed_uppers` asks
`reaching_definitions` for every 256-bit site once, in `collect`; where every path
arrives through a VEX.128 write the upper half is zero, and `lower_ymm_span` writes
sixteen zero bytes into that slot before the member reads it -- two immediate stores,
no register, and the slot is right again for every reader after. Where only some paths
arrive that way no constant is right, and the member is refused, so the site falls to
the repair that already handles a surviving reader.

**A compare is not a write, and the first version said it was.** `reaching_definitions`
stops at `vcomiss %xmm0,%xmm0` as though it wrote xmm0, and the fix refused that reader
-- which killed `regioncarry`'s region in `check-pe`. Such a field is now left exactly
as before.

`staleslot` is the shape, taken from the site: a poisoned 256-bit load above a branch
target, then `vpxor` and a 32-byte store. **167 without the fix -- 77 plus the poison
byte -- and 77 with it**; 29 under `--shadow-regs=off`, which leaves the load VEX.

    VEX in .text                                    752 ->  830    +78
      kept: its window was withheld                 313 ->  356
      kept: a repair left it in VEX form             11 ->   24
      declined: ymm value has no known upper half     0 ->   15
      declined: 256-bit: arithmetic rather than a copy  17 -> 26

**Seventy-eight sites are the price of not writing wrong bytes, and that is the right
trade** -- Finding 335 has since won back 75 of them by clearing the slot at the writer. A survivor faults where it stands; a wrong store corrupts something that fails
later, somewhere else, with nothing pointing back. The refusals are the 20 partial-path
reads and what the repair withheld around them, by the sign rule.

**What this does not cover.** A lowered read after `vzeroupper` takes the slot where
the original reads zero; `vzeroupper` is lowered to nothing and `reaching_definitions`
walks past it. A straight-line count says at most 153, and the one read checked is a
false positive -- the `vzeroupper` was on a path that never reached the read -- so the
real number is unmeasured. The 195 reads `reaching_definitions` cannot resolve are
untouched too.

Finding 320 named a block-layout change -- a scratch area above the sixteen permanent

    vcvtph2ps / vcvtps2ph has no legacy encoding      24   F16C, measured negative
    vpermd has no legacy encoding                      6   cross-lane
    too short to place                                10   next a branch target,
                                                           transfers control, or a
                                                           neighbour with no legacy form
    window outside .pdata                              2
    shape a register-to-register move                  2

The stash refusals exist only when the member-taking back-widening is in -- 22 under
Finding 325's A+B -- and that widening alone is neutral to the site (Finding 330). So
the layout change buys a resource nothing in the default build is short of. **Not
built.** It becomes worth pricing again only alongside a change that makes stash demand
appear and pays for it.

**And what stops the 96 `next instruction will not move` sites**, tallied from the

    after the site    vextractf128 41   vmovups 39   vaddss 9   vmulss 3   four others 1 each
    before the site   vextractf128 46   vmovups 33   vaddss 9   vmulss 2   six others 1 each

Perhaps fifteen sites, through the passenger borrow; not attempted.

### Finding 331 -- a short site jumps short, into the padding between functions

The three 128-bit floors were 402 of the 784 survivors, more than every 256-bit class
put together. Two of them are one problem: a site under five bytes cannot carry `jmp
rel32`, and its window can widen neither forward nor back -- 206 of the 228 `next
instruction is a branch target` are SANDWICHED, the site and its successor both branch
targets (Finding 299). Finding 299 measured the standard escape and set it aside: a
2-byte `jmp rel8` into inter-function `int3` padding that holds the `jmp rel32` reaches
only 28 of 228, and "a mechanism for 28 sites is not a mechanism". Ranked by sites it
had become the largest lever left.

**Re-measured across all three classes first**, a 5-byte slot in a run of `0xcc`
within `rel8` reach, each run's capacity shared out:

    declined: next instruction is a branch target   228   28 in reach   28 assignable
    declined: next instruction will not move        101    5 in reach    5 assignable
    declined: outside .pdata                         73   38 in reach   18 assignable

The third is declined for what `outside.py` refuses on purpose, not for size, so reach
does not help it. 33 predicted.

**Built as a fallback at the decline**, after both widenings have failed: the window
is the site alone, its first two bytes a `jmp rel8` to a claimed slot, the slot a `jmp
rel32` to the stub, which returns to the end of the site as any window's does. A slot
is padding only if nothing runs or reads it -- outside every function extent `.pdata`
describes or `outside.leaf_ranges` infers, outside every data island, holding no branch
target -- and each is handed out once. `TRAMPOLINE` maps site to slot, module-level
for `UNIT_ALTERNATIVES`'s reason.

    frontier                                          784 ->  752    -32
      declined: next instruction is a branch target   228 ->  200    -28
      declined: next instruction will not move        101 ->   96     -5
      declined: outside .pdata                         73 ->   74     +1
    detours                                       202,291 -> 202,323    +32

**33 for 33, and one of them is right to stay.** It took a slot and then failed the
`.pdata` check that still guards the site's own extent, so it moved class rather than
placing. 804,199 of 804,951, 99.91%. These are 128-bit sites, so no withheld window
was waiting on them: 265 not placed, unchanged.

`verify` learns one thing: five one-byte `int3`s become one instruction where a slot is
written, so four boundaries go, and it names them as such rather than calling them
swallowed. Only for windows actually placed. On Starfield it names 128, which is 32
slots times four, and every other check passes.

`tramp` (in `check-pe`) is the sandwiched shape executed: a four-byte `vaddss` whose
SSE form is seven, the site and its successor each named by a never-taken branch, and
`int3` padding after `func_end`. 29 originally, 77 rewritten through `eb 0f` and `e9`,
and 29 with `TRAMPOLINE_RULE` off and no detour placed.

**Three bugs in the first draft, each of which would have read as "padding is scarce"**:
the run lookup bisected on a nonsense key; the extent test looked at one range where
leaf ranges nest; and a range starting exactly at a run's end counted as overlapping it
-- which is where padding always ends, so nearly every run would have been refused.

The two `vfnmadd231ps` root blamers -- `0x142dcfd70` and `0x142dcfe1e`, both

addend - product` needs the addend as the subtract's destination while the product
is still wanted, and in the 231 order the only slot free to write is the destination's,
which holds the addend.

**The block has scratch slots nobody was using.** Transient indices below `TLS_SLOTS`,
addressed off the block pointer like any slot, with the mover and the stash drawing on

block tuple; the upper half becomes

    movups  <s1 slot>,%xmm5          the factor
    mulps   <rip>,%xmm5              the product
    movups  %xmm5,0x10(%r11)         out to the scratch slot
    movups  <dst slot>,%xmm5         the addend, which is the destination
    subps   0x10(%r11),%xmm5         addend - product, the product as an operand
    movups  %xmm5,<dst slot>

The same as the two-helper form except that the second register is a slot. Only where
the emitter used to refuse: the helper budget is untouched, Finding 326's rule.

`verify` passes, 19 checks. 804,167 of 804,951, 99.90%. **15 against a bound of 18**:

another blamer as the repair re-settled -- the shortfall Finding 306 describes for a

`fnm1` reproduces `0x142dcfd70`, memory multiplier and all, with one volatile helper and

### Finding 328 -- re-admitting the rootless cycle, and a closure the repair cannot draw

Finding 327's cycle -- four withheld windows at `0x142d8e4db` whose blame ends nowhere --
looked like a pass after the repair settles: find the largest set of dropped windows
closed under "every blamer lies inside a window of the set", re-admit it whole, keep it
only if the placement then has no stale read. The acceptance test is the loop's own, so
the bytes stay right by construction whatever the set is.

**It changed nothing, and the reason is the set, not the test.** Replayed offline on
`repair-blame.txt`, the fixed point closes **269 of the 274** dropped windows, not four.
Containment in a dropped extent is not "would be lowered if the window came back": the
40 root blamers Finding 327 counted -- refused stubs, overlaps, declined arithmetic --
all sit inside dropped extents, so they read as internal. The trial re-admitted 269
windows, came back guilty, and was refused; 274 not placed and 202,286 detours, as
before. Reverted, the measurement stopped at the census.

**The closure that finds four uses each reader's REASON**, followed into a holder only
when the reason is `kept: its window was withheld`. Inside the repair no reader has a
reason yet -- that is the census's work, done afterwards from the image. Drawing it in
the repair means classifying refused, overlapped and declined readers there, which is
more machinery than five sites pay for. Recorded so the next reader prices it with
that cost attached.

`build/` holds the stopped run's output, and `make census` rebuilds it. Its apply
reported the 799 build's counts exactly, but the image was not compared byte for byte
and the census was stopped partway.

### Finding 327 -- the silent exit was a label, and behind it a cycle with no root

The ranking's new row was one `vsubps` at `0x142d8e50a` in `the collector reached it and
recorded nothing`, holding four windows by the closure. Finding 319 had left it there as
"a genuine silent exit" and found no exit. A probe running the census's own steps for
that one address answered it:

    candidate  0x142d8e505  9 bytes, widened back over `vshufps $0xdd`   dropped by the repair
    withheld   0x142d8e4fa  to 0x142d8e517   and   0x142d8e505  to 0x142d8e529
    re-placed by the census, the candidate alone                          refused

**It is in two withheld windows and in neither one's extent as the census computes it.**
The census finds withheld sites by laying every dropped candidate's stub down again, all
together, and taking the extents that come back. A window that comes back refused or
overlapped contributes nothing, and a site with no other reason fell through every test.

**Two fixes moved nothing, and the third is the one that is right for a reason.**

- Keeping the re-placement's refusals in `place_stubs`' `detail`: filled on one refusal
  path only, so it stayed empty.
- Its returned refused list: the probe re-placed the candidate ALONE, and laid down
  together with the rest it is not refused but something else. A probe narrower than the
  thing it models answered a question the census never asks.
- A withheld candidate's own extent, checked LAST. 40 surviving sites lie in a withheld
  extent by `repair-blame.txt`, every root blamer among them, so an early check would
  have relabelled all forty and erased the reasons that make them roots. Last, it catches
  only what nothing else claimed.

    `the collector reached it and recorded nothing`     1 ->  0
    `kept: its window was withheld`                   325 -> 326
    every other site's reason                       unchanged, diffed line by line
    frontier                                          799 -> 799

**Worth nothing in sites, and the row it removes was worth nothing either** -- which is
Finding 319's own conclusion about this bucket, reached a second time. The ranking had
it at six.

**What the correct label shows is new.** The closure follows a withheld reader into its
holder, so the four windows that used to end at this "root" now end nowhere: `no-terminal
windows 4`. They are a CYCLE, withheld only by readers that sit inside each other, with no
unlowerable instruction anywhere behind them. The repair starts from "everything placed"
and only drops, so once the avalanche has dropped one member nothing re-admits the set.
Re-admitting it whole, and checking the stale reads again, is a repair change worth at
most the five sites inside: `vinsertf128` at `0x142d8e4db` and `0x142d8e4fa`, `vshufps`
at `0x142d8e500` and `0x142d8e505`, and the `vsubps`.

### Finding 326 -- `lanereg3` reads its second source out of the slot

Finding 325's lesson, applied: lower a ROOT blamer, and touch nothing else. The
closure on the rebuilt 808 rolls named three `vpshufb` sites -- `0x1434dc104`,
`0x14365ca76`, `0x14365ca81` -- as the only blamers of six withheld windows, and every
one was refused `lanereg3 wants a second helper` in `build/unit-refused.txt`.

The upper half of a three-operand lane op loaded both sources' slots into two helpers.
The second one need not be in a register at all: it is an SSE operation's memory
source, read straight from its slot off the block register, the move `span_slot_op`
already makes for the FMA forms on Finding 312's alignment argument:

    movaps  %xmm1,%xmm3              low half, unchanged
    pshufb  %xmm4,%xmm3
    movups  0x60(%r11),%xmm5         source 1's upper half
    pshufb  0x90(%r11),%xmm5         the control's, AS AN OPERAND
    movups  %xmm5,0x80(%r11)         into the destination's slot

**Only at the refusal.** `need` is untouched, which is the difference from Finding 325's
link 1: lowering the budget changed which windows formed everywhere and cost 18 sites
twice, while a fallback where the emitter used to refuse can change only the windows
that refused. At 808 that is exactly these three.

    frontier                                          808 ->  799     -9
      kept: its window was withheld                   331 ->  325     -6
      declined: 256-bit: arithmetic, not a copy        20 ->   17     -3
    windows not placed                                280 ->  274     -6
    detours                                       202,282 -> 202,286    +4

**9 for 9, the closure exactly**, and no other class moved. `verify` passes, 19 checks.
804,152 of 804,951, 99.90%. Of the uses Findings 306 and 324 tabulate, every one missed
the closure or beat it; this one met it, and it is the smallest -- three roots, six
windows, no window in the count with a blamer outside the class.

#### The fixture failed twice before it tested anything

`pshufb1` reproduces `0x14365ca76` register for register, with a lane-reversing control
so a dropped upper half and a low-lane-for-high mix-up each score differently from 77.

- **First version: the refusal reinstated and still 77.** It named every xmm but
  `xmm15`, meaning to leave one helper. Only `xmm0`-`xmm5` are candidates -- a
  non-volatile register is borrowed only where the function saves it -- so the window
  found NO helper, fell to the stash, and the stash takes two. Reading the stub showed
  `xmm0` and `xmm2` saved to scratch slots.
- **Second version: one volatile register free, and `off` answered 77 as well.** A frame
  span lowered the whole run with two helpers, so the fixture never needed a permanent
  slot and the gate's control refused it. Loading the sources above a branch target, as
  `crossregion` does, makes the shuffle read them from slots the region did not define.

    the fix                       77    through `pshufb 0x90(%r11),%xmm5`
    --shadow-regs=off             29    the VEX surviving
    the old refusal reinstated    29    and unit-refused.txt names `lanereg3 wants a second helper`

`check-shadow-pe` holds it.

**The negated FMA is not the same change.** `vfnmadd231ps` is the other one-helper
candidate, two roots and twelve windows, but `D = addend - product` needs the addend as
the subtract's destination: one register cannot hold both the product and the addend,
and the sign flip that would avoid it is the construction Finding 306 measured wrong for
NaN payloads. It wants a scratch slot for the product.

### Finding 324 -- `blendv` takes a stashed `xmm0` as its mask register

The handover ranked `vblendvpd %ymm2,%ymm1,%ymm3,%ymm3` at `0x14374ecee` the best ratio in
the project: one site, 25 withheld windows behind it, and a known refusal in
`build/unit-refused.txt` -- `blendv cannot borrow xmm0 as a helper`.

    frontier                                          960 ->  808   -152
      kept: its window was withheld                   481 ->  331   -150
      declined: no SSE form at any register             6 ->    5     -1
      excluded by a window the repair rebuilt           3 ->    2     -1
    windows not placed                                423 ->  280   -143
    detours                                       202,263 -> 202,282    +19

**152 against a predicted 26**, and the whole of `verify` passes, 19 checks. 804,143 of
804,951 sites, 99.90%. That is the fifth time a closure figure has proved a floor, and
by the widest margin: the closure counted the 25 windows whose ENTIRE terminal set was
this site, and 143 placed. **Why the other 118 were released is not measured**; the
avalanche Finding 305 describes, where a window withheld in one round blames others in
the next, is the likely route, and re-joining `build/repair-blame.txt` against the
960-site roll would settle it.

#### Why `xmm0` was a helper at all, and why that is the easy case

No register at the site is free by the whole-function rule, so `unit_candidate` takes
its helpers from the stash: every volatile `xmm` the window does not name, saved to a
block scratch slot and given back at the end of the stub. That list is handed out lowest
first, so `xmm0` comes first. The `blendv` emitter's own save-and-restore exists to put
whatever `xmm0` holds out of the way while the mask sits there -- and when `xmm0` IS the
helper, the place it would be saved is the register being saved, so it refused.

But a helper is by definition a register the window may clobber and no member names.
A stashed `xmm0` is already given back by the stub, so the mask goes straight into it
and the other helper accumulates:

    movaps  mask,%xmm0             the low mask, where SSE4.1 wants it
    movaps  src1,%H                accumulate in the other helper
    blendvpd src2,%H
    movaps  %H,dst
    movups  slot(mask),%xmm0       the upper mask
    movups  slot(src1),%H
    blendvpd slot(src2),%H
    movups  %H,slot(dst)

Four instructions shorter than the save-and-restore path, which is unchanged for the
case where neither helper is `xmm0`.

#### The fixture had to be forced onto the stash path, twice

`blendvx0` reproduces the site register for register, in the `pd` form no fixture
covered. **Its first two versions answered 77 with the refusal put back**, so they never
reached the new branch: `xmm0` carries a float return and is live at `ret`, so the
helpers came out as the whole-function-free `xmm4` and `xmm5`. Writing `xmm0` after the
blend did not help either, because `region_helpers` yields only whole-function-free
registers or ones dead INSIDE the window. Naming `xmm4` and `xmm5` at function entry is
what forces the stash, as at the real site, and the stub then shows `xmm0` saved,
loaded with the mask, and restored.

    the fix                       77
    --shadow-regs=off             29   SIGILL, the VEX surviving
    the old refusal reinstated    29   and unit-refused.txt names the site's refusal

`check-shadow-pe` holds it, and the gate passes whole.

### Finding 323 -- it runs, and the original dies in four seconds

Instructed by the copyright holder 2026-10-08, after a day of structural numbers was put
the obvious question: does the game run now. The honest answer at the time was that
nothing connected the frontier to it -- every figure since Finding 287 was `verify` plus
fixtures, and `project.md` had said since Finding 74 that the validation path was this
machine while nobody had taken it for the current default.

Taken now, both binaries, same prefix, same farm, same CPU:

    original     exit  29 after    4 s   EXCEPTION_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION
                                         addr=00000001422D2BF4   RVA 0x22D2BF4
    rewritten    exit 124 after  300 s   ZERO exceptions of any kind,
                 (960 survivors)         stopped only by the bound

**The original's fault address is the one Finding 74 recorded**, RVA `0x22d2bf4`,
`vpxor %xmm0,%xmm0,%xmm0`. Reproducing it across five months and two changes of default
is what makes this a control rather than an artifact of the environment: the same bytes,
the same prefix, the same Westmere, the same instruction, in four seconds.

**And the rewritten build does not stop there.** Finding 74's build died 866 bytes past
that point with 17,972 survivors. This one has 960 and raises no exception at all in
seventy-five times the original's lifetime, its last activity being `wineusb` device
enumeration -- real initialisation, well past the loader.

#### What this does and does not settle, corrected after an hour-long run

**It settles that the frontier is not on the first four seconds of the path.** The
original dies there and the rewritten build does not, which was never measured before;
the 2,687-to-960 progression was structural throughout.

**It does NOT settle that the build progresses, and the longer run showed it does not.**
Given an hour, a built prefix, a 1920x1080 Xvfb and `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` set:

    exit 124 after 3600s     the bound, not a fault
    exceptions                  0    throughout
    modules                   286    frozen from minute three
    RSS                   2120 KB    frozen
    display              mean = 0    nothing drawn

**It is hung, not running.** The log ends in `EnumProcessModulesEx` repeated to
exhaustion -- the process enumerating its own modules in a loop, which is a pre-gameplay
integrity or Steam-presence check, and with no Steam client it spins forever. Two
megabytes resident is a stub, not a game loading assets. So the AVX-dense rendering and
simulation code is never reached, and **"no exception in an hour" is evidence of being
stuck rather than of working.**

**The commit that recorded this finding was titled "the 960-site build runs where the
original dies in four seconds", and "runs" is too strong.** It gets past where the
original dies. What happens after the DRM loop is unmeasured, and the 252 MB RSS quoted
from the 300-second run cannot be compared to anything: that run had no `+loaddll`, so
its module count is zero in the log and what the memory belonged to is unknown.

This is the shape `running-code.md` warns about -- a comfortable explanation that ends an
investigation costs more than no explanation, because no explanation keeps somebody
looking. Running Steam, or a build with the check stubbed, is what would reach the code
the translation exists for.

#### Two environment findings worth more than the numbers

**The recorded reproduction no longer works as written.** Finding 74 copies the binary
into the Steam install beside `Starfield.exe`. The game is not in the local library at
all -- it is on an NFS mount, `/home/funk/mnt/dl180g6-03/SteamLibrary`, with Proton 10.0
beside it -- and both are `755 funk:funk` while this session runs as `claude`. Proton
also writes a lock file into its OWN directory, so even reading it is not enough.

What works instead, and needs no write anywhere outside scratch: **a symlink farm**. 38
links to the game's top-level entries, the two binaries copied in as the only real files,
Proton copied to scratch (1.4 GB) so it can take its lock, and `STEAM_COMPAT_DATA_PATH`
pointed at scratch. The install is untouched, which is better than the recorded method
rather than merely equal to it.

**And the first two attempts measured nothing, identically.** Under bare `wine` with no
game directory both binaries loaded 194 modules, the same module set, no illegal
instruction, exit 53 apiece. That is `evidence.md`'s probe that could not have succeeded
-- the control failing the same way is what said so, and without the control the 194
would have read as a result.

#### The claims this corrects

`project.md` line 37 said the Proton observation describes "a binary this tree no longer
produces" and that nobody had run the new one. True when written, false now. Line 3715's
"the validation path is this machine" is true only with the farm above. The
*What is still not verified* entry at line 20966 cites Finding 74's 866 bytes as the
honest scale of 17,972 survivors on a hot path; at 960 the hot path is clear.

### Finding 322 -- the mask extractors, whose destination is not a vector register

`vpmovmskb`, `vmovmskps` and `vmovmskpd` read a ymm and write a general-purpose
register. `span_shape_name` has called them "a register-to-register move" since Finding
253, and that bucket's own comment says they are not -- "7 are `vpmovmskb`, which writes
a general-purpose one". Being neither a move nor arithmetic, they fell past every branch
in `span_operand_shape` into None.

    frontier                                          996 ->  960    -36
      kept: its window was withheld                   502 ->  481    -21
      declined: 256-bit: arithmetic rather than a copy  31 ->   20    -11
      lost to an overlap                               15 ->   12     -3
      lost to a refused stub                           17 ->   16     -1
    windows not placed                                443 ->  423    -20
    detours                                       202,259 -> 202,263   +4

**36 against a predicted 30**, and the whole of `verify` passes -- 19 checks, including
`no surviving 256-bit read takes an upper half this rewrite left stale`. 803,991 of
804,951 sites, 99.88%.

The cascade ran further than the closure's 19 windows: releasing 11 sites freed 21
withheld windows and four more from the overlap and stub classes. That is the fourth time
a first-order closure figure has proved a floor rather than an estimate, which is now the
expected direction rather than a surprise.

#### A 256-bit form yields twice the bits, so the halves need a shift

    vpmovmskb   32 bits against 16    low | high << 16
    vmovmskps    8 bits against  4    low | high << 4
    vmovmskpd    4 bits against  2    low | high << 2

Eight instructions, two helpers, no extra general-purpose register, no FLAGS, no memory:

    movups slot(%block),%H1    H1 = the source's upper half
    pmovmskb %H1,%dst          dst = the high bits
    movd   %dst,%H2            them, in a vector register
    pslld  $n,%H2              shifted into place
    pmovmskb %src,%dst         dst = the low bits
    movd   %dst,%H1            them -- the upper half is spent
    por    %H2,%H1             combined
    movd   %H1,%dst            and back out

**Combining in a vector register is what makes it clean, and three other routes were
worked out and rejected first.** `shl` and `or` do it in two instructions and write
FLAGS, which a stub may not -- the constraint `vptest` is held out of `LANE_UNARY` for.
`lea` is flag-free and reaches `vmovmskpd` in one instruction and `vmovmskps` in two, and
cannot reach 16 at all because its scale stops at 8. Staging two halfwords through a
scratch slot works for `vpmovmskb` and not for the other two, whose halves are not
byte-aligned -- and it would draw on the block scratch slots that Finding 320 measured as
the scarce resource. `pslld` and `por` write no flags, take any shift, need no memory,
and serve all three mnemonics from one path with `n` from a table.

**No extra GPR either.** The destination is written by the original instruction anyway,
so using it as the temporary costs nothing and the borrow machinery is untouched. The
first design asked for a second GPR and `window_gpr_unnamed` would have supplied one;
not needing it is better, because `unit_candidate` already refuses when fewer than two
are unnamed.

#### Everything was checked against `as` before being written

All seven encodings, `encode_rr`'s REX behaviour, and the arithmetic -- `low` occupies
the bits below the shift, so addition equals OR, which is what makes the `lea` form
sound where it fits. The one detail memory would have got wrong: **`movmskps` carries no
`66` prefix** while `pmovmskb` and `movmskpd` both do.

#### Both controls fire, with different failure modes

    every shift forced to 8     exit 57   a wrong ANSWER
    the shape never returned    exit 29   SIGILL, the VEX surviving

The fixture sets one element in the low half AND its counterpart in the upper -- byte 0
and byte 16, float 0 and float 4, double 0 and double 2 -- so dropping a half gives 1
and shifting by 8 rather than 16 gives 0x0101, neither of which reaches 77. Each mask is
added and its expected value subtracted, so a correct lowering contributes nothing and
the constant alone carries the answer.

`check-shadow-pe` holds it, and the A/B is real: 29 without permanent slots, 77 with.

### Finding 321 -- a fingerprint that cried wolf

Finding 316 put a digest of the tool's sources in every roll header, because two rolls
from the same image and the same flags had differed only by the code that wrote them. It
hashed every `.py` beside `detour.py` -- 26 files, including the style gate, its test
suite, `pe_build.py` and a dozen oracles. **This program imports six of them.**

So when another session committed a change to `style_gate.py`, the fingerprint moved and
a join between this session's rolls was refused. The refusal was correct by the guard's
own rule and wrong about the world: a lint tool cannot move a bucket in the rewriter's
census.

**A guard that cries wolf is one somebody switches off**, which is `evidence.md`'s
long-ignore-list failure arriving from the other side -- there a gate is silenced by
instalments for reporting falsely, here it would be ignored for reporting irrelevantly.
Either way the next real divergence goes unnoticed.

The digest covers the import closure now, taken from `sys.modules` rather than from a
static scan -- an import made lazily is still an import -- and it is no longer cached,
because a value computed before a lazy import would cover less than the run did. It is
read when a roll is written, by which time everything is loaded, and six files cost
nothing.

#### The control has two sides now, which the first one did not

    scratch.py          moves=True   wanted=True
    patch.py            moves=True   wanted=True
    outside.py          moves=True   wanted=True
    lower.py            moves=True   wanted=True
    style_gate.py       moves=False  wanted=False
    pe_build.py         moves=False  wanted=False
    test_style_gate.py  moves=False  wanted=False
    why.py              moves=False  wanted=False

Finding 316's control proved only that the digest COULD move, which a digest over the
whole directory does readily. What it could not prove is that the digest stays still when
nothing relevant changed, and that is the half a guard is judged on in daily use.

### Finding 320 -- a three-link chain built on two refusals read as one

Findings 318 and the overlap measurement left what looked like a single item with three
symptoms and one root cause: `moved_instruction` cannot lower 256-bit, so a passenger
cannot be 256-bit, so a back-widened neighbour (39 refused stubs) and a rescued
candidate (10 of the 15 overlap losses) are both lost. Measured jointly the two classes
are worth **185** rather than the 120 and 65 they score apart.

Finding 318 had also measured why fixing it fails: 54 windows found no helper. So the
chain was

    1. `lanereg` takes one helper, not two, via `span_slot_op`
    2. then a backward 256-bit neighbour can be a member
    3. then a 256-bit passenger can ride in the rescuing window

each link individually neutral or worse, and links 2 and 3 impossible without 1.

**Links 1 and 2 were built. The chain does not pay.**

    baseline                                        996
    link 1 alone                                  1,014   worse by 18, verify clean
    link 1 + link 2                               1,014   no better
    no volatile xmm and scratch slot to stash it     54   UNCHANGED

#### The error, which is the finding

The 54 refusals are `no volatile xmm and scratch slot to stash it`. Finding 318's roll
listed `lanereg3 wants a second helper` as a **separate** reason, and that is the one
link 1 addresses. **Two differently-worded refusals were read as one shortage and a
three-link chain was built on it.**

Reading the refusal site is what settles it, and it is four lines:

    spare = [i for i in range(TLS_SLOTS) if i not in claimed]
    loose = [n for n in VOLATILE_XMM if n not in touched]
    if len(loose) < need or len(spare) < need:
            return refuse("no volatile xmm and scratch slot to stash it")

An **and** of two scarcities, on the non-volatile-borrow path. Lowering `need` from 2 to
1 cannot help where `spare` is already empty -- and that is the common case, because
Finding 267 seeds `claimed` from "the slots the members already occupy": the block's four
scratch slots share index space with the first four PERMANENT slots, so a window touching
`ymm0`-`ymm3` loses the corresponding scratch slot. With up to twelve members, four slots
run out.

**So the blocker is addressing, not register count**, and the chain's first link was aimed
at the wrong scarcity. What links 2 and 3 would actually need is more scratch slots --
the block growing and the scratch area moving above the sixteen permanent ones, with
`SizeOfZeroFill` raised to match. That is a change to the block layout and is bigger than
anything attempted here.

**The lesson is one this file already carries and I had just written down.** Finding 315
is about a reason that was true and described the wrong party; three times that day a
reason string sent me where the code was not. Here a reason string was READ CORRECTLY and
a DIFFERENT one was assumed to mean the same thing. A refusal's wording is evidence about
the refusal it names and about nothing else.

#### What survives

**The one-helper `lanereg` emission is sound.** Three instructions and one helper where
the old form was four and two, `verify` clean, every gate passing:

    paddd  %xmm1,%xmm2          low half, unchanged
    movups 0x70(%r11),%xmm4     the destination's upper half
    paddd  0x60(%r11),%xmm4     the source's upper half AS AN OPERAND
    movups %xmm4,0x70(%r11)

It costs 18 sites in placement economy, so it is reverted -- but the capability is real
and the alignment argument behind it (Finding 312) holds. If the block layout ever grows a
separate scratch area, this is the emission links 2 and 3 want.

**And the root-cause consolidation stands.** `moved_instruction` not lowering 256-bit does
explain 39 refused stubs and 10 of 15 overlap losses. What is disproved is that helper
demand was the obstacle.

#### Two process failures, recorded because both were avoidable

**The reason strings were distinct and in front of me**, in a roll I had printed twice.

**And `git checkout -- tool/detour.py` was executed by accident.** It was written as a
guard -- `git checkout ... && echo "WRONG -- would discard other work"` -- and the
command runs before the echo, so the echo merely reported that the discard had
succeeded. The loss was bounded to this session's own two uncommitted links, which were
being reverted anyway, and `23828fd` from the other session touched only
`style_gate.py` and `test_style_gate.py`. **The outcome was the intended one and the
route was forbidden**: `CLAUDE.md` requires reading `git diff -- <path>` and recognising
the content first, and in a tree where another session had uncommitted work in a
different file all day, the same slip in `detour.py` would have been unrecoverable.

### Finding 319 -- the bucket Finding 310 warned about, and an assertion made vacuous

`never a candidate` held four sites. Finding 310 emptied it from 31 to 4 and said the
part that mattered: a bucket named for the absence of information is where a mis-keyed
lookup goes to be invisible, and the only thing that makes one honest is an assertion
about what may land in it -- "`unaccounted` has one. This did not." It still did not.

    never a candidate                                4 ->  1
    excluded by a window the repair rebuilt               3
    the collector reached it and recorded nothing         1
    total                                          996 -> 996   image IDENTICAL

**Three of the four were rebuild casualties.** The stale-read repair substitutes another
ladder rung for a guilty window rather than dropping it. The replacement comes from
`UNIT_ALTERNATIVES`, so it may begin EARLIER as well as end sooner -- which is why the
excluded region is a set difference and not a suffix. A site the original covered and
the replacement does not is in no final extent, carries no decline because the collector
did produce a candidate for it, and is not dropped because the window was rebuilt. It
fell through every test into the fallback, and has done for as long as the repair has
been substituting windows.

**The fourth is a genuine silent exit** and is now labelled as a defect rather than as a
property of the binary, which is the distinction the bucket could not draw.

#### Two readings eliminated by measurement, not by argument

The loop head has exactly one guard that records nothing -- `if address in already:
continue`, the in-place patch set, "anything already rewritten in place needs nothing
further". Measured for all four: not in the patch set, and not in a data island either.
That is what moved the search past the head of the loop, where reading had put it.

#### And then the assertion was made vacuous in the same edit

The fix split the fallback into "the collector reached it" and "never reached it", keyed
on a `COLLECT_SEEN` set filled just past the head guards. The clear landed in
`repaired_placement`, which runs AFTER `collect` fills it. So the set was empty at census
time, the "reached" branch could never fire, and every site read **never reached** --
including one measured as passing all four head guards, which is what made the answer
impossible rather than merely wrong.

**A distinction drawn against an empty set is not a weaker distinction, it is a
constant.** `evidence.md`'s control-that-cannot-fail, introduced inside the fix for a
bucket that existed because nothing asserted what may land in it.

Two things keep it from recurring. The clear sits beside `UNIT_REFUSED.clear()` inside
`collect` now. And the census **names an empty set rather than classifying against it**:
`unclassifiable: COLLECT_SEEN was never filled`. The control runs both ways -- 0 entries
before a collect, 4 after.

#### What it is worth, which is nothing in sites

The pick was made on a cascade of 30 -- four sites and 26 windows waiting only on them --
and that figure assumed the four were a lever. Three are rebuild casualties, and
recovering those needs the repair to SPLIT a window rather than shorten it, which
Finding 281 measured as worse: 2,346 -> 2,349.

So the lever did not exist and what was wrong was the label hiding its absence. That is
Finding 310's shape exactly, which is the finding this one keeps rediscovering -- and the
reason to record it is that the next reader will otherwise price this bucket as work
again.

### Finding 318 -- the same class refused three ways, and a disproved objection

`lost to a refused stub` is 17 sites releasing 103 windows that depend on nothing else,
the largest cascading anchor in Finding 317's bound. It has now been attacked three ways
and held at 996 every time.

    refuse the backward widening       996 -> 996   Finding 315, reverted
    take the neighbour as a member     996 -> 996   here, reverted
    (and the shapes were never the obstacle: 33 of 36 windows carry a span
     shape for every member, measured before either attempt)

Both reverts proved byte-identical to the baseline image. **Three mechanisms, one
number: the class is a floor.**

#### The asymmetry is real and is the whole explanation

The forward walk states the rule: *a 256-bit neighbour is a MEMBER, never a passenger*,
because "emitting VEX into a stub is the one thing this tool exists not to do". The
backward path carries one into `preceding`, which IS the passenger path, so
`moved_instruction` is the only lowering offered it and `moved_instruction` cannot do
256-bit. That accounts for all 39 refused stubs -- strategy `unit` throughout, the roll
naming the carried instruction because a back-widened window starts at it.

**A rule written down and applied in one direction is worse than one not written**, since
the comment reads as the file's settled position and the other half of the file disagrees
with it silently.

#### The objection that blocked it was false, and that is worth more than the change

The comment said a member would be "emitted correctly and accounted nowhere". Measured:
taken as a member, **the whole of `verify` passes** -- every boundary, every branch
target, zero VEX in the stub section. `swallowed` never recorded FORWARD members either,
and `verify` derives an internal boundary from the window's extent. Ordering needed
nothing: the backward block runs before the site's own `take` and `span_entries` walks
`members` in list order with no sort.

The claim is corrected in place rather than argued with here, because the next person to
read it would be sent away from a route that works.

#### Why it still does not pay, and the dependency it exposed

    frontier                996 -> 996
    detours            202,259 -> 202,259   unchanged
    unit refused            92 ->  146      +54
    windows not placed     443 ->  471      +28

**The detour count is what settles it.** Thirty-nine stubs building would mean
thirty-nine more detours; there were none, so nothing was lowered. The +54 are a reason
that did not previously exist -- `no volatile xmm and scratch slot to stash it` -- because
a member's registers join the set the helper must avoid. The refusal moved from stub time
to collect time and the site was lost either way.

So this chains to the hypothesis dropped in Finding 317. Helper starvation was 1.6% and
not worth attacking; **this change creates it, 54 times**, which means the backward member
is only affordable if helper demand falls first -- a one-helper `lanereg` through
`span_slot_op`, the thing Finding 317 declined on its own merits. Two items that are each
not worth doing alone and might be worth doing together, and the dependency was invisible
until one of them was built.

The ladder confirms where the pressure came from: 97.9% at the full rung against 97.8%
before, so it is the member set rather than the window length.

### Finding 317 -- the ladder barely descends, and what that leaves

`unit_shortening` descends from 12 members to 1 because "a greedy window starves its own
helper", and it snapshots the refusal counters around the retries -- so a DESCENT leaves
no trace. The roll shows the 41 sites the whole ladder refused and nothing about windows
that placed shorter than they could have. `UNIT_RUNG` records the rung each one was
actually taken at:

    12 member(s) forward    35,028   97.8%
     3 member(s) forward       254
    12 member(s) back          196   not a descent -- reversed, same length
     6 member(s) forward       180
     1 member(s) back           83
     1 member(s) forward        62

**Helper starvation costs 579 windows of 35,803 -- 1.6%.** The 196 taken backwards are
Finding 277's widening rather than starvation, so they do not count.

#### The hypothesis it was measured to test, and dropped

`lanereg` demands two helpers because it loads both slot sources into registers, where
the FMA path reads one as a memory operand and accumulates in a single register.
Finding 301 excused the FMA form from the two-helper budget for exactly that and was
worth 66 windows; `TWO_HELPERS` has one consumer, inside `unit_candidate`, which refuses
without a per-thread block -- so the budget could honestly have asked for one.

**The criterion was written down before the measurement**: if most windows take the full
rung, starvation is rare and the change is worth the three `lanereg3` sites in the roll
and nothing more. 97.8% take the full rung. Dropped, for 25 minutes of measurement
rather than an implementation.

#### Overlap looks like the loss and is not

35,803 unit windows were taken and 19,255 placed; 15,900 candidates were foreclosed by a
placed window, and `place_stubs` resolves overlap by `sorted(candidates, key=c[0])` with
a running watermark -- purely positional, so a one-site `plain` window forecloses a
twelve-member `unit` window four bytes later. That is weighted interval scheduling solved
by the worst standard heuristic, and it reads like a large opportunity.

It is not. **`lost to an overlap` is 15 sites.** A foreclosed candidate's sites are
almost always lowered by the window that won or by a later one, so 15,900 foreclosures
cost 15 survivors. The frontier bounds the prize at 996 however many candidates compete,
and this is the shape `evidence.md` calls a price with two halves: the numerator looked
like 29,000 sites and the denominator is the frontier.

#### What the whole endgame is worth, which is the part worth keeping

The withheld class is 502 sites in 443 windows and 98.7% of its blame is internal, so it
moves only when the classes it terminates on clear. Those anchors are six classes holding
**75 sites** between them -- refused stub 17, arithmetic 31, overlap 15, no SSE form 6,
never a candidate 4, no known upper half 2. Clearing every one of them:

    blamed windows released    266 of 443
    blamed windows still stuck 177

The 177 wait on the withheld class itself -- self-blame, and passengers whose own window
is not a blamed start. At roughly 1.13 sites per window the 266 are about 300 sites, so

    75 anchor sites + ~300 released  ~375
    frontier 996 -> ~620

**That is the realistic floor of this approach**, and the 620 is mostly structural: 228
`next instruction is a branch target`, 101 `next instruction will not move`, 73 `outside
.pdata` and ~200 withheld sites whose blame is circular. Worth stating plainly rather
than discovering it one item at a time -- and worth stating that no single remaining item
is large: the biggest anchor is 31 sites, and two of the six are classes already measured
as negatives (F16C needs a call into injected code; refusing the backward widening moved
nothing).

### Finding 316 -- two rolls, byte-identical headers, different contents

    # Starfield-unpacked.exe	996 surviving	shadow-regs=all teb-scratch=auto ...   arith=31
    # Starfield-unpacked.exe	996 surviving	shadow-regs=all teb-scratch=auto ...   arith=57

Same image. Same flags. Same total. 31 sites against 57 in one bucket, because one was
written before an experiment was reverted and one after. **Every guard that exists
passed**, and a join built on the pair reported 26 sites in a class their own run does
not have.

This is the fourth variant of one hazard, and the only one nothing could have caught:

    image           Finding 240   the path is fixed, so the header names the image
    configuration   Finding 308   the same image under two flag sets
    extent          Finding 314   a window start where a range was meant
    the tool        here          the same image, the same flags, different code

So the header carries a fingerprint of the tool's own sources, `tool=ab3539a9fa2e`.
**Hashing the files rather than asking git is deliberate**: these trees are edited for
hours between commits, so `HEAD` is identical for every roll in a session and a dirty
flag says only that something changed, not what.

#### The control runs in three directions

    stable across two calls        True   ab3539a9fa2e
    moves when scratch.py changes  True   cfa103c6e688
    restores when reverted         True

The middle one is load-bearing and names a DIFFERENT file on purpose: it shows the
digest covers the collector, the patcher, the lowering tables and the scratch finder,
any of which can move a bucket. The third shows it is a function of content rather than
of time. An unreadable source folds in by name rather than being skipped, because a
fingerprint that ignores what it cannot read agrees across exactly the change it exists
to catch.

**The guard's first act was to refuse the rolls already in hand**, the apply-written
ones predating the fingerprint, which is the behaviour wanted rather than an
inconvenience.

### Finding 315 -- a reason that was true and described the wrong party

All 39 of Starfield's refused stubs say `moved: 256-bit, no Y strategy took it`. That
sentence says a Y strategy declined the window. **The strategy is `unit`, which is a Y
strategy, and it took it.**

The reason is `lower_vex`'s own words re-labelled with a `moved: ` prefix, and
`lower_vex` is right about its own situation: it was handed a 256-bit instruction and it
