`--teb-scratch=auto`, so its collector-side accounting described the baseline -- `detoured
201,733, refused 93` against the auto build's 201,833 and 149 -- and every attribution line
under the headline was the base model's verdict on the auto image's residue. The headline
itself is a direct count of the rewritten `.text` and was right either way, which is exactly
what made the wrong half quotable. `unaccounted 0` held under the mismatched model too, so
the reconciliation that normally catches this could not: it reconciles the residue against
whatever model it was given. What separates the two runs is that the corrected one's
`detoured` and `refused` match the apply log and the first one's do not -- the artifact,
not the tally.

**Slot k is `%gs:0x1480+8k`**, which is what makes this worth doing at all: still a complete
effective address with no base and no index, so the property that made mode "teb" the answer
for a site with no dead GPR survives being allocated rather than chosen. Both indices are
bounds-checked against 64 at load time and the callback refuses through
`GetCurrentProcess`/`TerminateProcess` above it, because past 64 a slot sits behind
`TlsExpansionSlots` and that is the dereference this exists to avoid.

#### A short jump that reached backwards out of the callback

The entry branch was `jne` in its two-byte form. With the TEB half the callback is 241 bytes
and `chain` sits at 0xe8, so the displacement wrapped: `75 df`, a jump to -33, taken on every
reason except `DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH` -- which is every thread attach. The 52-byte form without
the TEB half puts `chain` at 0x2b and hides it completely, so no build before this one could
have shown it. It is `0f 85` with a rel32 now.

**Widening it broke something four bytes away that nothing would have reported.**
`index_payload` reached the patch table with a displacement it computed by counting
instruction lengths in a comment, `code_off + 3 + 2 + 6 + 3 + 7`, and that `2` was the short
jne. The callback would have read its table from four bytes early -- inside the padding,
decoding as a plausible RVA. The fix is not a corrected constant: the caller now says WHERE
each table is and the emitter measures its own `lea`s. A hand-counted offset in a comment is
a second copy of the instruction stream, and it went stale the moment the first copy moved.

#### The control that made the 77 mean something, and the one that did not

`tebauto` is `nogpr` with an import table. The good build returns 77; the build whose callback
patches nothing returns **5**, because the stub then writes eight bytes at `%gs:0x5b5b5b00`
and that faults. `make check-teb-auto` runs both and refuses if the second also returns 77.

**The first version of that control returned 77 as well, and it was not a finding about the
TEB.** `ANTI_AVX_SABOTAGE=tebconst` emptied the patch tables and left the forcing condition
naming `teb` alone -- so the sabotaged build chose the callee home space and contained no TEB
write at all. Read as a passing control it would have said `%gs:0x5b5b5b00` was harmless. Both
names force the path now, and the gate asserts four `gs:0x5b5b5b` references in each build
before believing either exit code.

**The fixture builds its own import section rather than calling `detour.add_section`**, which
exists and works. A fixture assembled by the tool under test cannot detect a fault in that
tool: the image and the thing reading the image would agree because one produced the other.

#### A call counter is not a denominator, met a second time in the same file

The patch table was first checked against a counter incremented in `encode_gpr_teb`. It
reported 16 against the 4 that ship, because the collector emits for candidates it never
places and for every rung of the ladder. That is exactly what `INDEX_CONST_SITES` was measured
doing at 60 to 1 in Finding 293, and the remedy there -- count the artifact -- was in a comment
forty lines from where the counter was written.

What replaces it is structural rather than a tally: a TEB block saves exactly two registers,
one at the slot and one eight bytes above it, so the two tables must be the same length
whatever the collector did. Beside it is the refusal Finding 293 already carries, extended:
no image ships with an unfilled placeholder of either kind. The scratch one is the worse of
the two -- an unfilled index makes a stub READ the wrong block, an unfilled scratch makes it
WRITE eight bytes far outside the TEB.

#### The second borrowed register is dead, and is being left alone deliberately

Under the constant index `encode_tls_base` never touches the index register, so every TEB stub
saves and restores one for nothing:

    mov %r11,%gs:0x5b5b5b00
    mov %r10,%gs:0x5b5b5b08      <- saved
    mov %gs:0x58,%r11
    mov 0x5a5a5a5a(%r11),%r11
    mov %gs:0x5b5b5b08,%r10      <- restored, never read between

It is worth about 5 KB of the 4.57 MB stub section and one TLS slot per process. It unlocks
nothing: the collector's own `fewer than two dead GPRs for the block` class is 15 sites, and
the whole 1,878 wall was served WITH two registers, so those sites had two to give. Against
that, `window_borrow` is the function Findings 265, 268 and 269 were all about, all three
turning on `mover` having been chosen against the old block's registers. A size change to it
does not ride along with the pass being measured.

### Finding 296 -- the number that blocked the TEB route is 5, and it was measurable here

Finding 289 blocked the TEB route -- 1,878 refusals, the largest class left -- on
whether `TlsAlloc` returns an index below 64 when the EXE's TLS callbacks run, and
said that needed a machine with the game.

**It did not, and the reason it did not was in the README.** The rewritten binary
runs under Proton, which is wine, and wine is on this machine. Every slot gone at
that moment was taken by the imported DLLs initialising; the EXE's own code has not
executed. So the question is not about the game, it is about the game's IMPORTS
under this runtime, and a PE importing the same DLLs answers it.

    TlsAlloc at DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH, 59 of Starfield's 66 DLLs loaded:  5

Three runs, and a second call in the same callback returns 6 -- consecutive indices
being `TlsAlloc`'s contract, which is what shows the call reaches it rather than
some other export. Two slots would be 5 and 6 against a ceiling of 64.
`tool/tlsslots.py` is the method.

**The first answer was 53 three times and it was not an answer.** It is wine's exit
code for failing to load an image, which an absent file also produces, and the cause
was `bink2w64.dll` -- Starfield's Bink video library, not on this machine. A
load failure and a result are the same shape from outside; `WINEDEBUG=+loaddll`
separated them in one run.

**So the figure is a floor and is written that way.** Four of the 66 imports are the
game's own -- `bink2w64`, `libxess`, `sl.interposer`, `steam_api64` -- and are
dropped, so each could take slots this does not see. Five plus four libraries'
worth is still nowhere near sixty-four.

#### What this unblocked -- built, and the numbers are in Finding 297

The route was written the same day and the 1,878 it was worth are gone: 279 stubs
take two allocated slots, and the frontier is 2,346 with the flag against 2,687
without it. The callback does check both indices against 64 and refuses through
`TerminateProcess` above it, which is the one thing this entry left as a
requirement rather than a fact.

**The risk Finding 289 named is retired rather than accepted.** It was "probably
fine, unmeasurable from here, severe if wrong"; the middle clause was false.

**What the route did NOT do is shrink the frontier by 1,878**, and Finding 297 has
the reason: 870 sites left `declined` and 483 arrived in `dropped`, because serving
a site builds a window and a window can swallow a stale-read hazard. The net is 341.
A class the tool refused outright became a class the stale-read repair might yet
recover, which is a better place for it to be and is not the same as recovering it.

### Finding 295 -- the constant index becomes the default, and two gates had to learn it

Instructed by the copyright holder 2026-09-20.

    VEX in .text        2,889 -> 2,687        202 sites
    stub section    4,628,957 -> 4,540,587    88,370 bytes SMALLER
    index section                 98,256      the table and the callback
    stubs patched                 24,551

**The stub section shrank**, which is the part worth noticing: each of 24,551 chains
lost four bytes and an instruction, so the new section costs less than the old chain
did. The image grows by the table, and the hot path of every slot-using stub loses a
dependent load -- the thing Finding 288 measured at 2 to 3 ns per execution.

#### Making it the default broke every fixture, twice, in two different ways

**An image with no TLS directory has nothing to patch.** Most fixtures are like that:
no directory, no per-thread block, no stub standing a pointer up, no placeholder. The
installer raised "needs a TLS directory" and all forty-one failed to build. It is a
no-op where there are no placeholders now, which is the honest condition -- the
directory is not what it needs, the placeholders are.

**And a fixture keeps its callback array in `.text`.** Writing the tool's callback
into it changes eight bytes of `.text` that are not in any window, so the boundary
sweep decodes them differently and reports two lost boundaries. A real image keeps
that array in `.rdata`, which is why Starfield never showed it.

The fix is the one Finding 196 already made for the TLS directory, which sits in
`.text` in two fixtures for the same reason: name the structure from the PE header
and exclude exactly it. **Both exclusions are now written the same way**, and both
are about the same fact -- that a fixture is a smaller thing than a program, and the
places a real image keeps its data are places a fixture keeps its code.

#### What the default now does that no default here has done before

It **runs code at load time**. The tool has only ever rewritten bytes the loader then
executed; this emits a routine the loader calls before the entry point, and gives it
a section of its own. It also makes `.avxsse` writable and overwrites one slot of the
image's own TLS callback array, chaining ahead of the game's first callback.

Every one of those is argued in Findings 292 and 294 and checked by `verify`, which
now names both of its exemptions rather than one. **None of it has been executed by
the loader it was written for.** What has been executed is the fixture, under wine,
with a sabotage control either side: 77 with the patching and 5 without.

### Finding 294 -- the callback runs, and the checks were right about where it went

`--index-const` produces a working image. The TLS callback is emitted, the loader
calls it, it walks a table of RVAs and writes the index into 24,551 stubs, and then
tail-jumps to the callback it replaced.

    VEX in .text        2,889 -> 2,687        202 sites
    stubs patched      24,551
    index section     .avxidx, 98,256 bytes
    callback array     first slot was 0x14365d420, now the tool's

`verify` passes every check, including the two that had to learn something.

**Proven by making it fail.** `ANTI_AVX_SABOTAGE=indexconst` emits the callback and
an empty table, so it runs and patches nothing: the fixture answers **5** where the
real build answers **77**, three runs each, and the two images differ. The 77
depends on the patching rather than coinciding with it.

#### The first placement was wrong and four checks said so at once

The table went into `.avxsse` beside the stubs, and `verify` produced:

    98,261 bytes of stub outside every function table entry
    3,891 byte sequences in the stub section decode to nothing
    436 call instructions against 384 inside a placed window
    sections after .text changed

Three of those are one mistake: **the stub section is verified as pure code and the
table is data.** Every byte of it was being disassembled, which manufactured
instructions that decoded to nothing and calls that were never calls. The checks
were right and the placement was wrong; the table and the callback live in a section
of their own now, and the callback reaches its table rip-relative so the payload can
be built before it has an address.

#### Both remaining exemptions are written as identities

The fourth failure is not avoidable by any placement. **A load-time callback must be
reachable from the image's TLS callback array, and that array is after `.text` in any
real binary** -- so is the directory that points at it. The check now restores the
callback slot as well as `SizeOfZeroFill` and requires the rest to be equal again,
which is the form Finding 196 chose for the same reason: a skip would tolerate a
difference anywhere in an array of function pointers the loader calls.

**And the message understated what it allowed.** It read "byte-identical except
SizeOfZeroFill" while two fields were being restored -- in the one check whose whole
job is to say that nothing outside `.text` moved. It names both now. A gate that
permits more than it reports is the same defect as one that reports a failure and
returns success (Finding 281), one turn quieter.

#### What the image does not yet prove

Starfield has not been run. What is established is that the image builds, that every
structural check passes, and that the mechanism works end to end on a fixture under
wine with a sabotage control either side of it. The chain itself -- our callback
tail-jumping into Starfield's at `0x14365d420` -- has been assembled and verified as
bytes, never executed.

### Finding 293 -- the constant index dissolves three refusal classes

`--index-const` emits the block pointer as two instructions and one register:

    movq %gs:0x58,%block                 9 bytes
    movq <index * 8>(%block),%block      7 bytes, filled in at load time

against the three instructions and two registers it replaces. Disassembled for each
of the seven registers the collector can pick, all sixteen bytes, no SIB needed --
`rsp` and `r12` are the two that would want one and neither is in `VOLATILE_GPRS`.

**Measured on Starfield, and it beats the estimate:**

    refusals                              3,322 -> 2,521      -801
      mode True has no xmm to stash         360 ->     0      gone
      no non-volatile xmm this function     263 ->     0      gone
      no volatile xmm and scratch slot      154 ->     4
      no dead GPR and no home space       1,878 -> 1,878      untouched
    sites built                          33,888 -> 34,382      +494

I predicted "well under 360" and three whole classes went instead. The reason is
that mode True's xmm stash was competing for the same helpers the members wanted, so
removing the stash frees registers the other two classes were failing for. The 1,878
are untouched exactly as predicted: they have ZERO dead registers, so a chain needing
one still cannot run, and that is the TEB question rather than this one.

**No frontier number yet, and that is the point of the write guard.** The
displacement is a placeholder until a TLS callback fills it in, and `verify` has no
opinion about the value of a displacement -- it re-derives the placement and checks
structure. An image emitted with `--index-const` and no callback would pass every
check in this tree and address `0x5a5a5a5a` at run time. So `apply` refuses to write
one, and the flag cannot produce a usable image until the callback exists.

#### The guard's first counter was wrong by sixty times

It reported **1,163,501** stubs carrying a placeholder against 19,174 that stand a
block pointer up, because it counted calls to `encode_tls_base` -- which the
collector makes for candidates it never places and at every rung of the ladder.

A patch table built from that number would have been meaningless, and the number was
printed in a refusal message where it looked like a fact about the image. It counts
the blob now: the bytes that ship are what gets patched, so the bytes that ship are
what is counted. The search is anchored on the instruction rather than the value --
`8b`, a modrm with mod 10 and reg equal to rm, then the placeholder -- because
`0x5a5a5a5a` alone occurs in the constant pool.

**Same shape as Finding 290 one layer up**: a count taken from the process rather
than from the artifact. There it was the frontier counting rows that never decoded;
here it was a patch count counting work the collector threw away.

### Finding 292 -- the image is relocated, so chain the callback rather than add one

Both load-time routes -- Finding 289's reserved TLS slots and Finding 291's constant
index -- want a callback of the tool's own in the image's callback array. Neither
plan had accounted for the image being relocated, and that omission would have
shipped a pointer that is wrong the moment the loader moves the image:

    DllCharacteristics 0x8160   DYNAMIC_BASE set, HIGH_ENTROPY_VA set
    base relocations            rva 0x889f000, 953,060 bytes
    RELOCS_STRIPPED             no

A TLS callback array holds absolute VAs. Changing `AddressOfCallBacks` in place is
safe, because the relocation already covering that field applies to whatever value
is in it. **A new array in the stub section is not**: nothing relocates its entries,
so under ASLR the loader would call an address that has moved.

**The measurement offered one answer and the mechanism offered a better one.** There
are 284 raw bytes of slack after the relocation directory, all zero, so a block of
three DIR64 entries could be appended -- 8 bytes of header and 2 per entry, padded
to a multiple of four -- with the directory's size and the section's `VirtualSize`
grown to cover it. That works and it is surgery on a 953 KB structure in an image
that must still load.

**Chaining needs none of it.** Overwrite the FIRST entry of the existing two-entry
array with the tool's callback: that slot already carries a relocation, so the
loader fixes the new value exactly as it would have fixed the old one. The tool's
callback then tail-jumps to the original, which it locates as an RVA added to the
base the loader passes in `rcx` -- no absolute address anywhere, and the original
receives `rcx`, `rdx` and `r8` unchanged because a jump does not disturb them.

    tls_cb(rcx = module base, rdx = reason, r8 = reserved)
        cmp   $1,%edx            DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH
        jne   chain
        ...   patch, addressing everything as base + RVA ...
    chain:
        lea   <orig_rva>(%rcx),%rax
        jmp   *%rax              the original, arguments untouched

So the array is not relocated, not extended, and not moved; one slot changes value,
and the relocation that was already there does the rest. What remains for either
route is emitting the callback and its RVA table into the stub section and marking
that section writable.

**This is the second time on this item that measuring the environment produced a
better design rather than a number.** Reading the import table removed the need for
a PEB walk; reading `DllCharacteristics` removed the need for relocation surgery.
Neither was the question being asked at the time.

### Finding 291 -- the loader writes the TLS index before a callback runs

The block pointer needs two registers only because the index is in memory:

    mov %gs:0x58,%r11          9 bytes
    mov tls_index(%rip),%r10d  7 bytes   <- the whole reason for a second
    mov (%r11,%r10,8),%r11     4 bytes

Mode True exists solely to free that second register -- `encode_tls_base`'s `stash`
parks the index in an xmm for three instructions and puts it back -- and 360 of the
default build's refusals are sites with one dead GPR and no xmm to park it in.

**If the index were a constant the second register would not be needed**, and a TLS
callback can supply it: read `*AddressOfIndex` at process attach and patch it into
each stub as a displacement.

    mov %gs:0x58,%r11          9 bytes
    mov <disp32>(%r11),%r11    7 bytes, disp32 = index * 8

One register, one fewer dependent load, four bytes shorter, and a single disp32 per
stub so nothing changes length at load time.

**The precondition is that the loader has written the index by the time a callback
runs, and it has.** Measured under wine, three runs, exit code 100.

**The first version of that probe was vacuous and it is the part worth keeping.** It
left `tls_index` at 0 and read 0 back -- which cannot tell "the loader wrote 0" from
"the loader wrote nothing", the two answers being identical in the output. The
sentinel is what separates them: the field starts at 55, so 155 would mean untouched.
It reads 100, so the loader overwrote it. `tlscallback` in `pe_build.py` is the
method, kept rather than described.

It also establishes the mechanism that Finding 289 needed and could not test: a
fixture declaring `tls_cb` now gets a real TLS callback, the loader calls it, and
pe_build fills the callbacks array with its absolute VA -- `objcopy -O binary` on an
unlinked object cannot resolve one, which is why the directory is packed in Python
and now the array is too.

**Why this route rather than Finding 289's.** Both want a load-time callback and the
same patch table over the same 19,174 stubs. This one needs no `TlsAlloc`, so there
is no lowest-free-index question and no 64-slot ceiling, and no TEB byte belongs to
anybody else -- the index is this module's own. The thing that blocked 289 does not
arise.

**What is left to build**, and it is a session's work rather than a measurement:
emitting the one-register chain with a placeholder displacement, emitting the
callback and the patch table into the stub section, marking `.avxsse` writable, and
relocating Starfield's two-entry callback array to make room for a third. Finding 289
established the last of those is safe -- the array's VA occurs once in the image, in
the TLS directory's own field.

### Finding 290 -- 180 of the frontier were never instructions

The frontier is the number this project exists to drive down and the one both
documents quote. It counted **180 byte sequences that do not decode to an
instruction**, because `disassemble` selected a survivor on the first byte of the
encoding being `c4` or `c5` and an objdump `(bad)` row has three tab-separated
fields like any other.

    VEX in .text  805,131 -> 3,069      as it read
    VEX in .text  804,951 -> 2,889      decoded instructions only
                                        and 180 that decode to nothing

**They are not instructions.** `c5 32 00` is a two-byte VEX whose opcode is `00`,
which is not a VEX form in any map; one is a lone `c4`. Asked where they sit: 28
are outside every `RUNTIME_FUNCTION`, and of the 152 inside one, 136 are reached
by a disassembly starting at that function's own entry. That last figure is weaker
evidence than it looks -- a sweep desynchronises after inline data and then
"reaches" whatever follows -- but it does not matter which cause holds. **Real
compiled code does not contain an invalid instruction on a path anything reaches**,
so either the sweep walked into data, which is the hazard Finding 8 named, or they
are unreachable padding.

**They are reported rather than dropped**, and that is deliberate: `isa_guard`
already carries two known objdump misdecodes in this image, so silently discarding
every `(bad)` row could hide a real survivor. Both `verify` and `census` now count
the decoded ones and print the rest on their own line, which is one definition of a
surviving VEX instead of two.

**The removed count does not move** -- 802,062 either way, because the baseline
counted them too. What changes is the number that says how much work is left, which
was overstated by 5.9%, and the 180 phantom entries any future session would have
found on a list of things still to lower. The collector has refused them by rule
since Finding 223; nothing else had been told.

**Why it survived this long is the ordinary reason.** The frontier is computed by
one small function nobody had cause to read, it agreed with the census exactly --
both being wrong the same way, which is the corroboration failure `evidence.md`
opens with -- and every check around it passed. It surfaced only from asking what
the 180 in a census bucket named "undecodable, never classified" actually were.

### Finding 289 -- the TLS slot route is cheap, sound, and blocked on one number

`--teb-scratch` is worth 543 sites and has no default because nothing in the TEB is ours.
`TlsAlloc` is the documented way to own a slot, and four measurements were taken before
building anything. Three of them removed work:

  * **`TlsAlloc` is already imported.** `KERNEL32.dll`, IAT at VA `0x143a3f3a8`, beside
    `TlsGetValue`, `TlsSetValue` and `TlsFree`. No import-table surgery and no PEB walk to
    kernel32's exports -- the callback is `call *0x143a3f3a8(%rip)`. That was the one part
    of this with consequences outside the tree, since a PEB walk in a game binary is the
    shape anti-cheat and antivirus are written to notice.
  * **The callback array can be relocated safely.** Its VA `0x143a86ea0` occurs exactly
    once in the image, at file offset `0x4f06a98`, which is the TLS directory's own
    `AddressOfCallBacks` field. Nothing else holds the address. The two existing callbacks
    dispatch on the Reason argument as normal -- the first opens `cmp $0x2,%edx; jne` --
    so preserving order and content preserves behaviour.
  * **The patch scope is 19,174 stubs, not 200,000.** That is how many stand a block
    pointer up in the current default build; the rest of the 201,670 detours are `plain`
    and never touch the TLS block. A 77 KB table and 19,174 word writes at load time. The
    narrow scope -- only the teb-mode stubs -- is about 400.

#### The fourth measurement is the one that blocks it

**A TLS slot is addressable with no register only while its index is below 64.**
`gs:0x1480` is the 64-entry `TlsSlots` array; past that a value lives behind
`TlsExpansionSlots`, a pointer at `gs:0x1780`, which is another dereference and another
register -- the exact problem this exists to solve. `TlsAlloc` returns the lowest free
index, and the EXE's TLS callbacks run **after** every statically-imported DLL has had its
`DllMain`. Starfield imports 66 of them.

**Whether the lowest free index is under 64 at that moment cannot be measured here**, and
this is not a case where the risk can be engineered away:

  * There is no retry. `TlsAlloc` hands out the lowest free index; if that is 64 or more,
    asking again cannot do better.
  * There is no ordering fix. Putting our callback first in the array does not help,
    because DLL initialisation precedes the array entirely.
  * **There is no fallback once the stubs are emitted.** The sites that would use these
    slots are exactly the ones with no dead GPR and no home space -- that is why they are
    teb-mode -- so there is no cheaper form to patch them to. Restoring the original bytes
    is not a fallback either: it puts VEX back, which on the target host is a SIGILL.

So the honest failure mode is a process that refuses to start, and the honest risk
assessment is "probably fine, unmeasurable from here, severe if wrong". That is the shape
of Finding 268, which measured well and rested on an assumption about runtime behaviour
nobody in this tree could check, and which Finding 270 then had to revert.

**What would settle it is one number** and it needs a machine with the game: the value
`TlsAlloc` returns when called from the EXE's own TLS callback, with Starfield's 66 imports
loaded. Under 64 with room to spare and this is a day's work with the risk retired; at or
near 64 and the route is closed and the 543 sites stay where they are.

**A fixture cannot answer it.** These PEs have no import table by design -- "No imports and
no relocations", the first thing `pe_build.py` says about them -- so proving the mechanism
here would mean giving them one, and even then a two-import fixture's answer says nothing
about a 66-import game.

### Finding 288 -- what a lowered site costs, and why the comparison could not be made

Finding 287 took the uniform slots as the default and said runtime was not measured. It is
now, as far as this host allows, and the result has two halves: a number, and a reason the
number is not the one that was wanted.

**The number.** `bench` runs a lowered 256-bit zero-and-store fifty million times;
`benchempty` is the same program with those two instructions removed. Under wine on this
Westmere, six runs each:

    benchempty   0.075 0.085 0.086 0.087
    bench        0.209 0.230 0.259 0.289

About **2 to 3 ns per lowered site executed**, six or seven cycles at 3.06 GHz. That is
throughput and it flatters the figure: the iterations are independent so the processor
overlaps them, and a dependent chain would pay the latency of the three-load TLS walk
instead.

**The count had to be fifty million.** At two million the difference was about 15 ms against
a start-up spread of 46 to 90 ms, so it did not resolve -- the first version of this measured
noise, and reporting it would have been worse than reporting nothing.

**What the stub does every iteration is worth reading:**

    mov %gs:0x58,%r11          the thread's TLS array
    mov tls_index(%rip),%r10d
    mov (%r11,%r10,8),%r11     this module's block
    xorps %xmm3,%xmm3
    ... the slot traffic ...
    jmp back

The block pointer is stood up **per execution**. A compiler would hoist it out of a loop;
this cannot, because each stub is entered fresh from its own site and knows nothing about
being in one. In hot code that is three instructions and two dependent loads repeated for
every iteration, and it is the obvious thing to attack if the runtime ever matters.

#### The comparison against the old default could not be built, twice

The measurement that was wanted is `--shadow-regs=off` against `--shadow-regs=all` on the
same hot loop. Two fixtures were written for it and neither worked:

  * **The first** loaded both operands before the loop. `off` left the body in VEX and the
    build could not run at all on a host without AVX.
  * **The second** defined everything inside the loop. `off` lowered the two sites AFTER the
    loop and left the body in VEX again.

Both failed the same way: **`--shadow-regs=off` will not lower a loop body whose head is a
branch target**, which is exactly the class that is 95% of its refusals. A benchmark needs
ground both modes lower, and that excludes hot loops.

**On the ground they do share, the two modes emit instruction-for-instruction identical
stubs** -- only the slot offsets differ, 0x10/0x20 against 0x60/0x70. So the slot cost is not
a property of the new default at all; it is the cost of using a slot, which both modes pay
whenever they use one. What the default changed is how many sites take that path.

**Which makes the size-based worry about the new default weaker than it looked**, though not
disposed of. The old default's cheap strategies -- `zero` at 9.5 bytes a site against `unit`
at 31 -- were placing 10,018 and 7,232 sites; whether those sites are hot is exactly what
this could not measure, and two hand-written loops are evidence about two hand-written loops.
What would settle it is running the game, which nothing in this tree can do.

### Finding 287 -- the uniform slots become the default, and nine strategies stop firing

Instructed by the copyright holder 2026-09-18. `--shadow-regs=all` had been a flag since
Finding 244, and the record had said for some time that switching it was "worth more than
everything left in the list above combined" -- at a gap of 2,460 when that was written.
Measured on the day it was taken:

    VEX in .text        5,691 -> 3,069        2,622 sites
    stub section    3,778,502 -> 4,628,957    +850,455 bytes
    image         111,600,640 -> 112,437,760  about +0.8%
    detours           202,836 -> 201,670

**Why the gap was that shape.** 5,398 of the old default's 5,691 refusals -- 95% -- were a
single class: `reads a ymm defined outside the region`, split across after-a-call (3,385),
after-a-jump (1,079) and at-a-branch-target (934). A permanent per-register slot dissolves
the whole class by construction, because nothing has to be proved about where a value came
from. Nothing else in that census was above 311.

**What was not measured, and it is the number that would decide it for a game.** Every
lowered site now reaches its upper half through `gs:[0x58]`, an index and a load, where the
old default kept more of them in registers. This host has no AVX and nothing in this tree
runs Starfield, so the trade was taken on size and correctness with the runtime gap stated
rather than closed. `--shadow-regs=off` stays reachable as the A/B, the way `--spill=home`
stays beside `--spill=tls`.

#### Nine strategies stop placing anything, and a gate said so within the hour

The collector offers `unit` first under this mode and it takes what it can, so the placer
table is now three rows:

    plain   179,506      was 179,097
    unit     18,920      was 0
    spill     3,406      was 3,395

`zero` (10,018), `pair` (7,232), `run` (2,045), `region` (16), `span` (27), `zerorun`,
`splat`, `splatop`, `splatrun`, `longload`, `longstore` and `conststore` place **nothing**.

That is construction rather than regression: the uniform representation is coherent only if
EVERY writer maintains its slot, and `unit` is the strategy that does. Those twelve are the
`off` mode's path and are reachable there; none is dead code.

**`check-pe` caught the consequence immediately**, which is the part worth recording.
`regioncarry` exists to prove the region lowering actually runs, because four earlier shapes
of it silently became spans -- Finding 205. Under the new default `unit` took it, the fixture
went on answering 77, and the strategy assertion failed exactly as written. It runs under
`--shadow-regs=off` now, which is where the region strategy lives.

A fixture that asserts WHICH strategy answered is the only kind that could have noticed. The
exit code was 77 either way.

#### Two claims that had to be scoped rather than carried over

`project.md` and the README both said the rewritten binary loads 305 modules under Proton
before the frontier at `0x1428D1492` stops it. That was measured on the previous default and
nobody has run this one, so the module count and the address describe a binary this tree no
longer produces. Both now say so.

**A status line is the most-quoted sentence in a project and the least re-measured.** Ours
had been carried through this whole session as "the shipped build is unchanged at 5,691",
correctly as it turned out -- but I had been repeating it from a summary rather than from a
measurement, and only checked on the day it stopped being true.

### Finding 286 -- the window cannot be split, and that closes the largest class

The repair's dropped windows are 1,177 of 2,526 survivors, and Finding 283 shut the reshaping
route: shapes are not scarce, but nearly every one the ladder can build still covers the
instruction the window was blamed for. The one mechanism left was a window with a HOLE in it
-- two windows abutting the producer, leaving it in place -- which the strategy has no
representation for.

**Measured before building any of it, and it reaches zero sites:**

    1,136 dropped window(s)
      1 blamed                       439
      2 blamed                       287
      3 or more blamed               410

    of the 439 with exactly one blamed producer:
      neither side reaches 5 bytes   337
      only after is placeable         78
      only before is placeable        24
      five bytes on both sides         0

A split needs a five-byte jump on EACH side. Not one window of 439 has the room, and 337 do
not have it on either side. A unit window is as long as one jump and a member or two, which
is the point of the strategy; two jumps and a producer between them was never going to fit,
and the arithmetic says so in one run.

The 78 and the 24 are not a consolation. Those are windows one shorter or offset window could
take, which is exactly what the ladder already tries at four lengths in two directions and
what Finding 283 measured failing.

**So the class is closed on all three routes**, and they are worth keeping together because
the next person will think of them in this order:

  * **Lower the surviving reader.** The repair iterates for this already; what is left is
    readers nothing can lower, which is the declined class under another name.
  * **Zero the upper half from inside the stub.** Legacy SSE cannot touch bits 255:128 --
    that is why the zeroing is lost -- and a stub may hold no VEX because the host has no AVX.
    Impossible by construction rather than unbuilt.
  * **Split the window.** Zero sites, measured above.

#### Where that leaves the frontier

    in a window the repair dropped     1,177    closed, this finding
    declined by the collector            955    85% FMA, which has no SSE encoding
    refused, stub not buildable          190    128 of it the same FMA floor once removed
    undecodable, never classified        180    Finding 8's bytes; refused by rule since 223
    skipped for overlap                   13
    in-place patch reverted               11

**Every class is now a measured floor or derivative of one.** That is a different statement
from "the work is finished" -- it says the remaining 2,526 are not reachable by the mechanisms
this tool has, not that no mechanism exists. What would change it is a new representation
rather than a new shape: something that can lower a site whose upper half a surviving 256-bit
reader still needs, which is the one thing every route above runs into.

**The cost of learning this was one instrumented run**, against a mechanism that would have
taken a day and delivered nothing. That is the whole argument for pricing an item before
building it, and it is the third time this session the measurement disagreed with a prediction
I would otherwise have acted on.

### Finding 285 -- the per-lane conversions, and a bucket re-derived three times

`shape a register-to-register move` was the largest reachable refusal class after the FMA
floor. Finding 253 had dissected it once; re-derived rather than quoted, because a scope
number ages:

    emittable today : 108    vmovups 53, vbroadcastss 18, vpbroadcastd 18,
                             vmovdqu 12, vmovaps 6, vmovdqa 1
    refused         :  74    vcvtdq2ps 45, vcvtps2dq 12, vpmovmskb 7,
                             vmovapd 3, vrcpps 2, vmovmskpd 2,
                             vmovmskps 2, vptest 1

**A per-lane conversion splits by half because every element is decided by itself.** The low
half is the same instruction one width down -- a prefix drop `narrow_piece` already does --
and the upper half is the source's slot through a helper into the destination's. One helper,
not two: unlike `lanereg` the destination's upper half is wholly overwritten, so there is
nothing to load first.

    refusals                     730 ->  606
    shape ... register move      148 ->   24
    sites built               35,470 -> 35,532      +62
    VEX in .text               2,587 -> 2,526       61 sites

**62 predicted, 61 delivered** -- the closest this project has come, and the reason is that
the shape refusal really was the only wall for these: a conversion needs one helper and
nothing else, where Finding 271's immediate form needed registers it could not get.

**Width-changing conversions are the hazard and are excluded by construction.**
`vcvtps2pd` reads four floats from an xmm and writes four doubles to a ymm; the halves do not
correspond and splitting by half is meaningless. None occurs in Starfield in this shape, so
the data would not have caught the mistake -- `LANE_UNARY` excludes them by listing what is
safe rather than by filtering what is seen. `vptest` is out for a different reason: it writes
FLAGS, which a stub may not, and that is the constraint `encode_tls_base` is built around.

**And `vmovapd` was simply missing from `YMM_REGISTER_MOVES`**, which held `vmovups`,
`vmovaps`, `vmovdqu` and `vmovdqa` and neither `vmovapd` nor `vmovupd`. Three sites, one word,
and no argument for its absence -- a set written from the four spellings somebody met.

#### Three wrong measurements of one bucket, and the middle one was the dangerous one

I measured this population three times. The first mislabelled `vbroadcastss %xmm0,%ymm1` as
writing a general-purpose register, because it has one ymm operand and I tested the count
rather than the kind. The second reported **all 182 sites refused** -- including the
`vmovups` the tool plainly lowers -- and the cause was that my script never set
`SHADOW_REGS_RULE`, which the `regmove` branch is gated on.

**A probe that does not run the code under the mode the apply runs it in is measuring a
different program.** That one was dangerous rather than merely wrong: it said the tool refuses
what it handles, which would have sent the next piece of work at a gap that does not exist.
What caught it was the result being absurd, not any check of mine.

#### The fixture found the half of the change I had not made

`regmove` is handled in three places -- the classifier, the slot resolution in `span_entries`,
and the emission -- and I edited two. The third fills in `second`, the source's slot, from a
LIST of shape names that the new one was not in, so the emission refused `lanemove source is
in no slot` on every site. Nothing in the classifier or the emitter is wrong, and neither
reading them nor the type of the tuple would have shown it.

That is `evidence.md`'s least-wired-method rule met from the inside: a shape is not a shape
until every list that enumerates shapes has heard of it, and the only thing that knows how
many such lists there are is a fixture that fails.

### Finding 284 -- the aliasing shape, where the operation commutes

`op %ymmD,%ymmS,%ymmD` computes `D = S op D`: the destination is the OTHER source.
`SPAN_EMITTABLE` excluded it with the note that it is "the aliasing case `lower_vex` needs a
scratch for and this does not build", so the slot path refused a shape its in-place sibling
already emits.

**Where the operation commutes it needs no scratch at all.** SSE's two-operand form computes
`dst = dst op src`, so `op %xmmS,%xmmD` IS the wanted value with the sources read the other
way round. The same `lanereg` emission serves; only the low half changes, and only in which
register ModRM.rm names.

    refusals                     814 ->  730
    shape ... src2 is D          162 ->   78
    sites built               35,428 -> 35,470      +42
    VEX in .text               2,623 -> 2,587       36 sites

**162 was refusals, not sites**, and I quoted it as a site count twice before measuring it.
Classifying the listing directly with the tool's own `span_shape_name` gives **82 sites** --
a site is refused about twice, once per strategy that asks. Of the 82: 72 commute, 10 do not.

#### What is deliberately left, and why it is not mine to take

**Floating-point add and multiply are excluded** -- 30 of the 72, and the largest single
group (21 `vmulps`). They are commutative in arithmetic and not in x86: with two NaN operands
the result carries the FIRST source's payload, so exchanging them changes the bytes. This
project is bit-exact by rule, Finding 4 having made FMA's inexactness a finding rather than a
detail, so taking 30 sites on a NaN-payload argument is a decision for the copyright holder
and not one to make while in the file. Recorded here rather than done.

**FP min and max are excluded for a stronger reason** and are not a decision at all: they are
defined asymmetrically on NaN and on signed zero, so they do not commute. My first
commutativity list had them in it, which is the kind of error a list gets when it is written
from the word "commutative" rather than from the manual.

The remaining 10 need the scratch `lower_vex` already uses, which is a different piece of
work: an emission that wants a register, not a reclassification.

#### The encoder, and an instrument that lied twice

`narrow_piece` drops the VEX prefix and keeps the ModRM, which is right exactly when `vvvv`
already names the destination -- SSE has no room for a second source, so the one in `vvvv` is
thrown away. Where the destination is the other source, throwing it away turns
`vmulps %ymm1,%ymm0,%ymm1` into `mulps %xmm1,%xmm1`, which SQUARES. `commuted_piece` writes
`vvvv` into ModRM.rm instead and carries REX.B with it.

**Which of the two is used is read back off the bytes**, not passed down from the classifier:
`vvvv != ModRM.reg` is exactly the condition, and deriving it at the emission site is what
keeps the classifier and the emitter from disagreeing about a shape -- the drift
`SPAN_EMITTABLE` exists to prevent, met from the other side.

**My probe was wrong twice and the second one would have shipped.** The first version treated
`tail[0]` as the ModRM byte; it is the OPCODE, because `sse_encoding` supplies only the map
escape. So it overwrote the opcode and `vpaddd` came back as `psubq`. What caught it was
disassembling the emitted bytes with objdump rather than checking my own arithmetic -- and
the same check is what confirmed the fix, `vpaddd %ymm8,%ymm11,%ymm8` reading back as
`paddd %xmm11,%xmm8` with both REX bits right.

**The fixture separates the two emissions rather than merely passing.** `commute` holds 30
low and 3 upper against 40 and 4, so the answer is 70 + 7 = 77 and the doubling bug gives
60 + 6 = 66. A fixture whose two operands were equal would have passed either way, which is
Finding 205's rule applied to an arithmetic shape instead of a strategy.

### Finding 283 -- the shapes are there and every one of them is guilty

Finding 281's substitution allowed one attempt per window: an alternative that was itself
blamed meant the window was dropped with the rest of the ladder untouched. Lifting that --
offering every rung, against blame accumulated across rounds rather than this round's alone
-- is worth **7 sites**, 2,630 to 2,623.

**The seven are not the finding. The reason is, and it is the opposite of what I predicted.**
I expected the ladder to be producing one or two shapes per site, which would have made "try
them all" the same as "try one". Measured over the 1,276 windows that asked:

    0 alternative(s)      97
    1 alternative(s)     390
    2 alternative(s)      84
    3 alternative(s)     355
    4 alternative(s)      52
    5 alternative(s)     162
    6 or more            136

    ended dropped      1,136
    ended substituted    140
    rungs spent total    554

Shapes are not scarce: only 97 windows of 1,276 have none, and over half have three or more.
**554 rungs were spent across 1,276 windows**, so the overwhelming majority spent none -- not
because there was nothing to try, but because nothing on offer passed. Nearly every window the
ladder can build for a site still covers the instruction that site was blamed for.

That closes the line rather than continuing it. The 1,207 survivors in dropped windows are
**not a shape problem**, and no amount of further ladder work reaches them: a window built for
a site must contain that site, and the blame is on or beside it -- which the earlier position
probe already said, with 782 of 2,338 guilty producers sitting at the window start.

What remains is a different mechanism, and the options are worth naming because the shape
route is now measured shut:

  * **Lower the surviving reader.** The repair already iterates for this, so what is left is
    the readers nothing can lower -- which makes this the 1,059 declined class wearing another
    hat, not a separate item.
  * **Zero the upper half from inside the stub.** Impossible by construction: legacy SSE
    cannot touch bits 255:128, which is the whole reason the zeroing is lost, and a stub may
    hold no VEX because the host has no AVX.
  * **Split the window around the producer** -- lower the other members and leave the guilty
    one alone. The ladder cannot express this: it builds contiguous windows, and a window with
    a hole in it is a shape the strategy has no representation for. This is the only one of
    the three that is a piece of work rather than a floor.

The change is kept because it is correct and the "one attempt" limit was arbitrary, not
because 7 sites earned it.

### Finding 282 -- the census could not explain 85 of its own survivors

The census reconciles every surviving VEX instruction against a reason, and prints
`unaccounted` with a note saying it should be zero. After Finding 281's substitution it read
88, then 85. **Two bugs, and the first diagnosis was wrong**, which is the part worth keeping:

*The one I guessed.* `spread()` reconstructs a refused or overlapped window's extent by
looking its address up in `candidates` -- and a substituted window is refused under its
SUBSTITUTE's start, which appears in no original candidate, so the lookup silently
contributed nothing. Real, and it moved about eighty sites between buckets. It took
`unaccounted` from 88 to 85.

*The one that mattered.* `withheld` was built by walking `unrepaired` -- the placement taken
with the repair switched off -- and keeping the windows whose start is in `dropped`. A window
the repair drops need not be IN that placement at all: if something overlapped it there, it
contributes no range, and every site it covers falls through every bucket. A dropped window's
extent is a property of the CANDIDATE, not of some other placement of it.

    declined by the collector          1,059
    refused, stub not buildable          162
    in a window the repair dropped     1,207
    in-place patch reverted               13
    skipped for overlap                    9
    undecodable, never classified        180
    unaccounted                            0

**What found it was reading the addresses, not thinking harder.** Fifteen of the eighty-five,
printed with their flags, were `cand-span,dropped` to a row -- the survivor's own address was
a dropped window's start. That is one 12-minute run against two rounds of theorising that had
already produced one wrong answer.

**And the wrong answer was a plausible mechanism that fixed a real bug.** `spread()` WAS
broken, the fix WAS needed, and believing it had settled the question would have left 85
survivors unexplained behind a correction that looked like a diagnosis. A fix that moves the
number in the right direction is not thereby the explanation -- what settled it was that 85
is not 0.

#### What the substitution actually cost, which I reported wrongly

Finding 281's change was reported here as delivering sites while putting 148 into
`refused, stub not buildable` and 79 into `unaccounted`, as though those were its price. The
arithmetic says otherwise:

    in a window the repair dropped   -337
    refused, stub not buildable      +148
    unaccounted                       +79
    skipped for overlap                +7
                                     ----
                                     -103   = the frontier's fall, 2,733 -> 2,630

A window that is dropped loses its sites; a window that is substituted and then refused loses
the same sites. **Those 148 changed bucket, they were not newly lost**, and only the
`unaccounted` was a fault rather than a re-labelling. A price has two halves and I had given
the second one without checking whether it was a cost at all.

### Finding 281 -- the check that printed FAILED and returned success

**The item was the repair's dropped windows and the finding is the gate.** The census put
1,364 of 2,733 survivors in windows the stale-read repair withheld -- half the frontier, and
more than every refusal together. A window is dropped whole because of one instruction it
swallowed, 1,310 of the 1,318 are `unit`, and `unit` is the strategy that already knows how
to build a shorter window and one in the other direction. So the repair substitutes a rung
the ladder did not take, and drops only where none fits.

    default --shadow-regs=all     3,172 -> 3,114      58 sites
    with --teb-scratch            2,733 -> 2,630     103 sites
    windows not placed            1,318 -> 1,157     459 rebuilt

**Three of my own bugs on the way, and every one of them measured well.**

*A predicate standing in for the repair's question.* The first version decided up front which
windows were worth keeping alternatives for -- "does this window hold a VEX.128 write" -- to
avoid walking eight rungs at 35,428 sites. It excluded 34,367 of them **including 1,306 of the
1,319 the repair went on to blame**, so the substitution ran on 13 windows, found an answer
for one, and read as a mechanism that does not pay. A cheap predicate cannot stand in for a
question that depends on which windows are placed, which is the whole reason the repair
iterates. It is a closure now, walked only for the windows actually dropped: no predicate, no
wasted work.

*Keyed by the wrong start.* A substitute is a different window with a different start, so
keying `dropped` on the current start let a substitute's start collide with another
candidate's -- and `guilty - dropped` then read a guilty window as already handled and
settled the loop with it in the image. Everything is keyed by the original candidate's start
now, and the test is `not guilty`: a guilty window is by construction a PLACED one, so
subtracting the dropped set was always a no-op and only ever hid this.

*The loop validated one placement and the function returned another.* The final `place_stubs`
rebuilt its list from `candidates` alone and never applied the substitutions. `apply` reported
459 windows rebuilt and emitted none of them. **It survived because the loop and the return
computed the same list two ways**, which was true until one of them learned about
substitution.

#### And the check that would have caught all three on the first run

`verify`'s stale-read check -- the one guarding the exact defect Findings 187 and 197 are
about -- printed its finding to stderr and **never incremented `problems`**. Every other
branch in that function does. So an image shipping 186 stale upper-half reads passed `verify`,
with all 186 listed on screen and the exit code saying success.

    verify: 186 surviving 256-bit read(s) take an upper half this rewrite left stale
    verify exit=0

Nothing in the tree could have told me. `make check` was green, every fixture passed, and the
only reason anybody looked is that 186 happened to equal the fall in dropped windows and the
coincidence was too neat. **A gate that prints a failure and returns success is worse than one
that says nothing**, because it is quoted afterwards as having passed -- and this one had been
quoted, in every run of this session, as "no surviving 256-bit read takes an upper half this
rewrite left stale".

It counts now, and the broken image is kept as the proof: built by the unfixed repair, it
exits 1 through three checks at once -- 46 boundaries lost, 166 stale reads, 309 stubs
clobbering a register. Before the one-line fix that image was green.

**The lesson is not about this branch.** It is that a check's failure path is code nobody has
run. The pass path runs on every build and the failure path runs the day something breaks, by
which time it is load-bearing and unexamined -- so the sabotage discipline this file already
applies to `check-verify`'s fourteen controls is the thing that was missing here, and the
stale-read check had no control at all.

### Finding 280 -- the third register-free place, and 439 sites

Finding 270 closed the largest refusal class in the binary with an enumeration: a slot needs
the block pointer that a slot cannot hold, `(%rsp)` needs no register but cannot be described
in a chained fragment, **and those are the only two places that need no register.** The first
two clauses are right. The third is an enumeration, and nobody had checked it.

**`%gs:disp32` is a whole effective address.** Mod 00 with rm 100 selects a SIB, and a SIB of
0x25 is base 101 index 100: no base, no index, disp32. It is per-thread by construction, it
does not move `rsp`, and there is nothing in it for an unwinder to describe -- which is
precisely what mode "frame" was reverted for. Measured under wine before any of it was built,
three runs each:

    65 48 89 04 25 28 00 00 00   mov %rax,%gs:0x28     write, read back  -> 77 77 77
    65 48 89 04 25 c8 07 00 00   mov %rax,%gs:0x7c8    write, read back  -> 77 77 77

Nine bytes either way: an absolute address has no shorter form, so a far offset costs what a
near one does.

**Mode "teb" is mode "home" with the eight bytes somewhere else.** It borrows two live
unnamed registers and gives them back, exactly as "home" does, and the sequence between is
the same `encode_tls_base`. It needs no TLS callback, no load-time patching and no assumption
about the TLS index, because with both registers free the existing two-dereference chain
runs unchanged:

    mov %r11,%gs:0x1670          save, no register needed to address it
    mov %r10,%gs:0x1678          save
    mov %gs:0x58,%r11            the thread's TLS array
    mov tls_index(%rip),%r10d
    mov (%r11,%r10,8),%r11       this module's block
    mov %gs:0x1678,%r10          the index register, back before the body
        ... the members ...
    mov %gs:0x1670,%r11          the block pointer, at the single exit

Measured on Starfield, `--shadow-regs=all`, against 3,172:

    VEX in .text            805,131 -> 2,733        was 3,172      -439
    unconditional lowering  35,428 built, 814 refused, of 36,242
                                                    was 33,845 / 3,408 of 37,253
    sites through a slot    33,997                  was 33,173     +824
    windows not placed       1,318                  was   645
    stub section         4,669,539 bytes            was 4,623,702

**439 against a predicted 260.** The prediction came from Finding 268, which served the same
population by the unsound route and took 260 -- honest to quote, and stale, because the tree
has gained the immediate form and backward widening since. Refusals fell by 2,594 where the
two named classes total 2,155: dissolving the register wall also lets sites through that were
being refused behind it.

The withheld windows doubled again, 645 to 1,318, which is the same pull every lever here
meets and is now much the largest single class in the census.

**There is no default, and that is the finding's other half.** A stub cannot preserve what it
borrows in the TEB: preserving it means reading it first, into the register it has not got.
So the bytes have to be genuinely unowned rather than merely quiet, and every offset in the
TEB belongs to somebody -- `TlsSlots` is `TlsAlloc`'s to hand out, `ArbitraryUserPointer` is
read by some `NtCreateFile` paths, and the OpenGL reserved block is free only in a process
that never loads legacy GL. Starfield's own `.text` touches `gs:0x58` 12,887 times and
`gs:0x30` six times and nothing else, but that is the image and not the system DLLs it calls.

So `--teb-scratch=<offset>` has no default and the tool emits nothing without it, which is
what `--spill=stack` does for the stack borrow it is not allowed to take. The flag refuses an
offset overlapping the two fields this tool knows are in use and nothing more -- it cannot
establish that an offset is free, only that it is not obviously taken. **Settling ownership
for a real process is the work this does not do**, and until it is done the 439 are a
measurement rather than a shipped gain.

**The fixture had to be forced, for the reason Finding 268 recorded.** `lent is None` comes
from frame states that cannot be built by hand -- a leaf entered by the loader still has the
caller's home space above `rsp` -- so `ANTI_AVX_SABOTAGE=teb` takes the path on `nogpr`,
which would otherwise use mode "home". `check-teb` asserts the two images DIFFER, that the
stub really holds two segment-prefixed saves, and that no stub moves `rsp`, before believing
the 77. Without the middle assertion the target would be a control for nothing: a fixture
that answers 77 through mode "home" answers 77 either way.

**The liveness gate of Finding 266 needed no change and that was luck worth checking.** It
keys a save by the TEXT of its target and a restore by the text of its source, so
`%gs:0x1670` matches itself in both directions and the pair reads as preserved. It was
written for `offset(%rsp)` and an xmm stash, and happens to be general.

#### A fixed save location is not reentrant, and the thing that made it safe was a docstring

Mode "home" puts the block's two borrows in the CALLER's frame, so two stubs nested on one
thread cannot collide. Mode "teb" puts them at one address shared by every stub in the image.
A stub that swallowed a `call` whose callee held another teb stub would have its saves
overwritten and would restore rubbish -- silently, because nothing faults.

What rules that out is that a borrow window cannot contain a call, and `window_escape`'s
docstring says so while saying, in as many words, that it rests **"on a property asserted in
two docstrings rather than enforced by a check"**. For the home space that is second-order.
For a fixed global it is the entire safety argument, and `verify` reports 384 re-emitted calls
in the stub section, so the population is not empty.

So it is enforced rather than asserted: `verify` walks the stub disassembly and refuses a call
between a TEB save and its restore. **365 brackets on Starfield, zero calls inside any of
them** -- the property holds, and now something watches it. The check was made to fail before
being believed, by pointing its trigger at an instruction the fixture's bracket does contain.

### Finding 279 -- the guard that could not be watched, and a check the padding defeats

`unit_candidate` refuses to widen back over a site that is a branch target, because a
window's jump buries every byte after its first. **Three attempts to watch that refusal fail,
and the first two were worthless.**

The first ran against Starfield while Finding 278's `preceding` bug was still live. `verify`
exited 1 on lost boundaries before the branch-target check had anything to say, and that
check duly reported all 1,191,105 targets intact. A control that fails through the wrong
check has not run.

The second disabled the guard and compared images. Instrumented, **388 sites got past it** --
not the 30 the probe in Finding 277 suggested, which counted one rung of the ladder. Of those
388, 387 are refused further down for other reasons, one builds a candidate, and that
candidate loses at placement. The image comes out byte-identical, so the control reports "the
sabotage did not apply" and cannot fail. **Starfield is the wrong instrument here**: on a
binary this dense every window competes, and the one site where the guard decides anything is
a site something else already covers.

**The third attempt found that the check I was aiming at cannot see the fault.** A fixture
puts the window where nothing competes for it, and with the guard off the window is placed:

    140001034:  e9 3e 30 00 00    jmp 0x140004077
    140001039:  0f 1f 40 00       nopl 0x0(%rax)      <- the jne lands here

The site at `0x140001039` is one past the jump's last byte, and the four bytes its `vpaddd`
occupied are NOP padding. So the target **still begins an instruction**, `verify: all 2 direct
branch targets still begin an instruction` passes, and the program is wrong: arriving by the
`jne` runs the padding, falls out of the far end of the window, and skips everything the stub
would have done. Nothing crashes and the answer is silently different.

The swallowed-instruction check sitting directly above it does not cover this either, and
reads exactly as though it should. The buried instruction is the window's **member** -- the
site being lowered -- not a passenger the window swallowed, so it never enters `swallowed`.

So `verify` gains the check that was missing: **no direct branch target may lie strictly
inside a placed window.** The window start is excluded deliberately, being the one address in
a window it is correct to arrive at. It reports zero across Starfield's 201,624 windows and
names `0x140001039` on the sabotaged fixture.

**The first version of that check turned a 17-minute `verify` into one still running at
39 minutes.** It asked each of 1.19 million targets about each of 201,624 windows. Sorting
the targets once and bisecting per window makes it free. A gate that slow is a gate somebody
stops running, which costs the same as a gate nobody can make fail.

Two gaps closed on the way. `backward` was in no gate at all -- it needs `--shadow-regs=all`
and neither `PE_NAMES` nor `check-shadow-pe` listed it -- and both fixtures are in
`check-shadow-pe` now, with `backtarget`'s sabotage as `check-verify`'s fourteenth control.
And I read `apply=0 verify=0` for three unwired fixtures as evidence they worked under the
plain pattern rule: **`verify` exits 0 when nothing was lowered**, so that was a vacuous pass
of my own. What separates them is the strategy row, which is Finding 205's rule again.

### Finding 278 -- backward widening lands, and both bugs were in the bookkeeping

Finding 277 refused this twice and blamed a `call` between the loads and the site. Neither bug
was in the emission, which was correct in every version, and neither had anything to do with
the `call`.

**A name collision.** The new variable is `window_start` because `unit_candidate` already has
a `start` -- the enclosing FUNCTION's address, used forty lines below for the `SAVED_XMM`
lookup. The first two versions called it `start`, so every window that reached the xmm borrow
anchored at the head of its function, swallowing the prologue and a `call`. Only `nonvol` and
`unwindsave` broke because only they reach the borrow: a shadowed name is invisible to every
fixture that does not execute the line that reads it.

**The wrong tuple field.** A candidate is `(start, encoding, operands, mnemonic, window,
displaced, scratch, preceding, strategy)`. The swallowed neighbour went into field 5,
`displaced`, and belongs in field 7, `preceding`. `build_stub` emits it correctly from either,
which is why all 15 fixtures passed; `place_stubs` accounts it from `preceding` alone, so the
boundary it consumed was recorded nowhere -- `verify: FAILED -- 22 boundaries lost that were
not swallowed on purpose`.

**The second is the one worth keeping.** The image is byte-identical with the bug and without
it; the only difference is what the accounting knows. A change that emits correctly and
accounts wrongly passes every fixture and every behavioural test there is, and is caught by
exactly one thing -- a verifier that re-derives the placement and asks whether the bytes it
finds were meant to be there.

Measured, `--shadow-regs=all`, against the committed 3,199:

    VEX in .text            805,131 -> 3,172        was 3,199
    unconditional lowering  33,845 built, 3,408 refused, of 37,253
                                                    was 33,664 / 3,632 of 37,296
    unit                    18,435 placed, 14,619 overlapped, 18 refused
    boundaries lost         83,958, every one deliberate
    stub section            4,623,702 bytes         was 4,622,202

**27 sites, against the 795 Finding 277 priced**, and the gap is the one Finding 271 already
measured for the immediate form: a shape refusal is the first wall and never the only one.
Of the 795 that can reach five bytes backwards, almost all are then refused for a register, a
helper or a neighbour.

### Finding 277 -- the census row that was mine, and 795 sites behind a bookkeeping wall

**Two instrument faults in one change, and the second chose the next item.** Finding 276's
ladder recorded a failing site's reason from the SHORTEST rung, on the reasoning that it was
the most fundamental. It is the most degenerate: the widening condition is
`last - index < limit` with `last` already `index + 1`, so at `limit=1` the loop never
iterates and any site under five bytes refuses `too short to place, nothing follows`
unconditionally. That row reached **866** and was about to be picked as the second-largest
class in the binary. It is an artifact of the ladder.

The first rung's reason is kept now, which is also what the census said before the ladder
existed, so every earlier measurement stays comparable. `cmp` confirms the image is
byte-identical -- a reason-keeping change must be bookkeeping only, and that is cheaper to
check than to argue. The honest census:

    no dead GPR and no home space to save one    1,785
    mode True has no xmm to stash the index in     370
    no non-volatile xmm this function saves        285
    vfmadd231ps has no legacy encoding             186
    shape a register second source, src2 is D      162
    shape a register-to-register move              148
    no volatile xmm and scratch slot                108

#### Backward widening: 795 sites, priced here and landed in Finding 278

`unit_candidate` widens only forward; the plain path has used both directions since the
beginning. Measured at the refusal:

    too short, forward blocked            837
      BACKWARD would reach five           795
      the SITE is a branch target          30
      previous transfers control           12

**95% of them.** The window starts on the instruction before the site and swallows the site
itself, which needs only that the site is not a branch target -- an address strictly inside a
window is one nothing may branch to.

It was built twice and reverted twice, and the diagnosis written here was wrong. It said the
two failing fixtures had **a `call` between the loads and the site** in common and that the
next attempt should start there. They do, and it is a coincidence: what `nonvol` and
`unwindsave` actually have in common is that they are the two fixtures that reach the xmm
borrow, which is where the real bug -- a shadowed variable name -- did its damage. Finding
278 has both causes and the numbers.

The half of this that held is the pricing: **the 795 were behind a bookkeeping wall rather
than a semantic one**, and no part of the placer's swallow accounting had a case for a window
beginning before its own site. It delivers 27 sites rather than 795, for the reason Finding
271 already measured -- a shape refusal is the first wall and never the only one.

### Finding 276 -- a shorter window finds a helper, and the trade pays

Finding 275 measured the xmm shortage as register pressure and named one untried idea with
its risk attached: `unit_candidate` absorbs whole runs of adjacent 256-bit sites, so its
members name five to fourteen distinct xmm, and the helper must avoid every one -- a helper
is clobbered, so a register any member READS cannot serve. With six volatile registers that
is what leaves nothing. **A window with fewer members touches fewer.**

So where the long window refuses, ask for a shorter one. The ladder is the absorption limit
the function already took: **12, 6, 3, 1**, ending at a single site, which is the shape the
strategy is named for. No restructuring.

    unit placed              18,390  -> 18,401     +11
    unit overlapped          14,593  -> 14,613     +20
    windows not placed          583  ->    661     +78
    sites through a slot     33,101  -> 33,133     +32
    VEX in .text              3,231  ->  3,199     -32
    apply wall time             ~10m  -> 14m23s

**The trade landed the right way and it was genuinely a trade.** The greed is not
gratuitous: the first version of this strategy produced one window per site, each overlapping
the next -- three candidates built and one placed -- so a shorter window is one more likely
to be overlapped, and the repair withheld 78 more of them. It still places enough more to pay
32 sites. Nothing about that was predictable from the measurement; only the binary could say.

**And the first version of it corrupted the instrument.** The refusal counters were restored
when a retry SUCCEEDED and not when all four rungs failed, so a failing site recorded four
reasons instead of one: `14,724 refused of 48,388 sites`, against a true `3,632 of 37,296`.
Every measurement in this file is taken off those counters, so the inflation would have
travelled into the next several findings rather than staying in this one. Each rung starts
from the snapshot now, and a failing site keeps the SHORTEST window's reason -- the one that
says why the site itself cannot be lowered rather than what a window around it was carrying.

Confirmed by `cmp`: the counter fix leaves the image byte-identical, which is what a
bookkeeping change has to do and is cheaper to check than to argue.

The clean census, which is the one to quote:

    no dead GPR and no home space to save one    1,412
    too short to place, nothing follows            866
    mode True has no xmm to stash the index in     396
    vfmadd231ps has no legacy encoding             186
    no non-volatile xmm this function saves        184
    shape a register second source, src2 is D      162
    shape a register-to-register move              148

`too short to place, nothing follows` is new and is the limit=1 rung speaking: a four-byte
site with nothing absorbable beside it cannot reach the five a jump needs. That is the most
fundamental refusal in the list and it was previously hidden behind whatever a longer window
happened to complain about first.

### Finding 275 -- the xmm shortage is registers, and the mode is finished at 99.6%

The last class never looked inside was the 258-site xmm shortage. Measured at the refusal:

    reached the volatile borrow            987
      no free volatile xmm (need 2)        292
      block is None                          0
      no free scratch slot                   0
    members touch: 14 xmm (42), 9 (40), 7 (36), 13 (36), 5 (32), 10 (32), 12 (22)

**The slots are never the limit and the block is always there.** It is registers every time:
a window whose members name five to fourteen distinct xmm leaves nothing among the six
volatile ones. The exclusion is window-wide and has to be -- a helper is clobbered, so a
register any member READS cannot serve, and a borrowed one holds the helper's value for the
window's length rather than its owner's.

So it joins the 908 as register pressure rather than bookkeeping, and the frontier at 3,231
is:

    structurally impossible -- no register, nowhere to save          908
    in a window the repair dropped -- downstream of readers          529
    FMA and friends, no legacy encoding exists                      ~370
    xmm pressure                                                     258
    undecodable -- not instructions at all                           180
    shapes this could emit but placement absorbs                     155

**Only the last row is work, and the last attempt at that row produced a byte-identical
image.** Finding 273 lowered 97 sites' worth of shape, built 33 candidates, and placed none.
That is the evidence that the binding constraint has left the classes a census can enumerate
and moved into placement, and it is why `src2-is-D` and the register-to-register move are not
picked here: they are the same work whose last instance paid nothing.

**One idea remains untried and its risk is known.** `unit_candidate` absorbs the whole run of
adjacent 256-bit sites rather than stopping at five bytes, so its windows are large and their
members touch many registers -- which is exactly what starves the helper. A shorter window
would touch fewer. But the greedy absorption exists because the first version produced one
window per site, each overlapping the next: three candidates built and one placed. Trimming
trades a helper shortage for an overlap problem, and which wins is not predictable from here.

**The larger number is not inside this mode.** `--shadow-regs=all` reaches 3,231 where the
shipped default reaches 5,691 -- **2,460 sites** -- for about 20% more stub. Whether that
trade is taken is the copyright holder's, and it is worth more than everything left in the
list above combined.

### Finding 274 -- the repair's cost is mostly the site itself, and a fix for the rest lost

The stale-read repair withholds 583 windows and the census attributes 529 survivors to them,
which made it the largest single item left -- bigger than any shape class. **Two remedies are
closed by construction**: the lost zeroing cannot be reproduced, because only a 256-bit write
zeroes an upper half and the stub may contain no VEX; and `unit_candidate` widens only
forward, so there is no second direction to try.

**Measured before building**, over 1,481 guilty-window observations:

    producer at +0    460     the window's own SITE is the guilty write
    producer at +8     95
    producer at +5     90
    producer at +4     58
    window sizes: 5 (86), 8 (86), 9 (55), 6 (54), 16 (51), 10 (46), 24 (46), 26 (38)

**460 are irreducible**: a window cannot exist without its site. The rest are passengers in
windows of 16, 24 and 26 bytes, carrying length they did not need -- so the collector was
made to ask `upper_half_read_later` before swallowing a VEX.128 write, stopping the window
short rather than letting the repair drop it later. Local, no architecture change, and
conservative the safe way.

**It lost, and the numbers say why:**

    windows not placed          583  ->    585      +2
    too short to place, next loses a zeroing  -> 278
    unit candidates built    33,555  -> 33,316    -239
    sites through a slot     33,101  -> 32,890    -211
    VEX in .text              3,231  ->  3,258     +27

The check fires 278 times, costs 239 candidates, and prevents **essentially no drops**. It
cannot: the dominant case is the site itself at offset 0, which a check on SWALLOWED
NEIGHBOURS never sees, while `upper_half_read_later` returning "read" on an unresolved walk
refuses windows that would never have been guilty. Reverted.

**The measurement was right and the reading of it was wrong.** 460 of 1,481 was in front of
me before a line was written, and it says the majority is untouchable by anything that trims
a window. What it does not say -- and what I supplied without checking -- is that the
remaining 1,021 were reachable. A conservative walk aimed at a minority spent more on false
refusals than the minority was worth.

**So the repair is not the lever it looked like.** Its 529 survivors are downstream of
surviving READERS, and a reader survives because it is in the structural floor or a shape
this cannot emit. The way to shrink the repair's cost is to lower the readers, which is the
frontier problem itself rather than a separate one.

### Finding 273 -- the shape lands, the image does not change, and that is the finding

`op $imm,%ymmS2,%ymmS1,%ymmD` -- `lanereg3` with a selector. 95 `vshufps` and 2 `vpblendw`
of the 111 sites in the four-operand bucket, all per-lane. The other 14 are `vblendvps` and
`vblendvpd`, which carry a REGISTER mask that SSE takes only in the implicit `xmm0`; they are
excluded by requiring an immediate rather than by a list.

    shape four operands                    222  ->     28
    unit candidates built               33,522  -> 33,555     +33
    unit refusals                        3,912  ->  3,846     -66
    windows not placed                     550  ->    583     +33
    VEX in .text                         3,231  ->  3,231      0

**The output image is byte-identical.** Every one of the 33 new candidates was built and
none was placed: the placer table is unchanged to the site -- `unit placed 18,390` before and
after -- and the repair withheld exactly as many windows as the shape added. 111 sites
